data/sphere/anthroposphere/governance/in.title: Governance
data/sphere/anthroposphere/governance/in.content:
Administrative structures, legal boundaries, and the spatial frameworks through which authority and jurisdiction are expressed. Governance data underpins how all other spatial data is organised, reported, and regulated.
Scope

Administrative units and addresses as reference units that other data refers to by ID belong to the Reference Framework; leaves about them are usually also members here
Cadastral system: Land parcel boundaries, legal descriptions of ownership units
Planning and zoning: See Planning for plans, zoning, and protection designations
Statistical units: See Statistical Units in the Reference Framework
Resource permits: Fishing quotas, extraction licences, environmental consents

Key Distinction: Governance vs Infrastructure
Governance describes legal and administrative definitions of space. Infrastructure describes physical assets within that space. A municipality boundary is governance; the roads inside it are infrastructure.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/hazard_vulner.title: Hazard, Vulnerability, and Risk
data/sphere/anthroposphere/hazard_vulner.content:
Risk assessment data combining natural or anthropogenic hazards with human vulnerability and exposure. The hazard itself (earthquake, flood, storm) originates in a physical sphere. This twig addresses the risk to humans — what happens when the hazard meets human settlements, infrastructure, and populations.
The Risk Triangle
Risk = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability

Hazard: The physical event (from Geosphere Hazards, Hydrosphere flooding, Atmosphere storms)
Exposure: Which populations and assets are physically located in the hazard zone
Vulnerability: How susceptible those populations/assets are to damage

This twig stores the combined assessment — maps showing which areas face high risk from multiple hazards overlaid with population density and infrastructure value.
Scope

Multi-hazard risk mapping: Combined risk indices from multiple natural hazards
Population vulnerability: Socioeconomic vulnerability indicators spatially mapped
Critical infrastructure exposure: Which hospitals, power plants, transport links are in hazard zones
Climate adaptation: Future risk projections under climate scenarios
Insurance and loss models: Expected economic loss from natural disasters

data/sphere/anthroposphere/ict/index.title: ICT and Flows
data/sphere/anthroposphere/ict/index.content:
Information and communication technologies, movement traces, and the digital infrastructure that enables modern spatial data systems. This twig covers the flow layer rather than the physical cables (which are Infrastructure).
Scope

Geodetic reference frames: The mathematical models (ETRS89, DVR90, WGS84) that make all spatial data interoperable
Coordinate reference systems: Projections, transformations, datum definitions
Spatial data infrastructure (SDI): Metadata catalogs, CSW services, INSPIRE discovery services, WFS/WMS endpoints
Sensor networks: IoT streams and telemetry traces (the flow evidence, not the physical device)
Digital platforms: Data portals, APIs, digital twins, open data catalogues
Grid systems: Statistical grids, DGGS (H3, S2, DGGAL) as algorithmic spatial frameworks

Key Role: The Enabling Layer
ICT is the enabling layer for all other twigs. Without geodetic reference frames, no spatial data is interoperable. Without SDI, no data is discoverable. This twig doesn’t describe the world — it describes the systems we use to describe the world.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/informal_ephe.title: Informal and Ephemeral
data/sphere/anthroposphere/informal_ephe.content:
Informal, tactical, and short-lived human systems that are weakly represented in official registries.
Scope

Tactical urbanism and temporary installations
Informal service and mobility patterns
Short-lived event infrastructure and ad hoc land occupation
Unregistered anthroposphere behaviors that still affect spatial analysis

This twig is essential for capturing human systems that are real in practice but under-specified in formal cadastres and long-cycle registries.
Leaves

No leaves yet.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/infrastructur.title: Infrastructure
data/sphere/anthroposphere/infrastructur.content:
Physical and organisational networks form the backbone of urban and rural life. This twig covers the hard infrastructure that enables human settlement and economic activity — the roads we drive on, the pipes that carry water, the cables that transmit power and data, and the buildings that shelter activities.
Scope
Infrastructure data describes constructed physical systems and their spatial extent:

Transportation networks: Roads, railways, bicycle paths, pedestrian routes, bridges, tunnels, airports, harbours, ferry routes
Utility grids: Electricity transmission/distribution, gas pipelines, district heating networks, water supply mains, sewage/stormwater systems
Built environment: Buildings, structures, dams, levees, wind turbines, solar farms
Waste management: Landfills, recycling centres, waste treatment plants
Communication networks: Fibre optic routes, mobile tower sites (physical infrastructure aspect — data flows are in ICT)

Key Distinction: Infrastructure vs Services
Infrastructure is the physical asset; the service it enables sits in Services. A hospital building is infrastructure; the healthcare it provides is a service. A power line is infrastructure; the energy distribution service is Services.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/perception_th.title: Perception and Thematics
data/sphere/anthroposphere/perception_th.content:
Human thematic partitioning of space. This twig represents how humans classify, symbolize, and communicate territory through thematic and topographic interpretation products.
Scope

Thematic map products derived from imagery, surveys, and administrative interpretation
Historical and modern topographic map representations
Human zoning and categorization overlays used for planning and communication
Cartographic partitioning where the cognitive framing is part of the data meaning

Distinction

Raw observational image evidence is not in a sphere: it is a collection product of passive remote sensing (see Orthoimagery).
Physical surface geometry belongs in geosphere_landform_topography.
This twig stores the interpreted thematic framing used by humans.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/planning/inde.title: Planning
data/sphere/anthroposphere/planning/inde.content:
Human intent applied to space — plans, zoning, protection designations, and resource-management plans that decide what may happen where. Planning leaves are typically cross-domain: a nature protection area is both Planning and biosphere_ecosystems, and a drinking water protection zone is both Planning and hydrosphere_groundwater.
Key Distinction: Planning vs Governance
Governance is the administrative and legal framework: who has authority where (administrative units, cadastre, addresses, registers). Planning is the use of that authority to shape the future of an area.
Scope

Spatial plans and zoning: Municipal plans (kommuneplaner), local plans (lokalplaner), and national planning directives
Planning decisions: Permits, dispensations, and zoning decisions
Nature protection designations: Natura 2000, protected nature types (§3), and national parks
Water protection designations: Drinking water interest areas (OSD), abstraction catchments (indvindingsoplande), and water use restrictions
Resource-management plans: Fisheries management, forest management plans, and marine spatial plans

data/sphere/anthroposphere/resource_util.title: Resource Utilisation
data/sphere/anthroposphere/resource_util.content:
Quantification of human extraction, harvesting, consumption, and production from natural systems. This is where human activity physically takes from nature — measured volumes of water, harvested biomass, extracted minerals, caught fish, felled timber.
Scope

Water abstraction: Measured volumes of groundwater and surface water extracted for human use
Agriculture and aquaculture: Crop yields, livestock production, fish catches, timber harvests
Mining and quarrying: Mineral extraction quantities, gravel/sand extraction, fossil fuel production
Energy production: Renewable energy generation from natural sources (hydropower, wind, solar, biomass)
Fishing: Catch volumes, landing statistics, quota utilisation

Key Distinction: Resource vs Utilisation
The natural resource itself sits in the physical sphere — mineral deposits in Geosphere Resources, fish stocks in Biosphere Fauna, timber in Biosphere Vegetation. This twig records how much humans take — the utilisation volume that connects human activity to natural stock.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/services/inde.title: Services
data/sphere/anthroposphere/services/inde.content:
Organised activities and institutions that provide essential functions to populations. Where Infrastructure is the physical asset, Services describes what those assets deliver — healthcare, education, emergency response, commercial services, environmental monitoring.
Scope

Healthcare: Hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, ambulance stations, health districts
Education: Schools, universities, kindergartens, educational districts
Public safety: Police stations, fire stations, emergency services
Commercial services: Retail locations, financial services, postal offices
Environmental monitoring: Observation stations, measurement networks, sensors deployed to monitor physical spheres (a key thread — the stations are Anthroposphere services, but what they observe spans Atmosphere, Hydrosphere, Geosphere, Biosphere)
Water/energy services: Water treatment plants, wastewater facilities, power generation (the service dimension of utility infrastructure)

Key Thread: Environmental Monitoring
Environmental monitoring facilities are a classic cross-sphere concept. The station itself (its location, operator, calibration) is an Anthroposphere service. But the observations it produces belong to whichever sphere is being measured — air quality data goes to Atmosphere, water quality to Hydrosphere, soil samples to Geosphere.

data/sphere/anthroposphere/socioeconomic.content:
Data describing human populations, their economic activities, and social organisation. This is where demographics meet economics — population counts, workforce data, income levels, business composition, consumption patterns.

Economy: Business activity, industry composition, employment, GDP, trade, investment
Ownership: Property ownership, company ownership structures, beneficial ownership
Income and wealth: Personal income, corporate revenue, property values
Social indicators: Education levels, health outcomes, inequality measures

data/sphere/atmosphere/index.title: Atmosphere
data/sphere/atmosphere/index.content:
Description: This sphere is the gaseous envelope surrounding the Earth, encompassing its composition, dynamics, and energy exchanges. It drives weather patterns and influences climate.

Subclasses (Complexes):

atmosphere_climate: Long-term weather patterns and trends (e.g., temperature projections, historical climate data, climate zones, greenhouse gas concentrations affecting climate).
atmosphere_weather: Short-term atmospheric conditions and phenomena (e.g., temperature, precipitation, wind speed, atmospheric pressure, forecasts, severe weather events like storms and hurricanes).
atmosphere_composition: Data related to the general gaseous and particulate composition of the air (e.g., major atmospheric gases, aerosols, background trace gases not considered pollutants).
atmosphere_contaminants: Data related to the presence and distribution of pollutants in the atmosphere (e.g., NO2 levels, particulate matter (PM2.5), ozone-depleting substances, industrial emissions, air quality indices).


Common Overlaps & Distinctions:

Precipitation: While precipitation originates in the atmosphere, actual rainfall/snowfall data that interacts with the ground or water bodies is typically found under hydrosphere_atmospheric_water.
Surface Temperature: Air temperature is atmosphere_weather, but the temperature of the land or sea surface is geosphere_landform_topography.
Climate Change: The causes (GHG emissions from human activity) are anthroposphere_contaminants or anthroposphere_resource_utilisation. The atmospheric manifestations (temperature trends, changes in weather patterns) are atmosphere_climate. The impacts can span all other spheres.

data/sphere/atmosphere/climate/index.title: Climate
data/sphere/atmosphere/climate/index.content:
Long-term weather patterns and trends — the statistical description of the atmosphere over decades to millennia. Where Weather captures today’s conditions, Climate describes what is normal and how it is changing.
Scope

Historical climate records: Temperature series, precipitation normals, wind climatologies spanning 30+ years
Climate zones and classifications: Köppen-Geiger zones, bioclimatic regions
Climate projections: Future temperature and precipitation under IPCC scenarios (RCP/SSP pathways)
Greenhouse gas concentrations: Long-term CO₂, CH₄, N₂O trends as climate drivers (as atmospheric composition affecting climate — the emissions belong in Contaminants)
Climate indices: NAO, ENSO, PDO, drought indices, growing degree days

Denmark-Specific Context
Denmark’s climate data comes primarily from DMI (Danish Meteorological Institute). Key products include:

Climate normals (30-year reference periods)
Regional climate model projections for Denmark
Historical station records dating back to the mid-1800s

data/sphere/atmosphere/composition/index.title: Atmospheric Composition
data/sphere/atmosphere/composition/index.content:
The gaseous and particulate makeup of the atmosphere — major gases, trace gases, aerosols, and their spatial distribution. This is the background chemistry of the air, distinct from pollutant concentrations which are Atmosphere Contaminants.
Scope

Major atmospheric gases: N₂, O₂, Ar, CO₂ (as background composition)
Trace gases: Water vapour profiles, ozone column, methane background levels
Aerosols: Natural aerosol loading (dust, sea salt, volcanic), aerosol optical depth
Atmospheric profiles: Vertical soundings, radiosonde data, lidar profiles

Distinction from Contaminants
The boundary between composition and contaminants is contextual. Background CO₂ levels as an atmospheric property = composition. Elevated CO₂ from industrial emission = contaminant. If the focus is “what’s in the air naturally?”, it’s composition. If the focus is “what pollutants are present?”, it’s contaminants.

data/sphere/atmosphere/contaminants/inde.title: Atmospheric Contaminants
data/sphere/atmosphere/contaminants/inde.content:
Pollutants present in the atmosphere — measurements, models, and indices describing air quality. The source of emissions is Anthroposphere Contaminants; this twig records what is actually in the air.
Scope

Measured pollutant concentrations: NO₂, PM2.5, PM10, O₃ (tropospheric ozone), SO₂, CO
Air quality indices: AQI, CAQI, and national air quality classifications
Ozone-depleting substances: CFCs, HCFCs in the stratosphere
Modelled air quality: Dispersion models, chemical transport models
Emission inventories (atmospheric side): What goes into the atmosphere — the spatial distribution of emissions in the air column

data/sphere/atmosphere/weather/index.title: Weather
data/sphere/atmosphere/weather/index.content:
Short-term atmospheric conditions and phenomena — hours to days. Temperature, precipitation, wind, pressure, humidity, cloud cover, and their forecasts.
Scope

Observations: Station measurements of temperature, precipitation, wind speed/direction, pressure, humidity, visibility
Radar and satellite: Precipitation radar composites, cloud imagery, lightning detection
Numerical weather prediction: Forecasts from NWP models (HARMONIE, ECMWF)
Severe weather: Storm warnings, extreme precipitation events, heat waves, frost events
Derived products: Heat index, wind chill, evapotranspiration estimates

Key Distinction: Weather vs Climate
Weather is what you get; climate is what you expect. Weather data has temporal resolution of minutes to days. If the dataset describes conditions over 30+ years as statistical summaries, it’s Climate.
Precipitation Cross-Sphere Note
Precipitation falls as weather but lands in the Hydrosphere. Rainfall measurements are atmosphere_weather; the resulting streamflow is freshwater_surface; soil moisture response is Geosphere soil moisture.

data/sphere/biosphere/index.title: Biosphere
data/sphere/biosphere/index.content:
Description: This sphere encompasses all living organisms on Earth, including plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms, as well as their ecological communities and interdependencies. It focuses on life itself and the natural processes within ecosystems.
Subclasses (Complexes):

Vegetation: Specific information about plant life (e.g., forest types, crop health indices like NDVI, species distribution of plants, primary productivity).
Fauna: Data on animal life (e.g., species distribution, population counts, wildlife corridors, bird migration routes, fish stock biomass). Note: This excludes general human population data.
biosphere_microbial: Data on microorganisms and their activity (e.g., soil microbes, aquatic bacteria, fungal networks, distribution of pathogens where the primary focus is the organism itself).
biosphere_ecosystems: Data representing ecological units and their characteristics (e.g., ecoregions, habitat types, biodiversity hotspots, ecosystem health metrics).
biosphere_contaminants: Data related to the presence of pollutants within living organisms or their accumulation in biological systems (e.g., bioaccumulation of heavy metals in fish, pesticide residues in plants, spread of diseases/pathogens within non-human wildlife populations).

data/sphere/biosphere/contaminants/index.title: Biosphere Contaminants
data/sphere/biosphere/contaminants/index.content:
Pollutants within living organisms or their accumulation in biological systems — bioaccumulation, pesticide residues, disease spread in wildlife. This twig records what contaminants do within the living world.
Scope

Bioaccumulation: Heavy metals in fish tissues, persistent organic pollutants in marine mammals
Pesticide residues: Concentrations in crops, soil organisms, and non-target species
Wildlife disease: Spread of pathogens within non-human populations (avian influenza routes, chronic wasting disease)
Ecosystem disruption: Algal blooms from nutrient loading, invasive pathogen impacts

data/sphere/biosphere/ecosystems/index.title: Ecosystems
data/sphere/biosphere/ecosystems/index.content:
Ecological units and their characteristics — ecoregions, habitat types, biodiversity hotspots, ecosystem health metrics. Where Vegetation and Fauna describe individual organisms, Ecosystems describes communities and their interactions.
Scope

Ecoregions: Biogeographic zones with shared ecological characteristics
Habitat types: Natura 2000 habitat classifications, EUNIS habitat types
Biodiversity hotspots: Areas of exceptional species richness or endemism
Ecosystem health: Indicators of ecological integrity, disturbance levels, recovery status
Protected area ecology: Ecological justification for conservation — why a site is protected

Habitats and Protected Sites

data/sphere/biosphere/fauna/index.title: Fauna
data/sphere/biosphere/fauna/index.content:
Animal life — species distribution, population dynamics, wildlife corridors, migration routes. Fauna data covers all non-human animal life from insects to whales.
Scope

Species distribution: Occurrence records, range maps, habitat suitability models
Population counts: Census data for wildlife, fish stock assessments, bird colony counts
Wildlife corridors: Movement pathways, migration routes, ecological connectivity
Marine fauna: Fish stock biomass, cetacean sightings, benthic community surveys
Invasive species: Distribution and spread of non-native animal species

Key Distinction

Fish stock (the biological population) → Fauna
Fish catch (how much humans harvest) → Resource Utilisation
Aquatic habitat (the water body) → Hydrosphere

Human population data is explicitly excluded from Fauna — it belongs in Socioeconomic.

data/sphere/biosphere/microbial/index.title: Microbial Life
data/sphere/biosphere/microbial/index.content:
Microorganisms and their activity — soil microbiomes, aquatic bacteria, fungal networks, pathogen distribution. This twig covers life at the microscopic scale, which plays outsized roles in nutrient cycling, decomposition, and disease.
Scope

Soil microbiomes: Bacterial and fungal communities in soil, mycorrhizal networks
Aquatic microorganisms: Freshwater and marine bacteria, phytoplankton, algal blooms
Pathogen distribution: Spatial occurrence of disease-causing organisms in the environment (the pathogen as organism, not human disease — that’s Contaminants)
Decomposition: Microbial activity rates, organic matter breakdown

data/sphere/biosphere/vegetation/index.title: Vegetation
data/sphere/biosphere/vegetation/index.content:
Plant life in all its forms — from individual species to forest ecosystems. Vegetation data describes the presence, type, health, and productivity of plant cover.
Scope

Forest types: Deciduous, coniferous, mixed forest classification and boundaries
Crop types and health: Agricultural crop identification, NDVI, chlorophyll indices
Species distribution: Where specific plant species occur (presence/absence, abundance)
Primary productivity: GPP, NPP, biomass estimates from remote sensing
Phenology: Green-up dates, senescence, growing season length

Cross-Sphere Connections
Vegetation sits at the intersection of several spheres:

Geosphere (soil): Soil properties determine what grows — and plant roots shape soil development
Atmosphere: Vegetation drives carbon cycling, transpiration, albedo modification
Hydrosphere: Riparian vegetation influences water quality and bank stability
Anthroposphere Perception & Thematics: Vegetation classification is a major component of interpreted surface partitioning and thematic map products

Agricultural crops here represent the biological organism. The harvest yield (how much humans take) is Resource Utilisation.

Pollutants within rock and soil — what is in the ground, whether geological in origin or deposited by human activity. The human source of emissions is Anthroposphere Contaminants; pollutants carried in water are Hydrosphere Contaminants.

Geological origin

Radon mapping: Natural radon emission from geological formations
Heavy metals in bedrock: Naturally elevated arsenic, lead, or cadmium in geological units
Source zone characterisation: DNAPL plumes, contaminant migration in fractured rock

In the soil matrix

Heavy metal contamination: Cd, Pb, Zn, Cu, Hg concentrations in topsoil
Organic pollutants: PAHs, PCBs, PFAS, petroleum hydrocarbons in soil
Pesticide residues: Agricultural pesticide concentrations in soil profiles
Nutrient excess: Nitrate leaching risk, phosphorus saturation levels

Registers

Contaminated land registers: Sites where the subsurface is contaminated (industrial legacy, landfills)

data/sphere/geosphere/geology/index.title: Geology
data/sphere/geosphere/geology/index.content:
Rocks, minerals, and geological formations — the structure and composition of the Earth’s crust. Geological data describes what the ground is made of and how it got there.
Scope

Geological maps: Bedrock geology, surficial geology, geological unit boundaries
Borehole data: Subsurface stratigraphy from drilling logs, geological cross-sections
Structural geology: Fault lines, fold axes, dip/strike measurements
Geochemistry: Chemical composition of rock formations, radiometric dating
Geomorphology: Landform classification based on geological processes (glacial, fluvial, aeolian)

Denmark-Specific Context
Denmark’s geology is dominated by Quaternary deposits (glacial tills, outwash sands) overlying Cretaceous–Paleogene chalk and limestone. GEUS (Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland) is the authoritative source. The Jupiter database contains tens of thousands of borehole records.

data/sphere/geosphere/index.title: Geosphere
data/sphere/geosphere/index.content:
Description: This sphere covers the solid Earth from bedrock to the soil surface: the crust’s rocks and structure, the processes that move and shape it, the form of the land surface, and the unconsolidated soil layer formed by the interaction of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, and time. It replaces the former Lithosphere and Pedosphere spheres and the terrain part of the former Toposphere. Geology and soils are treated as a continuum, as UN-GGIM’s Geology and Soils theme does.
Subclasses (Complexes):

geosphere_geology: Rocks, minerals, and geological formations (e.g., bedrock and surficial geology maps, borehole data, subsurface stratigraphy, structural geology, geochemistry).
geosphere_tectonics: Crustal movements, earthquakes, and volcanic activity (e.g., fault lines, seismicity, post-glacial rebound, plate boundaries).
geosphere_resources: Geological resources where they exist in the ground (e.g., mineral deposits, raw materials, fossil fuel reservoirs, geothermal potential).
geosphere_hazards: Hazards originating in the solid Earth (e.g., landslide susceptibility, ground stability, sinkholes, coastal erosion).
geosphere_landform_topography: The shape and elevation of the land surface and lake/sea floors, and properties derived from it (e.g., DTMs, DSMs, bathymetry, slope, aspect, curvature, solar exposure, surface roughness, geomorphological features).
geosphere_soil: What the soil consists of, its types, its moisture and temperature, and how it erodes (e.g., texture, organic carbon, soil maps, soil moisture, erosion rates).
geosphere_contaminants: Pollutants within rock and soil, whether geological in origin (radon, naturally elevated heavy metals) or deposited by human activity (heavy metals, PFAS, pesticides, hydrocarbons in soil, contaminated land registers).


Common Overlaps & Distinctions:

Rock ↔ Soil: Bedrock is the parent material for soil. Both are in this sphere, so a dataset that crosses the boundary (e.g., GEUS surficial geology) can belong to both the geology and the soil twig without needing a cross-sphere link.
Terrain ↔ Water: Elevation determines where water flows and floods reach. Terrain leaves typically also belong to hydrosphere_freshwater_surface; bathymetry links to hydrosphere_marine.
Imagery: General-purpose aerial and satellite imagery is not part of this sphere; it belongs to the Reference Framework. Imagery-derived products enter through their analytical focus (a DTM from photogrammetry belongs here).
Agriculture: Agricultural activity happens on soil, but land use partitioning is anthroposphere_perception_thematics and yields are anthroposphere_resource_utilisation.
Resources vs Extraction: The natural occurrence of minerals and fuels is geosphere_resources; the quantity extracted is anthroposphere_resource_utilisation.
Hazard vs Risk: The hazard itself (e.g., an unstable slope) is here; the risk to people and assets is anthroposphere_hazard_vulnerability_risk.

data/sphere/geosphere/landform_topograph.title: Landform and Topography
data/sphere/geosphere/landform_topograph.content:
Historically, terrain information has been represented and visualized as couture lines, i.e. lines connecting points with identical elevation values. This was primary because of the way this information was collected, first through field mapping and later through stereoscopic Stereoscopic photogrammetry. While couture lines are still used for terrain visualisation on many maps, they are unsuitable for digital representation aimed at 3d visualisation and modelling.  For these purposes, a Raster Data-based representation or a 2.5D Triangulation model [TIN model]
Representation of Buildings and Tunnels
There are several problems in relation to the representation of bridges and tunnels namely:

How do bridges influence the terrain model, and how does this affect hydrological modelling

Topography related to the shape and elevation of the Earth’s land surface and ocean/lake floors (e.g., Digital surface Models (DSM’s), Digital Terrain Models (DTM’s), bathymetry charts, derived slope, aspect, and curvature maps, geomorphological features).
Derived surface properties
Properties computed from the terrain surface, or describing the surface as a boundary for water and air, also belong here. They were previously the Toposphere twigs Surface Physical and Surface Radiative and Thermal.

Terrain derivatives: Slope, aspect, curvature, flow direction, and flow accumulation
Solar exposure: Insolation, hillshade, and sky-view factor computed from the DSM/DTM
Surface roughness: Aerodynamic roughness length (z₀) for wind modelling, and hydraulic roughness for overland flow
Albedo and emissivity: Surface reflectivity and thermal emission characteristics

Related properties sit elsewhere in the network:

Land surface temperature links to atmosphere_climate.
Sea surface temperature belongs to hydrosphere_marine.
Infiltration capacity belongs to geosphere_soil.
Impervious surface is land cover, so it belongs to anthroposphere_perception_thematics.

data/sphere/geosphere/soil/index.title: Soil
data/sphere/geosphere/soil/index.content:
The unconsolidated layer formed by climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time: what it consists of, how it is classified, its current state, and how it moves.
Scope
Texture
The sizes of the mineral particles (clay, silt and sand fractions), and the physical properties that depend on them: structure, porosity, bulk density, infiltration rate and hydraulic conductivity.
Organic matter and lime
Organic carbon and humus, carbonate, and the rest of the soil’s chemistry and biology: pH, cation exchange capacity, nutrients, microbial biomass.
Soil types and classification
What type of soil is where: WRB, USDA Soil Taxonomy and national systems (in Denmark the JB numbers), soil maps and mapping units, and how they relate to the parent material. Danish soil mapping is well developed for agricultural land; the deposits beneath belong to Geology.
Moisture and temperature
The current condition of the soil, which changes with time: water content, matric potential, soil temperature and frost, satellite-derived moisture, drought indicators.
Erosion and sedimentation
How soil is lost, moved and deposited: erosion rates, erodibility, sediment yield, deposition zones, compaction and degradation.

data/sphere/geosphere/tectonics/index.title: Tectonics
data/sphere/geosphere/tectonics/index.content:
Crustal movements, earthquakes, and volcanic activity. Denmark is tectonically quiet but not inactive — the country experiences minor earthquakes, and the subsurface is influenced by post-glacial rebound and salt tectonics.
Scope

Seismic activity: Earthquake epicentres, magnitude, depth, focal mechanisms
Fault lines: Mapped tectonic faults, potential rupture zones
Crustal deformation: Post-glacial rebound rates, GPS-measured uplift/subsidence
Volcanic activity: Not relevant for Denmark, but included for completeness

data/sphere/hydrosphere/atmospheric_wate.title: Atmospheric Water
data/sphere/hydrosphere/atmospheric_wate.content:
Water in the atmosphere — precipitation, humidity, cloud properties, water vapour. This is the hydrological view of atmospheric moisture, complementing the meteorological view in Weather.
Scope

Precipitation: Rainfall totals, snowfall amounts, mixed precipitation, gauge and radar data
Humidity: Relative and absolute humidity, dew point
Cloud properties: Cloud cover, liquid water content, cloud type
Water vapour: Column-integrated water vapour, vertical profiles
Evapotranspiration: Actual and potential ET as the return flux

Why This Exists Alongside Atmosphere Weather
Precipitation is simultaneously an atmospheric phenomenon and a hydrological input. The measurement of rainfall is Weather. The hydrological significance — how much water reaches the ground and enters the water cycle — lives here. Many precipitation datasets serve both purposes, so this twig enables discovery from the water cycle perspective.

data/sphere/hydrosphere/contaminants/ind.title: Water Contaminants
data/sphere/hydrosphere/contaminants/ind.content:
Pollutants in water bodies — chemical, physical, and biological water quality measurements. This twig records what is in the water, not where the pollution comes from (that’s Anthroposphere Contaminants).
Scope

Chemical pollutants: Heavy metals, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, microplastics in water
Nutrient loading: Nitrogen, phosphorus concentrations causing eutrophication
Physical parameters: Turbidity, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, temperature anomalies
Biological indicators: E. coli counts, algal bloom extent, chlorophyll-a concentrations
Water quality indices: WQI, ecological status under the EU Water Framework Directive

data/sphere/hydrosphere/cryosphere/index.title: Cryosphere
data/sphere/hydrosphere/cryosphere/index.content:
Frozen water in all its forms — glaciers, ice sheets, sea ice, permafrost, seasonal snow cover. While Denmark proper has limited cryosphere data, Greenland makes this twig critical for the Danish realm.
Scope

Glaciers: Ice mass, flow velocity, calving fronts, volume change (Greenland ice sheet)
Sea ice: Extent, thickness, concentration, ice type classification
Permafrost: Distribution, active layer depth, ground temperature (Greenland, Arctic)
Seasonal snow: Snow cover extent, snow depth, snow water equivalent (SWE)

Greenland Context
The Greenland Ice Sheet is one of the most studied cryospheric features on Earth. Danish institutions (GEUS, DMI) produce critical datasets on ice mass balance, firn temperature, and meltwater runoff that feed into global sea level projections.
Leaves

No leaves yet.

Classical Theme Mappings
No direct classical theme — cryosphere data is typically classified under Inland Waters (ISO) or Hydrography (INSPIRE) for ice sheets, and Meteorological Features for snow cover.

data/sphere/hydrosphere/freshwater_surfa.title: Freshwater Surface Water
data/sphere/hydrosphere/freshwater_surfa.content:
Rivers, lakes, wetlands, reservoirs, and drainage systems — the visible freshwater on the land surface. This is the twig for hydrographic data describing water bodies, their flow, and their characteristics.
Scope

Rivers and streams: Channel geometry, streamflow measurements, catchment boundaries, stream order
Lakes and ponds: Extent, depth, volume, water level monitoring
Wetlands: Bog, fen, marsh classification and delineation
Reservoirs: Artificial water bodies, dam locations, storage capacity
Drainage: Drainage networks, tile drain systems, storm drainage routes
Estuaries: Transitional waters where freshwater meets marine (shared with Marine)

Key Distinction: Water Body vs Water Quality
This twig describes the water body itself — its geometry, flow, and physical state. The quality of the water (pollutant concentrations) is Hydrosphere Contaminants. The organisms in the water are Biosphere.

data/sphere/hydrosphere/groundwater/inde.title: Groundwater
data/sphere/hydrosphere/groundwater/inde.content:
Water beneath the Earth’s surface in soil pores and rock fractures. Groundwater is invisible but accounts for a vast share of freshwater resources, making it critical for water supply and ecosystem support.
Scope

Groundwater levels: Monitoring well data, piezometric surfaces, hydraulic head
Aquifer characteristics: Permeability, transmissivity, storage coefficient, aquifer boundaries
Groundwater flow: Flow direction and velocity, recharge zones, discharge areas (springs)
Groundwater–surface water interaction: Base flow contribution to rivers, spring-fed wetlands

Cross-Sphere Connections

Geosphere (geology): Aquifer geometry is determined by geological formations — Geology
Geosphere (soil): Infiltration through soil recharges groundwater — Soil
Anthroposphere: Water abstraction volumes — Resource Utilisation

data/sphere/hydrosphere/hazards/index.title: Water Hazards
data/sphere/hydrosphere/hazards/index.content:
Water-borne threats and events — where harm from water can or did occur. This covers natural hazards (floods, storm surge) and pollution hazards (spills and incidents that put water bodies at risk).
Key Distinction: Hazard vs Contaminant vs Risk

Contaminants is the state: pollutant concentrations measured in the water (PFAS, pesticides, nitrate, heavy metals).
Hazards is the threat or event: flood extents, inundation scenarios, spill locations, and pollution incidents.
Risk is the hazard combined with human exposure and vulnerability. It belongs to the Anthroposphere, and hazard leaves usually also belong there.

Scope

Flooding: Pluvial, fluvial, and coastal flood extents, return-period scenarios, and inundation depth
Storm surge and sea level: Extreme water level statistics and sea level rise scenarios
Groundwater flooding: Rising groundwater tables affecting the surface and buildings
Pollution incidents: Spills, discharges, and accidents that put water bodies at risk
Hazard zoning: Areas designated by the hazard itself (e.g., EU Floods Directive risk areas)

data/sphere/hydrosphere/index.title: Hydrosphere
data/sphere/hydrosphere/index.content:
Description: This sphere includes all of Earth’s water, whether in liquid, solid (ice), or gaseous (water vapor) form, focusing on the water body or phenomenon itself.
Subclasses (Complexes):

hydrosphere_freshwater_surface: Data related to freshwater bodies on the Earth’s surface (e.g., rivers, lakes, ponds, wetlands, estuaries, streamflow, lake levels).
hydrosphere_groundwater: Information about water found beneath the Earth’s surface in soil pores and fractures (e.g., groundwater levels, aquifer characteristics, groundwater flow).
hydrosphere_marine: Data related to oceans, seas, and coastal waters (e.g., sea surface temperature (water mass), ocean currents, salinity, marine water column temperature, tides, waves, bathymetry of water column).
hydrosphere_cryosphere: Data related to frozen water bodies (e.g., glaciers, ice sheets, sea ice extent and thickness, permafrost distribution).
hydrosphere_atmospheric_water: Information about water in the atmosphere (e.g., precipitation totals, humidity, cloud properties, water vapor content).
hydrosphere_contaminants: Data related to the presence and distribution of pollutants within water bodies (e.g., water quality measurements for specific pollutants such as PFAS, pesticides and nitrate, microplastic concentrations in water).
hydrosphere_hazards: Water-borne threats and events (e.g., flood extents and scenarios, storm surge, groundwater flooding, spills and pollution incidents).


Common Overlaps & Distinctions:

Ice/Snow as Surface Interpretation: While hydrosphere_cryosphere describes the physical properties of ice bodies, interpreted thematic surface partitioning belongs in anthroposphere_perception_thematics.
Water Utilization: Data on the amount of water extracted or used (e.g., cubic meters of water abstracted) is in anthroposphere_resource_utilisation.
Flooding/Pollution Incidents: The hazard itself (e.g., flood extent maps, spill locations) belongs in hydrosphere_hazards; the measured pollutant state belongs in hydrosphere_contaminants. The risk to human assets/populations is in anthroposphere_hazard_vulnerability_risk.
Life in Water: The water body is Hydrosphere, but the fish and other aquatic organisms are biosphere_fauna.

data/sphere/index.title: SPHERE
data/sphere/index.content:
This view organises spatial data by semantic domain or sphere of interest. Rather than thinking about “which registry?”, think about “what kind of questions am I asking?”
What is a Sphere?
Spheres are part of the SPHERE protocol (Semantic Protocol for Human and Earth Relational Environments). Each sphere is a thematic cluster of interests and phenomena—a hub in the SPHERE network, divided into narrower twigs. Leaves decompose datasets into purpose-specific semantic aspects that answer specific kinds of questions, and each leaf is connected to every twig it is relevant to, so the same leaf can be reached from several spheres.
For example:

Anthroposphere: Companies, people, governance, planning, infrastructure, services, thematic perception, flow systems

domain-hubs/agriculture/2026-norms-and-n.title: 2026 norms and NUAR at Ledreborg (Example)
domain-hubs/agriculture/2026-norms-and-n.content:
A worked case for the course Environmental Regulation and Management with GIS, Theme 3.1 (nitrogen in the agro-environment: pollution and regulation). It builds on Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR (Example), which runs the NUAR model for one point, and Crop rotations at Ledreborg (Example), which gives the crops of each field. Hub: Agriculture.
Until 2026 a field’s nitrogen was set by a norm: a number per crop and soil type, the same everywhere in Denmark. From 2027 the discharge-based regulation (NUAR) ties it to how much nitrate the field is modelled to leach. Run for the fields of the Ledreborg landscapes, the two regimes give the same answer for many cereal fields, but only if the fields have a catch crop. Without catch crops almost no arable field reaches NUAR’s yardstick even with no fertiliser at all. With catch crops, winter wheat and spring barley stay close to their norms, winter canola loses most of its nitrogen (38 instead of 188 kg N/ha), and grass is barely limited.
Example data
ledreborg_nuar_example_data.zip (0.3 MB), a snapshot package: one row per field piece with every input the model got (crops 2024–2026, soil, subsoil, lowland, retention, climate cell, covers) and both results, the landscapes, and the crop code table. The NUAR workbook’s own tables are not included: they are SEGES’s.
1. Spatial Intent
Question: how much nitrogen may each field at Ledreborg receive under the 2026 norms, and how much under NUAR? Where, and for which crops, do the two differ, and what decides the difference?
Study area and units: the five landscapes of the Ledreborg study area; the fields of 2026 as pieces of land with the same crops in 2024, 2025 and 2026, from the flattened Marker layers (History from yearly snapshots (Task)).
Theory:

The 2026 norm (Vejledning om gødsknings- og harmoniregler 2025/2026, chapter 4 and Bilag 1, table 1): each crop has a nitrogen norm per soil group (JB 1+3, JB 2+4, irrigated JB 1–4, JB 5–6, JB 7–9, JB 11), set at the economic optimum. The field’s norm is the crop’s norm minus the value of last year’s crop (forfrugtsværdi), and minus 21 kg N/ha after a catch crop. The farm’s quota is the sum over its fields. The norm says nothing about where the field lies or what happens to the nitrate.
NUAR (Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR (Example)): the leaching from the root zone is modelled with NLES5 from the crops of three years, the autumn cover, soil, subsoil, climate and nitrogen, and the discharge to the coast is the leaching minus the retention on the way. The SEGES spreadsheet (NUAR-regneark v1.3) has no quota; it compares each field with a reference, spring barley with a catch crop on the same site. This example asks how much spring mineral nitrogen a field can get and still discharge no more than its reference.
Targeted regulation (Christensen et al. 2021): general rules apply the same number everywhere; a targeted regulation lets the soil, the crops and the way to the coast decide.

2. Auditing the data





















































DataSourceWhat it isChoicesCrops 2024–2026Marker, flattened as in Crop rotations at Ledreborg (Example)crop code per piece and yearpieces of at least 0.05 ha with a crop in all three years: 517 pieces, 1,490 haSoil (JB)Jordbundskort 2024 (SGAV), WFS Jordbunds_og_terraenforhold:Jordbundskort_2024JB number of the topsoilthe JB covering the largest part of the piece, as the guidance prescribes (§4.3); 491 pieces JB 6SubsoilGEUS Jordartskort 1:25 000 (WMS, read at a point inside each piece)geological typeNUAR knows seven subsoils; other GEUS types set to the nearest (meltwater gravel → meltwater sand, meltwater and freshwater clay → moraine clay, freshwater peat → freshwater sand); combinations NUAR lacks for eastern Denmark set to moraine clay. About 110 pieces, recorded per pieceLowlandKulstof 2022 and DJF_LAVBUND (Miljøportalen)carbon-rich and other lowland soilsorganogen where more than half the piece has over 12 % peat (none at Ledreborg), minerogen where more than half is lowland (23 pieces)RetentionKvælstofretention UMR 2027 (SGAV), WFSshare of the nitrate removed on the way to the coastthe value covering the largest part of the piece; 40–95 % at LedreborgClimateDMI 10 km gridclimate cellfrom the piece’s location (see Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR (Example))ModelNUAR-regneark v1.3 (SEGES Innovation and Aarhus University), through the nuar codeNLES5 leaching, discharge, N-normthe code reads the workbook’s tables, exported once; checked against Excel
What the data cannot say:

Catch crops and covers are not in Marker. The autumn cover after each crop is set by a rule: winter cereal or winter rape when one follows, grass or clover grass before grass, the perennial cover for grass and fallow that continue. Where a spring crop follows, and after the 2026 crop, two scenarios: A no catch crop, B a catch crop (sown 20 August). The truth lies in between, field by field.
The fertiliser actually used is not known. Each field is modelled as fertilised at its norm in all three years (NUAR’s default), with no manure.
NUAR’s reference is not a quota. The legal discharge allowance per field from 2027 is not published per field. With the reference as target, retention cancels out, because the field and its reference share it. Where retention matters is shown separately, as the discharge at the 2026 norm (map 4).
NUAR is preliminary. SEGES’s v1.3 says that soil data and the runoff map are not settled; the final regulation may differ.
Grass. For grass and seed grass, NLES5 is asked about nitrogen far beyond the range it was fitted on; such results are shown only as not limiting.

3. The Analytical Schema
flowchart LR
  M[Marker 2024–2026] --> F[Flatten: crops per piece]
  F --> I[Inputs per piece]
  S[Soil, subsoil, lowland, retention, climate] --> I
  I --> N26[2026 norm]
  I --> NU[NUAR: leaching, discharge]
  NU --> SOL[Solve: N for the reference]
  N26 --> C[Compare per piece, crop, landscape]
  SOL --> C































TaskImplementationOperator families usedHistory from yearly snapshots (Task)History from yearly snapshots (Recipe - QGIS)Overlay, Attribute calculationCategories from register codes (Task)the crop codes as NUAR’s crop and cover codesAttribute calculationSoil, subsoil, lowland and retention per piecelargest share of each piece; a point inside it for the subsoilOverlay, AggregationLeaching, discharge, norm and the N that meets the referencethe nuar code (Python port of the SEGES workbook)(model-specific)
Settings used

Flatten (Flatten snapshot series): Marker 2024–2026 from the crop rotation example’s package, fields Afgkode, crop_en, acr_class, tolerance 2 m.
Inputs: JB, lowland and retention by largest share of each piece; subsoil from GEUS at representative_point(); climate cell with nuar.grid.
Covers: the rule above; scenario A cover 4000 (weeds and volunteers), scenario B cover 968 (catch crop) with catch_crop_date 20. aug.
Model: nuar.model.compute for the norm, leaching and discharge, fertiliser left blank (= the norm in all three years); nuar.model.solve_mineral_n with the default target (the reference). Harvest year 2027 as in NUAR.
Script: scripts/examples/ledreborg_nuar.py in semanticGIS-code.
Classes on the maps: more than 25 kg below the norm, within 25 kg, more than 25 kg above; not limiting for grass and where the allowance is 100 kg or more above the norm; above the reference even at 0 kg N.

4. Results
401 pieces (1,420 ha) could be computed. 71 ha could not: fallow and set-aside that NUAR cannot model, and a few crop and cover sequences the workbook marks as invalid. 142 ha have no norm (fallow, unfertilised grass).
The 2026 norm

The norms follow the crop: winter wheat about 200 kg N/ha, winter canola 188, spring barley 125–145, permanent grass up to 158. Almost all the fields are JB 6, so the soil hardly changes the norm here.
NUAR against the norm





































A: no catch cropsB: catch cropsAbove the reference even at 0 kg N817 ha39 haMore than 25 kg below the norm213 ha252 haWithin 25 kg of the norm21 ha643 haMore than 25 kg above the norm—86 haNot limiting (grass, seed grass)226 ha258 ha
By crop, for the arable crops (kg N/ha, area-weighted; scenario B for the norm after a catch crop):











































































Crop class 2026Area (ha)2026 normNUAR, ANUAR, BWinter wheat3522014201Spring barley3121231127Winter canola171188038Winter barley631775196Oats40830131Rye4014310132Spring wheat111410119Horticulture, maize19114–12000All arable1,0331645145
And by landscape (arable crops, scenario B):



























































LandscapeArable (ha)2026 normNUAR, BRetentionLeaching at the normDischarge at the normTill plain46215312276 %25.16.1Glacial lake deposit20917918387 %22.12.9Hummocky topography16018514665 %25.48.8Strongly undulating hummocky topography11217517773 %22.96.5Valley system9013512857 %24.410.2
Leaching and discharge in kg N/ha, area-weighted.
Where the nitrate goes

At the 2026 norm, with catch crops, the fields leach 20–25 kg N/ha from the root zone almost everywhere, but what reaches the coast differs fourfold: 2.9 kg N/ha from the glacial lake deposit, where 87 % is retained on the way, against 10.2 from the valley system, where 57 % is. Half the fields discharge less than 3.4 kg N/ha; a tenth more than 13.
5. Points for the discussion

Catch crops decide more than fertiliser. Without them, 817 ha are above NUAR’s reference even with no nitrogen at all. The reference itself has a catch crop, so a field without one starts behind. Under the 2026 norm a catch crop costs 21 kg N/ha the following year; under NUAR it decides whether the field can be fertilised at all.
Winter canola is the loser. Its 2026 norm is 188 kg N/ha; NUAR allows 38 with catch crops. At its norm, canola leaches 33 kg N/ha in the model, half again as much as the reference (149 %), and only a much smaller dose brings it down. Under NUAR the choice of crop has a price in nitrogen that the 2026 norms did not show.
The same crop, different fields. Winter wheat averages its norm under scenario B, but not everywhere: wheat after spring barley gets 176 kg N/ha against a norm of 206, while wheat after wheat (213 against 209) or after canola (193 against 188) gets its norm or a little more. The 2026 norm sees the previous crop only through a fixed deduction; NUAR sees the crops and covers of two years back.
Retention is where the place enters. With the reference as target, retention cancels out, and NUAR’s verdict depends on crops and soil only. The coming regulation sets a discharge allowance per coastal catchment; then a field in the valley system (57 % retention) will be held to much less leaching than one on the glacial lake deposit (87 %). That is the core of targeted regulation (Christensen et al. 2021), and map 4 shows where it will bite. Read retention with the caveats of Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR (Example): it is a catchment value towards one coastal water, not a property of the field.
The inputs are choices. Covers by rule, fertiliser at the norm, subsoil from a point and set to the nearest type NUAR knows, lowland by a 50 % rule: each changes the answer for some fields. They are in the package per piece, to change and rerun.
One soil type. Almost all of Ledreborg is JB 6 on moraine clay, so the soil hardly separates the fields here; on sandy soils in western Jutland the norms and NUAR would differ in other ways.
A preliminary model. NUAR v1.3 is SEGES’s preview; the runoff map and soil data are still being settled, and the legal allowance is not yet set per field.

Sources

Styrelsen for Grøn Arealomlægning og Vandmiljø (2025). Vejledning om gødsknings- og harmoniregler, planperioden 2025/2026. Chapter 4 and Bilag 1, table 1.
SEGES Innovation and Aarhus University: NUAR-regneark v1.3 (16 June 2026); Børgesen, C. D. et al. (2019). NLES5 – An empirical model for predicting nitrate leaching from the root zone of agricultural land in Denmark. DCA report No. 163.
Christensen, A. Aa., Andersen, P. S., Kjeldsen, C., Graversgaard, M., Andersen, E., Piil, K., Dalgaard, T., Olesen, J. E. and Vejre, H. (2021). Achieving sustainable nitrogen management in mixed farming landscapes based on collaborative planning. Sustainability 13, 2140. doi:10.3390/su13042140
Data: Marker, Jordbundskort 2024 and Kvælstofretention UMR 2027 (SGAV); Jordartskort 1:25 000 (GEUS); Kulstof 2022 and DJF_LAVBUND (Miljøportalen); DMI’s 10 km grid. Fetched 12 November 2026.

domain-hubs/agriculture/index.title: Agriculture
domain-hubs/agriculture/index.content:
Agriculture studies ask what is grown where, under which management regime, and what that regime costs the environment — nutrient leaching above all. In Denmark the question is increasingly a regulatory one: from 2027 the new discharge-based area regulation (Udledningsbaseret Arealregulering, UMR) ties a field’s permitted fertilisation to a statistical model of its own nitrate leaching (NLES5, run through Aarhus University’s and SEGES’s NUAR calculator) and to the share of that leaching retained before it reaches the coast. The questions therefore sit across three registers that rarely line up at the same resolution: the declared crop and management per field, the soil and subsoil under it, and the hydrological model of what happens to the water afterwards.
Typical questions

How much nitrate leaches from a field’s root zone under its crop, soil and management, and how much of that reaches the coast after retention?
Which measures (catch crops, cover crops, reduced fertilisation, precision farming) bring a field’s discharge within its quota?
What crop and cover has a field or block carried over time, and how is a declared crop code turned into a model category?
Where are soils organic, drained or otherwise under special management rules?

Often used data
Through the SPHERE leaves: Land use and agriculture, Soil properties.
Not yet leaves in their own right, but in active use: the national nitrogen retention map (geodata.fvm.dk, WFS layer Kvaelstofretention_UMR_2027), DMI’s 10 km climate grid, and the field-block/declared-crop series from Landbrugsstyrelsen (mirrored as GeoParquet by Fields of the World). A worked pipeline against all three is at github.com/Esbern/nuar.
Tasks

General: Aggregating points to zones (Task), Categories from register codes (Task), History from yearly snapshots (Task), Vegetation index from satellite imagery (Task)

Examples

Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR
2026 norms and NUAR at Ledreborg: the 2026 nitrogen norms against NUAR for every field, with and without catch crops
Crop rotations at Ledreborg: crops, legumes and crop combinations 2021–2026 from Marker
Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg: NDVI from Sentinel-2 (in the Landscape ecology hub)

Related hubs
Land use planning, Soil, Hydrological modelling

domain-hubs/agriculture/calculating-perm.title: Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR (Example)
domain-hubs/agriculture/calculating-perm.content:
A worked case for the agriculture hub, on Denmark’s discharge-based area regulation (Udledningsbaseret Arealregulering, UMR) entering force in 2027. Code: github.com/Esbern/nuar.
From 2027 a field’s permitted mineral fertiliser is tied to how much nitrate it is modelled to leach from the root zone, and how much of that leaching is retained before it reaches the coast. The calculation runs through NLES5, Aarhus University’s statistical leaching model, as implemented in SEGES’s reference “NUAR-regneark” (Excel, v1.3) — an authoritative but partly provisional tool: SEGES’s own documentation states outright that several of its inputs (soil data, the runoff map) are not yet finalised. This example works one point through the full chain: crop and soil → leaching → retention → discharge, and treats the retention step on purpose as a modelling question, not a lookup.
1. Spatial Intent
Question: given a field’s crop, soil and climate, and the nitrogen retention between it and the coast, how much mineral fertiliser N can be applied without the field’s net discharge exceeding its 2027 quota?
Theory: NLES5 is a regression model fitted to suction-cup leaching measurements; it estimates root-zone leaching (kg N/ha) from crop, cover, soil texture, climate and fertilisation. What actually reaches the coast is leaching × (1 − retention) — and retention, as published, is not a property of the field but of the catchment it drains through on the way to a named recipient. That distinction is the point of this example.
2. Auditing the data









































DataSourceWhat it isChoicesNLES5 / NUAR calculationSEGES Innovation / Aarhus University, “NUAR-regneark” v1.3 (16.06.2026)~2,100-formula Excel engine; also ported to Python and checked against real Excel on 10,500+ scenarios, 0 mismatchessoil input discretised to 56 (region × JB-group × subsoil) combinations, each given one representative clay % and topsoil-N valueNitrogen retentiongeodata.fvm.dk, WFS layer Udledningsbaseret_mark_regulering:Kvaelstofretention_UMR_2027catchment polygons (up to ~80 km²) with RetTot (retention %) and KystvandIDfield point joined to polygon by within; points outside farmland coverage, or exactly on a boundary, get no valueClimate gridDMI’s DKN_10km_ETRS89 grid (vendored from dmidk/Climate-Data-Grid-Map)609-cell national grid, real ETRS89 geometryNUAR’s legacy sequential grid id (10001–10609) is not published by DMI; the crosswalk used here is inferred and strongly evidenced, not officially confirmedCrop and covernot yet wired incandidate: LBST’s “Marker” field/crop dataset, mirrored as CC0 GeoParquet by Fields of the World (data.source.coop/ftw/harmonized-field-data/dk), one file per year 2008–2026—Soil class, subsoil, lowlandnot yet wired incandidates on landbrugsgeodata.fvm.dk: Jordbundskort_2024, Afstroemningsvaerdier_2027, Organisk_kvælstof_i_overjorden_2027, several Lavbund layersdownloaded as zip, format and field-vs-grid resolution not yet verified
Known limits: the soil input is a 56-bin simplification of what Aarhus University’s own newer soil mapping treats as a continuous clay-content surface. The runoff/percolation lookup (AfstrDat) has the largest single effect on the result of anything tested (~17% of leaching variance in sensitivity runs, against ~1% for climate-grid/region) and was, as of SEGES’s 16.06.2026 note, still “under udvikling” at Aarhus University. See Soil for the broader question of modelled vs. surveyed soil data in Denmark.
3. Retention is a hydrological model output, not a field property
The retention layer looks, at first glance, like any other lookup: join a point to a polygon, read off a percentage. Two things about its schema argue against treating it that way.
First, every polygon carries a KystvandID — the id of the specific coastal water body the retention value is accounted toward. The number published is not “the fraction of this field’s nitrogen lost in transit,” independent of where it ends up; it is already attributed to one recipient. A field at the edge of two catchments draining to different coastal waters will see different retention even if the land between it and the coast looks identical, because the two numbers are computed against two different recipients, not two different transport distances.
Second, a retention percentage of this kind is normally derived from a hydrological model — flow paths, travel time, subsurface denitrification potential — run against some reference loading, not measured per field. That makes it a direct output of the same kind of model this vault’s Hydrological modelling hub covers, with the same caveats: sensitive to how the underlying terrain/flow model was built, and to assumptions baked in at calibration time rather than stated on the data layer itself. Some retention maps of this type in Denmark show a 10 km homogeneity in places — a resolution that would be unremarkable for a national groundwater flow model (such as DK-model/HIP) but is unexpected for something published as a field-relevant agricultural layer. Whether that is in fact inherited from reuse of a coarser hydrological model’s own grid, rather than being resolved at the retention calculation itself, is an open research question, not yet confirmed from this layer’s own metadata.
Practical consequence: retention_pct should be read, and taught, as “this catchment’s modelled retention toward this specific recipient, under the assumptions of whatever hydrological model produced it” — not as a fixed physical constant of the land between a field and the sea.
4. The Analytical Schema
flowchart LR
  P[Field point x/y] --> CR[Categories from register codes: JB, crop code]
  P --> AZ1[Aggregating points to zones: retention polygon]
  P --> AZ2[Aggregating points to zones: DMI grid cell]
  CR --> M[NLES5 / NUAR calculation]
  AZ2 --> M
  M --> L[Root-zone leaching, kg N/ha]
  AZ1 --> R[Retention %, tied to a KystvandID]
  L --> D[Net discharge = leaching × 1 - retention]
  R --> D
  D --> S[Solve: mineral N for a target discharge]































StepTaskImplementationPoint → retention polygonAggregating points to zones (Task)nuar/retention.py, join_retention()Point → climate grid cellAggregating points to zones (Task)nuar/grid.py, grid_for_points()JB / crop code → model categoryCategories from register codes (Task)nuar/tables.py, VLOOKUP-equivalent lookupsLeaching, discharge, solve for N(no general Task yet — model-specific)nuar/model.py, compute() / solve_mineral_n()
5. Results
A single demonstration point (not a real farm; coordinates in northern Jutland, near the Limfjord, EPSG:25832), run through the full pipeline from coordinates alone. For real fields, with every input fetched and the 2026 norms beside NUAR, see 2026 norms and NUAR at Ledreborg (Example).
mamba run -n nuar python -m nuar run examples/points_fetch_auto.csv -o result.csv \
    --fetch-retention --fetch-grid




























xyjbcrop/coverretentiongridleaching (kg N/ha)discharge (kg N/ha)% of reference52935063015506 (Moræneler)spring barley, no catch crop99.0%1018627.770.28101%
The reference is NUAR’s own built-in comparison case (spring barley with no measures), so 101% reads as “about what an unremarkable spring-barley field is expected to leach” — the retention step, not the leaching estimate, is doing almost all of the work in bringing discharge down to 0.28 kg N/ha at this particular, very high-retention point.
6. Points for the discussion

Retention is recipient-conditioned, not a transport coefficient (§3). Before using RetTot across fields draining to different coastal waters, check whether it is meant to be comparable at all, or whether it is only valid relative to each polygon’s own named recipient.
A 10 km artefact, possibly inherited. Where the retention layer shows unexpectedly coarse, grid-like homogeneity, the likely explanation is reuse of a national hydrological model’s own resolution (HIP/DK-model) rather than a resolution chosen for retention itself — worth confirming against the layer’s methodology documentation, which is not published alongside the WFS service.
Soil input is categorical by construction, not by necessity. NUAR discretises soil into 56 (region × JB-group × subsoil) bins; Aarhus University’s own newer soil maps are built from a continuous clay-content surface. SEGES’s 11.05.2026 note states plainly that whether soil type “documented via jordprøver” can enter the regulation at all is still undecided.
The highest-leverage input was, by SEGES’s own account, still being built. AfstrDat (runoff/percolation) affects the result roughly 17× more than the climate grid does, and was “under udvikling” as of June 2026. landbrugsgeodata.fvm.dk now lists an Afstroemningsvaerdier_2027 layer that may be its finished replacement — not yet checked against the workbook’s own lookup.
The climate grid id is a reconstruction. NUAR’s legacy 10001–10609 numbering of DMI’s 10 km cells is not published anywhere; the crosswalk used here is strongly evidenced (an exact 18-cell match against the workbook’s own picture, the isolated Bornholm cluster landing correctly) but should be flagged as inferred whenever it is relied on.

Sources

Børgesen, C.D., Sørensen P., Blicher-Mathiesen G., Kristensen M.K., Pullens, J.W.M., Zhao J., Olesen J.E. 2019. NLES5 – An empirical model for predicting nitrate leaching from the root zone of agricultural land in Denmark. Aarhus University, DCA – Danish Centre for Food and Agriculture. DCA report No. 163.
SEGES Innovation, “NUAR-regnearket kan beregne kvælstofudvaskning,” Landbrugsinfo, 11.05.2026, updated 16.06.2026.
Kvælstofretention UMR 2027 — WFS geodata.fvm.dk, layer Udledningsbaseret_mark_regulering:Kvaelstofretention_UMR_2027.
DMI climate grid documentation, dmi.dk/frie-data/dokumentation/climate-data/parameters-for-10x10km-20x20km-municipality-and-country; grid geometry from dmidk/Climate-Data-Grid-Map (GitHub).
Code: github.com/Esbern/nuar

domain-hubs/agriculture/crop-rotations-a.title: Crop rotations at Ledreborg (Example)
domain-hubs/agriculture/crop-rotations-a.content:
A worked case for the course Environmental Regulation and Management with GIS, Themes 3.1 (nitrogen in the agro-environment: pollution and regulation) and 3.2 (cultivation and food consumption). Companions: Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example) (NDVI), Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example). Hub: Agriculture.
Within the Ledreborg landscapes, farmers declared about 1,520 ha of fields each year from 2021 to 2026, 56 % of the area. Most of it is in cereal–oilseed rotations: a third of the fields (515 ha) grew only winter wheat, spring barley and winter canola, with or without seed grass, in those six years. Legumes are rare. Pulses (peas and faba beans) were grown on 65 ha in all, each field in one year only, and on none in 2025 and 2026. Clover and lucerne, mixed into grass, cover 80–110 ha every year.
Example data

Ready to use: ledreborg_crops_example_data.zip (1.5 MB), a snapshot package: Marker 2021–2026 as this example used it (clipped to the landscapes; the applicant’s identifiers left out), the landscapes, and the crop code table (codelists/crop_codes_dk.csv), with snapshot.json and a README.
Or fetch it yourself with Download snapshot series (step 2 below), for these years or others, and for your own landscape.

1. Spatial Intent
Question: which crops have the fields of the study area carried from 2021 to 2026, where are the legumes, and which crop combinations cover the most land? What does that mean for nitrogen leaching and for a regulation targeted at where leaching does the most harm?
Study area and zones: the five landscape types of the Ledreborg study area (Landscape delineation (Task)), 2,704 ha.
Units: the fields as declared each year; after flattening, pieces of land that keep their identity through the six years.
Theory: nitrate leaches when there is mineral nitrogen in the soil and water draining through it, which in Denmark is mostly from autumn to spring. A field with a growing crop in autumn and winter (winter cereals, winter canola, grass, catch crops) takes up nitrogen that a field left bare after a spring crop loses. Legumes fix nitrogen from the air: they need little or no fertiliser, but their residues and ploughed-in clover grass release nitrogen to the following crop, and to the drainage water if nothing takes it up. Danish nitrogen regulation has mostly been general: the same rules for all farmland in the country. Christensen et al. (2021) argue that further reductions need targeted regulation, planned in ecologically meaningful units: landscapes, where the same pattern of land use repeats across many farms, or watersheds, where the farms share the same recipient water. In their six case watersheds, farmers and other stakeholders built land-use scenarios with a GIS landscape tool that estimated leaching field by field from soil, hydrology, nitrogen retention and crop rotation. Mapping the crop rotations of a landscape, as here, is the first step of such a tool.
2. Auditing the data





























DataSourceWhat it isChoicesFields and cropsMarker 2021–2026, WFS Marker:Marker_<year>, fetched 12 November 2026the fields farmers declared for EU area payments, with the crop code Afgkodeclipped to the landscapes; 2026 is preliminaryCrop classesData/Inner workings/Code lists/danish-crop-codes-afgkodeeach code’s English name and a simplified class (acr_class, 25 classes)the classes are a choice, made for teaching; see below for legumesLandscapesthe example’s landscapes (Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example))five landscape typesas delineated for the Ledreborg examples
What the data cannot say:

Marker is what was applied for, not what grew; NDVI from a satellite image can check it (Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example)).
Catch crops and green cover after harvest are not crop codes in Marker; a winter NDVI image shows where the soil was green and where bare.
The field boundaries are drawn anew each year and differ by a metre or two; flattening moves older boundaries onto the newest (2026).
The simplified classes put clover grass and lucerne grass into Grass in rotation or Permanent grass. A legume map from the class alone shows only the pulses (class Leguminous seed). This example therefore maps the clover and lucerne from the English crop name as well.

3. The Analytical Schema
flowchart LR
  F[Fetch 2021–2026 for the landscapes] --> J[Codes to crop classes]
  J --> S[Area per class and year]
  J --> T[Flatten: one piece, one column per year]

Settings used

Fetch (Download snapshot series): Series Marker, First year 2021, Last year 2026, Area the landscapes layer (all features), Buffer 0, Only features that touch the area on, Clip features to the area on, Output CRS EPSG:25832. 2,814 features (445–488 a year).
Crop classes (Join attributes by field value): Afgkode = afgkode of the crop code table; fields crop_en and acr_class; one-to-one. All 2,814 features matched.
Area per class and year (Statistics by categories): $area / 10000, categories acr_class and snapshot_year.
Flatten (Flatten snapshot series): Period field snapshot_year, Fields to keep acr_class and crop_en, Tolerance 2 m, Column prefix y. About 1,650 pieces, 1,559 ha; about 1,900 slivers merged on the way.
Combination (Combination of values): the six y<year>_acr_class columns, field name rotation, without frequencies. 184 combinations.
Pulses, year grown (map): CASE WHEN "y2021_acr_class" = 'Leguminous seed' THEN 2021 WHEN "y2022_acr_class" = 'Leguminous seed' THEN 2022 … END.
Years with clover or lucerne (map): one term per year, if(regexp_match(lower("y2021_crop_en"), 'clover|lucerne') > 0, 1, 0) + ….

4. Results
Crops per year

Winter wheat, spring barley and winter canola take about half of the fields every year (49–57 %); the shares shift between them from year to year, as rotations do. Seed grass falls from 170 ha in 2021–2022 to about 25 ha in 2024 and 2026.
Legumes


























Pulses (peas, faba beans), any year65 ha, each piece in one year onlyPulses per year2021: 16 ha (faba beans 12, peas 3) · 2022: 11 ha (peas) · 2023: 27 ha (peas) · 2024: 11 ha (peas) · 2025, 2026: noneGrass with clover or lucerne, per year78–108 haGrass with clover or lucerne, any year195 ha; 18 ha in all six years
Most of the pulses (40 of 65 ha) lie on the till plain in the north-west; the rest in the hummocky topography and the valley system. Clover and lucerne grass is found in every landscape, most on the till plain (91 ha) and in the strongly undulating hummocky topography (53 ha), where some fields keep it for five or six years.
The 20 largest crop combinations

95 % of the flattened area (1,477 ha) has a crop in all six years; the rest are pieces that were a field in only some years, mostly along edges.
5. Points for the discussion

Winter cover. Winter wheat, winter canola, rye and winter barley (610–770 ha a year) are green through the winter; spring barley, oats and spring wheat (205–365 ha) leave the soil bare or in stubble from harvest to spring, unless a catch crop is sown. The winter NDVI the assignment asks for shows which fields were actually green; Marker alone cannot.
Where to target. Arable rotations cover 81–88 % of the fields on the till plain and the glacial lake deposit, but only 41 % in the strongly undulating hummocky topography, where a third of the fields are grass. The landscapes are units of the kind Christensen et al. (2021) propose: each has its own pattern of land use, repeated across several farms. Combined with soil, drainage and the national nitrogen retention map (see Calculating permitted fertiliser with NUAR (Example)), the rotations show where changing a rotation, or taking land out of it, would reduce the load on the water the most. Their study also shows the limits: the stakeholders agreed that there was a nitrogen problem, but not on its size or on how to solve it, and a map like this is an input to that negotiation, not its answer.
What is a legume? By the simplified classes there are 65 ha of legumes; with clover and lucerne grass, three to four times as much. The definition decides the map; record it (Categories from register codes (Task)).
Unordered on purpose, and what it loses. The combination puts fields at different stages of the same rotation together, which is why the largest combinations are clear. It also drops the order: grass ploughed before a cereal, or a pulse before wheat, releases nitrogen in a particular year. For that, read the year columns of the flattened layer.
Short histories. Six years is one or two rotations. Permanent grass in the table includes pieces that are permanent grass in every declared year, but a piece declared in fewer years gets the same label; rotation_periods says how many years a combination is based on.
Preliminary 2026. The 2026 layer is still being updated; the 2026 column will change.
Boundaries. At a 2 m tolerance, about 1,900 slivers from re-digitised boundaries are merged away. Strips narrower than 2 m go too; wider fallow strips along the field edges stay, which is why thin red strips show along many fields on the map.

Sources

domain-hubs/biodiversity/index.title: Biodiversity
domain-hubs/biodiversity/index.content:
Biodiversity studies ask where species and habitats are, in what condition, and how they are protected. In GIS the work is mostly about habitats: defining which areas count as habitat, mapping their types and condition, and relating them to the protection and land use around them. How the habitats are arranged and connected is the concern of landscape ecology.
Typical questions

Which areas are habitat, of which types, and in what condition?
How much habitat is protected, and by which rules (§3, Natura 2000, forest designations)?
Where are species observed, and how do observations relate to habitats?

Often used data
Through the SPHERE leaves: Habitat extent, Habitat condition, Nature protection areas, Natura 2000 habitats, Species observations, Species of conservation concern, Biodiversity priority indicators, Forests.
Tasks

Nature content layer (Task)

Examples

Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example) (in Landscape ecology)

Related hubs
Landscape ecology, Soil

domain-hubs/biodiversity/nature-content-.title: Nature content layer (Task)
domain-hubs/biodiversity/nature-content-.content:
Implementation: Nature content layer (Recipe - QGIS).
Nature content layer is the Task of bringing the different kinds of semi-natural habitat in an agricultural landscape into one polygon layer: protected nature (§3), larger woodlands, hedges and streams. Together they are the landscape’s nature content, the patches that species live in and move between. Every later habitat analysis starts from this layer, so what goes into it decides what the network can show.
Used in examples: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Decide what counts as nature content (decision point) — which habitat types, and with which thresholds (minimum woodland size, which hedge types).
Get each source for the study area plus a margin (Operator: clip to extent) — a margin of about 1 km, so patches just outside the area still count.
Select what qualifies (Operator: selection by attribute) — e.g. woodland ≥ 5 ha, living hedges only, open (not piped) streams.
Give lines a width (Operator: dilation) — hedges and streams are lines in the data but strips of habitat in reality.
Label each source (decision point) — a field saying which kind of nature each patch is.
Put the sources together (Operator: merge) — one layer, features unchanged, overlaps kept.

Output: one polygon layer of nature patches with a type field, covering the study area and its margin.
Epistemic Choices to record

Thresholds: “larger woodland” as ≥ 5 ha (or 0.5 ha, or all woodland) changes the number of patches a lot; say why the chosen threshold fits the question.
Data quality of each source: in GeoDanmark most hedges have no recorded type (Ikke tildelt); keeping only the ones marked as living hedges leaves real hedges out, keeping all of them adds garden hedges and fences. Say which and why.
Widths given to lines: a 5 m hedge, a stream with its 2 m cultivation-free bank zone. The widths affect areas, not connectivity at distances of 50 m or more.
Overlaps: a §3 bog inside a woodland is counted twice if areas are summed per type; dissolve before measuring total nature area.
Date: each source has its own date; the layer is as old as its oldest source.

domain-hubs/climate/index.title: Climate
domain-hubs/climate/index.content:
Climate questions in GIS come in two kinds: how the climate shapes a place (temperature, precipitation, flooding, sea level), and how land use affects the climate (carbon in soils and vegetation, emissions). Soil carbon links this hub to Soil.

How much carbon is stored in soils and vegetation, and how does land use change it?
Which areas are exposed to flooding or rising sea level?
Where do emissions and deposition occur?

domain-hubs/energy/index.title: Energy
domain-hubs/energy/index.content:
Energy planning in GIS is about where energy is produced, moved and used: siting wind turbines and solar parks, the grid that connects them, and the land and transport that biomass such as straw needs.
The main actors in Danish Energy planning are the Danish Energy Agency (Energistyrelsen) and the dedicated organisation (EnergiNet).
