domain-hubs/soil/soil-carbon-and-land-us.title: Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example)
domain-hubs/soil/soil-carbon-and-land-us.content:
A worked case for the course Environmental Regulation and Management with GIS, Theme 2.2 (carbon storage in land-use systems). Companion: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
At Ledreborg the topsoil holds the most organic carbon where the landscape holds the most nature. The valley system averages 2.2 % SOC in 0–30 cm, the till plain 1.6 %. The difference comes from the wet areas: in wet nature the topsoil holds 6.4 % SOC, in intensive arable land 1.5 %.
Example data
Everything this example uses, frozen as it was used (27 October 2026), so its numbers can be reproduced without API keys: ledreborg_example_data.zip (2.9 MB), a snapshot package. It holds one GeoPackage with the landscapes, protected nature, woodland, hedges and streams; Basemap04 land use and soil organic carbon (0–30 cm) as 10 m rasters with their styles; the Basemap04 class list (codelists/); and snapshot.json and a README with sources, licences and attribution. The same data serve Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example) and Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example).
1. Spatial Intent
Question: how do land use and soil organic carbon (SOC) differ between the landscapes of the study area, and how does carbon follow land use?
Study area and zones: the five landscape types of the Ledreborg study area (Landscape delineation (Task)).
Theory: photosynthesis takes carbon from the atmosphere into biomass. Part of it ends up in the soil, where microbial activity breaks it down or binds it. How much stays depends on land use (tillage, permanent cover) and on water: in wet soils breakdown is slow, and peat builds up.
2. Auditing the data























DataSourceWhat it isChoicesLand useBasemap04, lu_agg_2021 (10 m)35 aggregated classeslegend from the attribute table (lu_agg_2021.qml); classes grouped into ten for the chartSOC 0–30 cmKulstofkort i 10 m opløsning, Aarhus University (10 m)% organic carbon by mass, modelled from >83,000 samples with Sentinel-1/2 time series and environmental layersused as a concentration, not a stock; mean and median reported
Known limits: SOC is modelled, with its own error. The model predicts values under lakes and buildings too. 3.4 % of the landscape area has no value. A concentration in % says nothing about tonnes per hectare without bulk density.
3. The Analytical Schema
flowchart LR
  L[Landscape delineation] --> C[Land-use composition per zone]
  L --> Z[Zonal summary of a surface]
  LU[Basemap04 land use] --> C
  SOC[SOC 0–30 cm] --> Z
  LU --> Z





















TaskRecipeOperator families usedAggregating a categorical raster to zones (Task)Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS)Geometry restructuring, ZonalAggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task)Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS)Geometry restructuring, Zonal
Settings used

Land use per landscape (Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS)): raster lu_agg_2021.tif (Basemap04, 10 m, 35 classes) with its style lu_agg_2021.qml (English labels; lu_agg_2021_da.qml for Danish), made from the raster’s attribute table. Landscapes dissolved by type; Tabulate area with Report as percent.
SOC per landscape (Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS)): raster kulstof_kombineeret.tif, SOC 0–30 cm in % by mass, NoData −1. Landscapes dissolved by type; Zonal statistics Count, Mean, Median.
SOC per land use: Raster layer zonal statistics with lu_agg_2021 as zones; both rasters on the same 10 m grid.

4. Results
Land use

Soil organic carbon

High SOC values follow the valleys and the hollows between the hummocks: the wet areas and former peatland. On the till plain the topsoil is uniformly low.
Land use and SOC per landscape






















































LandscapeIntensive arableForestWet natureMean SOCMedian SOCValley system38 %29 %12 %2.18 %1.50 %Glacial lake deposit65 %14 %3 %1.95 %1.60 %Strongly ondulating hummocky topography21 %28 %4 %1.94 %1.50 %Hummocky topography50 %18 %4 %1.91 %1.50 %Till plain62 %9 %1.5 %1.57 %1.44 %
Intensive arable includes permanent crops; wet nature includes wet nature with extensive agriculture.
Mean SOC 0–30 cm by land use, within the landscapes: wet nature 6.4 %, wet nature with extensive agriculture 5.0 %, lakes 3.9 % (a model artefact, see below), forest 1.9 %, extensive agriculture 1.7 %, intensive arable 1.5 %.
5. Points for the discussion

The mean hides where the carbon is. In the valley system the median (1.5 %) is the same as elsewhere; the high mean comes from a small wet area with very high values. Carbon management there is about a few hectares of wet soil, not the whole landscape.
Land use or landform? Wet nature has high SOC, but wet nature also lies where the soil was always wet. The map shows co-occurrence, not that changing land use would change SOC at the same rate.
Concentration is not stock. 6 % SOC in a light peat soil and 2 % in a dense clay soil can hold similar amounts of carbon per hectare. A carbon budget needs bulk density and depth.
Habitat and carbon together. The wet areas that hold the most carbon are also §3 nature and part of the habitat network (Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example)). Taking low-lying arable land out of drainage would serve both; the till plain’s stepping stones would mostly serve biodiversity.
Modelled values under lakes. The SOC model gives lakes 3.9 %; that is the model’s prediction for a soil that is not there, and such cells should be left out of a careful analysis.

Sources

Møller, A. B., Nyborg, L., Grogan, K., Druce, D., Svane, S. F., Greve, M. B., Gutierrez, S., Styczen, M., Greve, M. H., Knudsen, L. and Beucher, A. (2025). High-resolution 3D soil texture mapping in Denmark using satellite time series and bare soil composites. Advances in Agronomy 194, 133–. doi:10.1016/bs.agron.2025.07.001

domain-hubs/transport/demand-response-tr.title: Demand Response Transport (DRT)
domain-hubs/transport/demand-response-tr.content:
Analysis
Demand-responsive transport (DRT) is a type of public transportation service that operates based on passenger demand rather than fixed routes or schedules. Unlike traditional buses or trains that run at specific times along predetermined paths, DRT services are flexible, adjusting their routes and pick-up and drop-off locations in real-time according to the requests of passengers. This allows DRT to provide more personalised and efficient transportation, particularly in areas where demand is too low to justify the cost of regular public transport services, such as in rural or suburban regions.
DRT typically utilises technology such as mobile apps or call centres to manage bookings and optimise routes, ensuring that the service is both responsive to passenger needs and economically viable. It can be used as a standalone transport service or integrated with existing public transport networks to enhance accessibility and connectivity, especially in areas underserved by traditional transit options.
Demand-Responsive Transport (DRT) plays a crucial role in providing mobility solutions in rural areas, where low population density and passenger numbers often make traditional public transport services economically unfeasible. In these regions, DRT offers a flexible, cost-effective, and accessible alternative to fixed-route buses and trains, ensuring that rural residents remain connected to essential services and opportunities.
Key Benefits of DRT in Rural Areas

Flexibility and Adaptability:

In rural areas, where the population is spread over large distances and the demand for public transport can be unpredictable, DRT’s flexibility is particularly valuable. Unlike fixed-route services, DRT does not require a constant stream of passengers to justify its operation. Instead, it adapts its routes and schedules based on real-time passenger requests, allowing for efficient transport even in sparsely populated areas.

Cost-Effectiveness:

Operating traditional fixed-route services in rural areas can be prohibitively expensive due to the low number of passengers and long distances between stops. DRT addresses this challenge by only running services when and where they are needed. This on-demand approach minimises wasted resources, reducing operational costs while still providing essential transport services to rural communities.

Increased Accessibility:

For many rural residents, especially those without access to a private vehicle, DRT can be a lifeline, providing access to healthcare, education, employment, and social activities. DRT services can be tailored to meet the specific needs of these communities, offering door-to-door service and accommodating passengers with mobility challenges. This ensures that even the most remote areas remain accessible.

Integration with Broader Transport Networks:

In rural regions, DRT often acts as a feeder service to connect passengers with fixed-route buses, trains, or other modes of public transport in more populated areas. This integration is crucial for maintaining a seamless transport network, allowing rural residents to reach larger towns and cities for work, shopping, or other activities.

Support for Rural Sustainability:

By providing an alternative to car dependency, DRT contributes to the sustainability of rural communities. It helps reduce the environmental impact of transport by optimizing vehicle usage and lowering emissions. Additionally, by supporting mobility, DRT can help sustain rural economies by keeping residents connected to local businesses and services.
Challenges and Considerations
While DRT offers many advantages in rural areas, there are also challenges to consider. These include ensuring adequate coverage across widely dispersed populations, maintaining service reliability, and integrating DRT with existing public transport networks. However, advances in technology, such as real-time booking systems and route optimisation algorithms, continue to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of DRT in rural settings.
In relation to Public Transportation Analysis and Accessibility Planning, DRT poses its own unique problems.

domain-hubs/transport/public-transportat.filePath: Domain hubs/Transport/Public Transportation Analysis and Accessibility Planning.md
domain-hubs/transport/public-transportat.title: Public Transportation Analysis and Accessibility Planning
domain-hubs/transport/public-transportat.content:
Public Transportation Analysis and Accessibility Planning involve the study and optimisation of public transit systems to ensure that communities are well-served by transportation networks. This field leverages geospatial data to analyse how effectively public transport connects people to essential services like healthcare, shopping, and schools and how well different areas are covered by transit routes.
Key Concepts: Modal Split and Journey Segments


Modal Split:
Modal split refers to the distribution of travellers among different modes of transportation—such as walking, cycling, public transit, and private vehicles—within a specific area or journey. Understanding the modal split is essential for planning and optimising public transport, as it reveals how different segments of the population prefer to travel and highlights areas where public transport can be improved or better integrated with other modes.


Journey Segments: First Mile, Transfer, and Last Mile:
A typical public transport journey can be divided into three key segments:


First Mile: This is the initial segment of the journey, where a traveller moves from their starting location (e.g., home or workplace) to the nearest transit stop. This phase is crucial for accessibility, as inadequate first-mile options (e.g., long walks, poor cycling infrastructure) can deter people from using public transport.


Transit Segment (also known as Main or Core Segment): This is the central part of the journey, where the traveller uses the primary mode of public transport, such as a bus, train, or tram. The efficiency, comfort, and reliability of this segment are key to the overall satisfaction with public transport.


Last Mile: The final segment of the journey, where the traveler moves from the transit stop to their final destination. Like the first mile, the quality of last-mile connections (e.g., sidewalks, bike-sharing systems) plays a significant role in the overall convenience and attractiveness of public transport.




Understanding and optimising these journey segments, particularly the first and last miles, are essential for enhancing public transport accessibility and ensuring that the entire journey is efficient and user-friendly.
Key Data Sources and Formats


OpenStreetMap (OSM):
OpenStreetMap is a vital data source for public transportation analysis, offering a detailed and continuously updated map that includes roads, paths, and other transportation infrastructure. Its strength lies in its granularity, particularly for modeling the first and last mile of travel—critical for understanding access to and from public transit.


General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) and NeTEx:
GTFS and NeTEx are essential formats for representing public transit data. GTFS provides information on schedules, routes, and stops, while NeTEx (Network Timetable Exchange) offers a more feature-rich alternative that supports advanced transit features like fare zones and flexible service areas. These formats are indispensable for modelling and analysing the complexities of real-world transit operations.


Route Planning and Analysis Tools


OpenTripPlanner (OTP):
OpenTripPlanner is an open-source tool designed for individual route planning across multiple transportation modes, including walking, cycling, driving, and public transit. By integrating OSM for street and path data with GTFS/NeTEx for transit information, OTP excels at providing detailed, multimodal itineraries that consider the entire journey, including the first and last miles.


Conveyal R5:
Conveyal R5 is an advanced routing engine designed for large-scale transportation analysis. Unlike OTP, which focuses on individual routes, R5 is geared toward analysing broader mobility patterns across entire metropolitan areas. It’s particularly useful for scenario planning and evaluating the impact of infrastructure changes on accessibility, making it a powerful tool for public transportation planning.


Integration and Impact
The integration of OpenStreetMap, GTFS, NeTEx, OTP, and R5 has significantly enhanced the ability to analyse and optimise public transportation systems. OSM provides the necessary street and path data for modelling critical aspects of transit access, while GTFS and NeTEx offer detailed and structured transit data. Tools like OTP and R5 leverage these datasets to provide powerful capabilities for both individual route planning and large-scale transportation analysis.
In conclusion, public transportation analysis and accessibility planning are essential components of modern urban planning. The use of OSM, GTFS, NeTEx, OTP, and Conveyal R5 enables detailed and accurate modelling of transit systems, ensuring that transportation networks are efficient, accessible, and meet the needs of the population. By considering key concepts like modal split and journey segments (first mile, transfer, and last mile), these tools and data sources will be crucial in shaping the future of urban mobility.

domain-hubs/urban-design/urban-design-vi.title: Urban Design Visualisation (Example)
domain-hubs/urban-design/urban-design-vi.content:
Domain: urban design and landscape architecture. Case: the redesign of a town square — Hestetorvet and Algade, Roskilde. Stack: QGIS → Blender → Twinmotion → Affinity.
In most Domain Projects the Geospatial Workflow exists to answer a question: where are the party zones, which rooftops suit solar panels. Urban design is different. Here the Geospatial Workflow rarely produces the answer — the answer is the designer’s proposal for the square. What the workflow must produce is a faithful, legible spatial context in which that proposal can be drawn, rendered and judged.
This makes urban design visualisation a useful counterweight to the case studies elsewhere in the book, for two reasons. First, the weight of the workflow sits at Designing Spatial Results Communication (Vantage Point 4), not at the Analytical Schema. Second, it is an almost pure Prescriptive (Teleological) workflow (see 1.2 The workflow): the deliverable — an A0 poster — is fixed before any data is touched, and every earlier Vantage Point is reverse-engineered from it.





























Vantage PointWhat it settles in this domain1. Scoping the WorkflowWhat the context is for: a stage for the proposal, not a portrait of the existing city2. Establishing the Data FrameworkWhich parts of the city are represented, at which Level of Detail, from which data3. Authoring the Analytical SchemaHow heights, roofs, ground surfaces and shadows are derived from official data4. Designing Spatial Results CommunicationHow the reader’s attention is directed to the proposal — the centre of gravity of this workflow5. Executing the Analytical SchemaThe Stack: QGIS, Blender + BlenderGIS, Twinmotion, Affinity, and the hand-over formats between them

1. Scoping the Workflow
Spatial Intent. Present a proposal for the square in its urban context, so that a jury and the public judge the proposal — not the existing city around it.
The second half of that sentence is not decoration. It is the constraint that shapes every later Vantage Point, and it was learned the hard way (see Workflow Stewardship below).
Workflow type. Prescriptive. We run the preliminary pass in reverse:

Communication — an A0 poster: site plan 1:500, concept diagrams, a line section, perspective renders.
Analytical Schema — those drawings require building heights, roof forms, ground surfaces, terrain and shadows.
Data Framework — those derivations require building footprints, two elevation models, edge lines for streets and pavements, and a site visit.

Universe of Discourse. The square and its edges; the buildings that frame it and the wider block structure; the terrain (the Roskilde square slopes); the ground surfaces — roads, cycle paths, pavements, plazas, planting; existing trees; sunlight and shadow; people and how they use the space; and the elements of the proposal itself — planting, water, paving, furniture, pavilions.
Operational context. Student groups over one semester; one site visit; free official data from Dataforsyningen; free or educational software; a large-format printer. A deliberately tight time budget: the context model should take one working session, not one week. Time spent modelling window frames on existing buildings is time not spent on the proposal.
A note on persuasion. A visualisation of a proposal is advocacy. It shows a future that does not exist, populated by people doing what the designer hopes they will do. That is legitimate — but it puts a Duty of Disclosure on the workflow: the reader should be able to tell what is recorded (the existing city), what is derived (heights, shadows), and what is proposed.

2. Establishing the Data Framework
Formalising the Domain of Discourse





























































Cognised ExistenceSpatial CharacterThematic specificationResolutionTypingRelationship constraintsStudy areadiscreteThe area within which the existing city is represented — 200–300 m around the square. Bigger is not better.—PolygonContains every other context RealisationContext buildingdiscreteInherited from GeoDanmark Bygning (see Buildings) — including its contested edges, which we accept rather than re-openGeoDanmark’s MMU (25 m², 10 m² inside an area polygon); vertical: LOD1 or LOD2 (below)Polygon footprint, extruded to a solid. height, eave, roof_rise: ratio. ground (DVR90 elevation): interval. roof_type: nominal. lod: ordinalFootprints do not overlap; every building stands on the terrainTerraincontinuousBare ground surface (see Elevation)0.4 m cellFieldBuildings and surfaces sit on itGround surfacediscreteThe paved and unpaved surfaces of the public realm: road, cycle path, footpath / pavement, plaza, parking, green, water, building, otherPrecise in and around the square; rough elsewherePolygon; surface: nominalPlanar partition: no gaps, no overlaps, complete coverage of the study areaExisting treediscreteA tree standing in the study area todayIndividual treePoint—Proposal elementdiscretePlanting, water, paving zone, furniture, new tree, pavilion — authored, not observedDesign-ledPolygon / PointLies within the study area; may replace ground surfaces
Three of these commitments deserve comment.
Level of Detail is a resolution commitment. “Detail follows distance” sounds like a rendering tip, but it is a decision about resolution, and so it belongs here. Borrowing the CityGML convention, LOD1 is a flat-topped block extruded to the building’s height; LOD2 adds the roof form. We commit to LOD2 only for the four to eight buildings that frame the square and appear in the perspectives, and LOD1 for everything else. A Cognised Existence with deliberately uneven resolution must say so in its own data — hence the ordinal lod field. Without it, the finished poster silently implies a uniform accuracy the model does not have.
The ground surface is a partition. Its topological constraint — no gaps, no overlaps, full coverage — is what makes a site plan readable as a continuous ground. It is also exactly what the existing data does not offer (see the audit below).
Proposal elements are a different kind of thing. Every other Cognised Existence here is observed: it belongs to the World of Observation. The proposal belongs to the World of Proposition. It is formalised with the same five commitments, but it is never audited against existing data or confronted with the Sensoric Manifold, because there is nothing yet to confront. This is why it is recorded separately (below).
Auditing existing data


















































Cognised ExistenceCandidate dataAudit outcomeContext building (footprint)GeoDanmark BygningAcceptContext building (height, eave)Not in the footprint dataTransform from Danmarks Højdemodel: surface (DSM) minus terrain (DTM)Context building (roof form)Not in any registerCollect — orthophoto, oblique photos (skråfoto), site visitTerrainDHM Terræn (DTM), 0.4 mAcceptGround surfaceGeoDanmark offers only road edges (Vejkant) and centre lines (Vejmidte) — lines, not areasTransform (partition the edge lines into polygons) and Collect (draw the boundaries the data lacks: plaza edges, kerbs, planting beds)Existing treeGeoDanmark, where presentAccept, completed from orthophoto and site visitOrthophotoDataforsyningen WMS/WMTSWorking reference only — used to check and digitise, never shown in the final deliverablesPhotogrammetric city modelRealityScan meshes, Google Photorealistic 3D TilesReject
The rejection of photogrammetry is worth spelling out, because it is usually argued on aesthetic grounds alone. The aesthetic argument belongs at Vantage Point 4. There is also an ontological argument, and it belongs here: a photogrammetric mesh does not Realise Context building at all. It realises one undifferentiated visible surface, in which a facade, a parked car, a sign and a tree are the same continuous skin. It cannot be split into buildings, cannot carry a height or lod attribute, and cannot be edited when the proposal changes a building edge. It answers a different question — what does this place look like? — from the one the Domain of Discourse asks. See also Photogrammetry.
Confronting the Sensoric Manifold — the site visit
The site visit is not an excursion. It has both of this Activity’s functions:

Validation — do the derived heights survive contact with the street? A very large roof_rise usually means a lower wing or annex inside one footprint, which no elevation model will tell you. Does the square slope the way the terrain model says?
Collection — roof forms (gable, hipped, mansard, flat with parapet), and the boundaries the existing data lacks: where the plaza ends and the pavement begins, the kerb of a planting bed, the steps.

Recording the Domain of Discourse

One master GeoPackage for the context (context.gpkg), in ETRS89 / UTM 32N (EPSG:25832) with heights in DVR90. The CRS is fit for purpose: metric, and native to all Danish source data, so nothing is reprojected.
A separate GeoPackage for the proposal (design.gpkg). Observed and proposed Cognised Existences have different epistemic status and are kept physically apart, so the proposal can change without touching the record of the existing city.
Shapefile, GeoTIFF and FBX are transport formats, not Recording. They carry data between programs at the Execution stage; the master data always stays in GeoPackage.


3. Authoring the Analytical Schema
The analytical core of this workflow is small. Most of its Operators derive representations rather than answer a question — which is typical of communication-led domains, and a reason not to skip this Vantage Point: the derivations still contain judgements.
flowchart LR
    SA[Study area] --> CL{{Clip}}
    FP[Building footprints] --> CL
    DSM[DSM] --> CL
    DTM[DTM] --> CL
    EL[Edge lines] --> CL
    CL --> ND{{"DSM − DTM<br/>(local)"}}
    ND --> NDSM[nDSM]
    CL --> IB{{"Inward buffer −0.5 m"}}
    IB --> ZS{{"Zonal statistics<br/>outlier filter, p95 / p10"}}
    NDSM --> ZS
    ZS --> H[height, eave]
    H --> RR{{"roof_rise = height − eave<br/>reclassify at 1.0 m"}}
    RR --> RT[roof_type]
    CL --> ZG{{"Zonal statistics on DTM"}}
    ZG --> G[ground]
    CL --> PL{{"Node + snap<br/>polygonize"}}
    PL --> SF[Ground surface polygons]
    H --> EX{{"Extrude:<br/>LOD1 to height,<br/>LOD2 to eave + roof"}}
    RT --> EX
    G --> EX
    EX --> M3[3D context model]
    M3 --> SH{{"Shadow casting<br/>sun position: place, date, time"}}
    SH --> SR[Shadow raster]
    CL --> CT{{"Contour, hillshade"}}
    CT --> TR[Terrain graphics]

The parameter choices are Epistemic Choices and belong in the Design Rationale:

95th percentile, not maximum, for building height — chimneys, antennas and overhanging trees would otherwise set the height of whole buildings. The 10th percentile of the same pixels estimates the eave.
Inward buffer of 0.5 m — keeps street and wall-edge pixels out of the zonal statistic.
Flat-roof threshold of 1.0 m — a building whose roof_rise is below this is typed flat.
Centre lines are not partition boundaries. Vejmidte is used only as a classification hint; if it enters the partition, every road is cut lengthwise in two.

Two Intermediate Realisations matter in practice: the nDSM (height above ground), which is the quickest visual check on the heights, and the dangles (loose line ends) of the partition, which show exactly where the planar-partition constraint is still violated.
Tasks used at this Vantage Point:

Building heights from elevation models (Task)
Surface partitioning (Task)
Context massing (Task)


4. Designing Spatial Results Communication
What kind of deliverable. On MacEachren’s cartography cube the poster sits firmly in one corner: a public audience, presenting knowns (the proposal is a set of claims, not an exploration), and no interaction. That justifies a static, printed artefact, read from one to two metres away.



































DeliverableWhat it must showMade withSite plan 1:500The proposal in plan, on a quiet groundQGIS, finished in AffinityConcept diagrams (3–4)One idea each: zones, flows, connectionsQGIS, finished in AffinityLine drawing or section perspectiveExisting vs. proposed, from the same cameraBlenderPerspective renders (2–3) + one season variantThe proposal as experienced at eye heightTwinmotionA0 posterAll of the above, in one hierarchyAffinity
How the deliverable represents the data. The governing principle here is not specific to urban design. Every map must decide where the reader looks first; the general rule is set out in Visual hierarchy and figure-ground. In this domain the figure is the proposal and the ground is the existing city, and the principle translates into three representational rules:

The context is one neutral material. Matte white in renders; white with a thin black outline in plans. No facade textures, no photo meshes.
Colour belongs to the proposal. Planting, water, paving, furniture and people carry the colour. Nothing in the context competes with them.
Atmosphere over accuracy. Haze, soft shadows and light do more for the context than modelled detail — haze literally pushes the white city back and brings the proposal forward.

Professional competition material uses the same grammar. MASU Planning’s proposal for Hestetorvet and Algade shows white or grey context, with realistic trees, people and paving only where the design happens.

Test: if someone looks at the render and talks about the existing buildings first, the context is too loud.

Backward Glances. Several representational choices must be checked against what was actually recorded and computed:

Camera placement depends on the lod field. A perspective that puts an LOD1 block in the foreground exposes a resolution the Data Framework never committed to. Either move the camera or go back and raise that building to LOD2.
Shadows are either a convention or a claim. A drop shadow on a site plan is a graphic convention that implies nothing about the sun. A shadow render cast from the 3D model at a stated place, date and time is a claim about the proposal’s microclimate — so it should be labelled with that date and time.
Existing vs. proposed must share a camera. Otherwise the comparison measures the change of viewpoint, not the change of design.
The orthophoto is turned off in every final drawing. It was a working reference (Data Framework), not a Realisation of anything in the Domain of Discourse.
People in the renders are a claim about use. Place them doing what the design invites — sitting, playing, crossing, meeting — in small groups, and be ready to defend each one.


5. Executing the Analytical Schema
The Analytical Schema is translated into a chain of Recipes across four programs. Data flows one way. Each program is used for what it does best, and the hand-over format between them is fixed in advance.

























StackRole in this workflowQGISInstrument of record (the master GeoPackage) and of analysis (heights, partition, contours); 2D plans and diagramsBlender + BlenderGISExtrusion to LOD1/LOD2; line drawings; sun-correct shadow renderTwinmotionPerspective renders, seasons, atmosphereAffinityFinishing plans and diagrams; A0 poster layout and print PDF





































































StepTaskRecipeInputOutputHand-over format1Building heightsBuilding heights from DHM (Recipe - QGIS)GeoDanmark, DHMClipped data; buildings with height, eave, roof_type, groundShapefile + GeoTIFF2Surface partitioningSurface partitioning (Recipe - QGIS)Vejkant, buildingsClassified ground surfaces(stays in GeoPackage)3—Site plan and concept diagrams (Recipe - QGIS)Surfaces, buildings, design layersSite plan 1:500, concept diagramsPDF / SVG4Context massingContext massing (Recipe - Blender)Shapefile with heights, terrain GeoTIFFWhite LOD1 context, LOD2 roofsFBX5—Line drawings and shadow plans (Recipe - Blender)Context + design modelLine perspective/section; top-down shadow renderPNG / SVG / world file6—White-context rendering (Recipe - Twinmotion)context.fbx, design.fbxPerspective renders, season variantsJPG / PNG / video7—A0 poster layout (Recipe - Affinity)Everything aboveA0 posterPrint PDF (PDF/X-4)
Recipes differ in how reproducible they are. Steps 1 and 2 are scripted QGIS Processing tools: given the same inputs and parameters, they give the same result, and can be handed to another practitioner or an agent. LOD2 roof modelling in step 4 is not — every roof is a human decision point checked against photographs. That asymmetry is fine, but it must be recorded: the lod field says which buildings were hand-modelled, and the Design Rationale says from which sources.
Project folder. Every group uses the same structure, and no file is renamed once another program links to it:
plaza_project/
  01_data/        downloaded raw data (never edit)
  02_qgis/        QGIS project + GeoPackages (master data)
  03_exchange/    shp, tif, fbx, obj between programs
  04_blender/     .blend files
  05_twinmotion/  .tm files
  06_output/      renders, plans, diagrams, poster


Workflow Stewardship
A Backward Glance across iterations. The previous run of this workshop built its context from RealityScan meshes of oblique aerial photos and Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles. The renders were impressive and the juries talked about the existing buildings. That observation, made at Vantage Point 4, cascaded back to Scoping — the Spatial Intent was rewritten to say whose judgement the context must serve — and from there to the Data Framework, where photogrammetry was rejected and LOD1/LOD2 massing adopted. This is the Backward Glance working as intended: the fix was not a better render setting, but a re-stated intent.
Design Rationale entries owed by every group:

Study area extent, and why
Which buildings are LOD2, and the sources used for each roof
Height-derivation parameters, if changed from the defaults — and any heights corrected by hand
Ground surfaces classified by judgement rather than by hint
Sun position (date, time) of every shadow render
What in each render is proposed rather than recorded

Before hand-in:

Context is one neutral material in every render and plan
LOD2 roofs only on the buildings that frame the square; no LOD1 block in a foreground
All colour and detail is in the proposal
Site plan at 1:500 with north arrow and scale bar; orthophoto turned off
Ground surfaces classified in and around the square (no red outlines left)
Building heights checked (h_check)
3–4 concept diagrams, one point each
At least one line drawing, existing vs. proposed from the same camera
2–3 perspective renders + one season variant
A0 poster from the course template, images at 150 ppi, PDF/X-4 checked and test-printed at A3
Someone outside the group looks at a render and talks about the design first


Related

Visual hierarchy and figure-ground — the general map design principle behind the context rules
The use of 3D geospatial data in urban planning, Urban design
2.5D geometries, 3D geometries, Digital Twin
Data: Buildings, Elevation, Orthoimagery, Transport networks

domain-hubs/urban-design/index.title: Urban design
domain-hubs/urban-design/index.content:
Urban design works with the form of places: buildings, streets and spaces, usually in three dimensions and at the scale of a site and its surroundings. GIS supplies the context — terrain, buildings, parcels, plans — that a design is drawn into and shown against.
Typical questions

What does a site and its context look like in three dimensions?
How high are the surrounding buildings, and how would a new one fit?
How can a design be shown to people who do not read plans?
