learning-paths/environmental-management-.title: Environmental Management with GIS
learning-paths/environmental-management-.content:
Course path for Environmental Regulation and Management with Geographical Information Systems, autumn 2026. See Learning paths for how paths work.
The course uses GIS to model the socio-ecological world, so that regulation and planning can rest on informed choices. It starts with observation: what is out there, and how do we record it so that it can be modelled? It then works through three themes (landscapes, resilience, ecosystem services) and ends at the science–policy interface. Each session has a lecture on the theme and a GIS lab that applies it.
The thread through the course
Three drawings return throughout the course:

The five activities of a geospatial workflow: the workflow every lab follows.
Design rationale of a geospatial workflow: why each choice in a workflow is recorded.
Mapping and data: from field observation to map.

Sessions
Introducing the course and key skills

































#WeekSessionReadWork through138Introduction. Modelling and recording the socio-ecological world with GIS: making informed choices in regulation and planning.GIS, GIS project, From Reality to Geospatial Data238Ontology-based field observations. Ontologies, data types and observation protocols; field excursion to a landscape near campus, recording observations with an ontology.Ontology, world of observation, world of discourse, Entity-based modelling, Field-based modelling, The Four NOIR Data Types, Geospatial Data Collection339Modelling field observations in GIS. Geodata and processing tools; describing an area in a map from spatial environmental data and field observations.Geospatial data, vector representation, raster representation, Coordinate Reference System (CRS), [[Data/Inner workings/Platforms/where-to-find-danish-dataWhere to Find Danish Data]], Basemap
Theme 1: Landscapes


























#WeekSessionReadWork through441Landscape systems. Scale, interaction, functionality, feedback and emergence in environmental systems; recognising and delineating patterns of interacting features in heterogeneous landscapes.Landscape ecology, scale, Modifiable areal unit problemLandscape delineation (Task) (Recipe), building on Surface partitioning (Task)543Land use regulation and planning. The Danish Planning Act and the countryside; basic layout and symbols for a synoptic presentation.Land use planning, General-purpose Map, Visual hierarchy and figure-ground, Classification for mapsSite plan and concept diagrams (Recipe - QGIS)
Theme 2: Resilience


























#WeekSessionReadWork through644Biodiversity and area-based conservation. Protected areas, landscapes and their biotopes; depicting land use and the (re)establishment of historic and new habitats.Biodiversity, Spatial relationsNature content layer (Task), Habitat network (Task), Network gaps and stepping stones (Task); example: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example)745Carbon storage in land use systems. Obtaining and analysing data on vegetation from satellite-based observation platforms.Remote sensing (chapters 1–6)Vegetation index from satellite imagery (Task) (Recipe), Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task); examples: Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example), Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example)
Theme 3: Ecosystem services


























#WeekSessionReadWork through846Nitrogen in the agro-environment. Nitrogen as pollutant and resource: geodata and tools to model and intervene with emissions. Lab: mapping winter-green fields (fields with plant cover through winter, which take up nitrogen that would otherwise leach) from Sentinel-2 NDVI, and selecting those fields.Spectral signatures and vegetation indices, SelectionVegetation index from satellite imagery (Task) (Recipe) on a winter image, then Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task) with the fields of Marker as zones; data: Målrettede efterafgrøder947Cultivation and food consumption. Mega-trends in food consumption; changed crop selection and its environmental effects. Lab: extracting the historical crop choices of the fields within each landscape from Marker, comparing extract by location (whole fields, selected by a spatial relation) with intersection (fields cut at the landscape border).Spatial relations, Selection, Overlay (intersection and clip)the landscapes from session 4 (Landscape delineation (Task)); Categories from register codes (Task) for grouping crop codes
The policy dimension



















#WeekSessionReadWork through1048Working at the science–policy interface. Public authorities’ work with environmental assessments; presenting results in a poster; poster presentations and course evaluation.A0 poster layout (Recipe - Affinity)
Exam

Week 50, Monday 7 December: written assignments handed in as PDF on eksamen.ruc.dk.
Week 51, 15–16 December: oral exams.

learning-paths/learn-gis-the-semantic-wa.filePath: Learning Paths/Learn GIS the semantic way/Learn GIS the semantic way.md
learning-paths/learn-gis-the-semantic-wa.title: Learn GIS the semantic way
learning-paths/learn-gis-the-semantic-wa.content:
An open learning path: for anyone learning GIS on their own, at their own pace. See Learning paths for how paths work.
Most GIS courses start with the software: this button buffers, that one clips. This path starts with the world. You learn to say what you are looking at and what question you are asking of it, to find the data that can answer the question, and to choose the operation that turns the data into an answer. The software comes last, as the Recipe that carries the operation out. Once you work this way, changing tools (QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, Python) changes only the last step.
You need: a computer that can run QGIS (free), and curiosity about a place you know. No earlier GIS experience.
Afterwards you can: turn a question about a place into a documented GIS workflow: what you observe, which data stand for it, which operations answer the question, and why you chose them.
The path
Each stage starts with the question it answers. Read the notes in the “Read” column first, then work through the Tasks and Examples.
1. Seeing the world as data
What is in the world, and how does it become data?








































StepReadWork throughWhat GIS is forGIS, Geospatial data, 1.1 IntroductionThe workflow1.2 The workflow, GIS projectObserving before recordingOntology, world of observation, world of discourse, From Reality to Geospatial DataWhat kind of value is it?The Four NOIR Data TypesObjects or fieldsEntity-based modelling, Field-based modelling, vector representation, raster representationWhere on EarthCoordinate Reference System (CRS), ESPG code, Shortlist of Danish, European and Global CRS, Projection
2. Finding data the semantic way
Which datasets stand for the thing I am asking about?






























StepReadWork throughFrom question to dataSPHERE: start from a leaf (a question you can ask of the data) and follow it to the datasets that realise itHow data are servedGeographical Web Services, [[Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Geospatial Data Access Methods/WFSWFS]], Where to Find Danish DataGetting started in QGISQGIS, Managing QGIS plugins (the SemanticGIS plugin loads SPHERE data directly)Placing register units on the map (Task)Good data habitsFAIR principles, Snapshot packages
3. Operating on space
Which operation turns the data into an answer?
The Operators are the families of spatial operations. Each Task below is written with Operators, and its Recipe shows how to carry it out in a specific tool.













































StepReadWork throughMaking your own dataBasemapGeoreferencing (Task), Backdrop digitalisationSelecting by locationSpatial relations, SelectionSummarising to areasAggregation, Modifiable areal unit problem, Square and hexagonal gridsAggregating points to zones (Task); example: Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example)Distance and neighbourhoodProximityDistance to habitat (Task)Combining layersOverlayAggregating a categorical raster to zones (Task)SurfacesSlope and flow direction (Task), Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task)Seeing from aboveRemote sensingVegetation index from satellite imagery (Task); example: Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example)
4. Communicating
How do I show the answer so that it is read correctly?




















StepReadWork throughThe map as an argumentGeneral-purpose Map, Visual hierarchy and figure-ground, scaleClasses and coloursClassification for mapsComparable choropleth maps (Task)
5. Specialising
What do the questions of my field look like?
Choose a Domain hub close to your interests: landscape ecology, biodiversity, soil, climate, housing, hydrology, urban design, transport, energy, land use planning or ethnography. Each hub lists the questions the field asks, the data it often uses, and worked Examples. Work through one Example from start to end, and write down your choices as a Design Rationale.

learning-paths/index.title: Learning paths
learning-paths/index.content:
A learning path is an ordered route through the notes on this site. It adds no new content of its own: each step points to the Supporting concepts to read, and to the Tasks, Recipes and Examples to work through. SemanticGIS can be entered in three ways:

by data: SPHERE starts from what exists in the world and which datasets describe it;
by domain: Domain hubs start from the questions a field asks;
by learning: a learning path starts from what you want to be able to do, and takes you through the other two in an order that builds up.

Every path follows the same semantic way of working. A step starts with a question about the world. It finds the data that can answer the question, chooses the operation (an Operator), and only then the tool and its Recipe. You meet the question before the button.
Two kinds of path

Open paths are for anyone learning GIS on their own, at their own pace. They have no dates.
Course paths follow a course taught on site. A course path uses the same steps as an open path wherever it can, and adds what belongs to the course: the schedule, the lectures and field work, and the drawings used in teaching.

Paths




















PathKindForLearn GIS the semantic wayOpenAnyone learning GIS on their own; no earlier experience neededEnvironmental Management with GISCourseStudents of Environmental Regulation and Management with GIS, autumn 2026

operators/aggregation-(operator-family).title: Aggregation (Operator family)
operators/aggregation-(operator-family).content:
Aggregation Operators summarise many values into one per zone or group: the values of one layer inside the zones of another, or of the features that share an attribute. For example the mean soil carbon per landscape, the area of each land use per landscape, the number of dwellings per district. The zones can be polygons (landscapes, districts, a grid) or the patches of a network. Dana Tomlin’s map algebra calls the raster versions zonal operators. What is aggregated decides the Operator: points or polygons, a continuous raster, a categorical raster, or a table grouped by an attribute.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Task), Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task), Habitat network (Task), Aggregating points to zones (Task).
Zonal statistics (continuous surface)
Operator Schema: for each zone, statistics of the raster cells inside it: count, sum, mean, median, minimum, maximum, standard deviation.
Choices to record: which statistic (mean and median differ when a few extreme cells pull the mean); how cells on the zone edge are counted (QGIS counts a cell when its centre is inside); cell size against zone size (a zone smaller than a few cells has an unreliable value).
Tools: QGIS Zonal statistics (Tool - QGIS) (polygon zones), or Zonal statistics by class (Tool - QGIS) (SemanticGIS plugin: the classes of a categorical raster as zones, with legend names in the table).
Tabulate area (categorical raster)
Operator Schema: for each zone, the number of cells (or the area, or the share) of each class of a categorical raster such as land use.
Choices to record: which classes to keep or group; area or percentage; how the zone’s total is defined (all cells, or only cells with a class).
Tools: QGIS Tabulate area (Tool - QGIS) (SemanticGIS plugin, with legend names as column names), or QGIS’s own Zonal histogram (column names are the raster values).
Summary by location (vector)
Operator Schema: for each zone, statistics of the features of another layer that fall inside it: count, sum, mean of a field.
Choices to record: the spatial relation and its direction (zones contain points); what to do with points on borders and with polygons that cross them. See Spatial relations.
Tools: QGIS Join attributes by location (summary) (Tool - QGIS) (counts, sums, means, medians in one run) and Count points in polygon (Tool - QGIS) (counts or sums only); Join attributes by location (Tool - QGIS) to give each point its zone instead.
Group-by statistics (by attribute)
Operator Schema: statistics of a field for each value of another field, without any geometry: the mean dwelling area per construction period, the number of patches per cluster.
Choices to record: which field groups; what to do with empty values in the grouping field.
Tools: QGIS Statistics by categories (Vector analysis), Aggregate (Vector geometry; also merges the geometries per group), or aggregate expressions in the Field calculator (Tool - QGIS).
Rule: never average averages upwards
Counts, sums and areas from small zones can be added up to a larger zone that contains them. Means, shares and medians cannot: average the cells again, or add up sums and counts and divide. See Modifiable areal unit problem.

operators/attribute-calculation-(operato.title: Attribute calculation (Operator family)
operators/attribute-calculation-(operato.content:
Attribute calculation Operators derive new values from the attributes and geometry of each feature, or from the values of each raster cell, without moving anything: a 0/1 indicator from a code, an area from a geometry, a density from a count and an area, a total over a group. They are how register codes become the variables an analysis needs.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Categories from register codes (Task), Aggregating points to zones (Task), Habitat network (Task), Vegetation index from satellite imagery (Task), Scoring criteria (Task), Multi-criteria suitability (Task).
Derive a value per feature
Operator Schema: a new field computed from other fields and the geometry of the same feature: a recoding (if(code = 1, 1, 0)), a ratio, an area ($area), a length.
Choices to record: what the new value means, its unit, and what happens to empty values (a NULL in, a NULL out, unless you decide otherwise with coalesce).
Tools: QGIS Field calculator (Tool - QGIS).
Indicator (0/1) variable
Operator Schema: a category turned into 1 (has it) and 0 (does not). The sum of an indicator over a zone is a count, and its mean is a share. That makes any tool that sums or averages compute counts and shares of a category.
Choices to record: which codes count as 1, and whether “unknown” or “not in use” counts as 0 (it stays in the denominator) or is left out.
Tools: QGIS Field calculator (Tool - QGIS).
Aggregate over a group
Operator Schema: a value per feature computed from all features that share a group value: the number of patches in a cluster, the area of a cluster, a feature’s share of its group’s total.
Tools: QGIS Field calculator (Tool - QGIS) with aggregate expressions such as count($id, group_by:="cluster_id").
Rescale to a common scale
Operator Schema: the values of a criterion turned into a common scale, so that criteria measured in metres, square metres and classes can be added: divided by the maximum (0–100), min–max (lowest 0, highest 100), z-score (mean 0, standard deviation 1), or percentile rank (the share of features with a lower value, 0–100).
Choices to record: the method, and why. Division by the maximum and min–max keep the shape of the distribution, so one extreme value squeezes all the others towards 0. A z-score gives every criterion the same spread, but extreme values remain extreme. A percentile rank is not moved by extreme values and suits ordinal values, but it discards the distances between values. Also record the direction: whether a high value is good or bad for the question.
Tools: QGIS Field calculator (Tool - QGIS), e.g. 100 * "x" / maximum("x") or ("x" - mean("x")) / stdev("x"); for a percentile rank, Add autoincremental field (Tool - QGIS) first. All the functions, and NULL for held-out units: Scoring criteria (Task).
Weighted sum
Operator Schema: several rescaled criteria combined into one value per feature, each multiplied by a weight: suitability = w₁·c₁ + w₂·c₂ + …. A negative weight turns a criterion where a high value is bad (a long distance) into a penalty.
Choices to record: the weights and the argument for them. A weight only means what it says when the criteria have the same spread: with a criterion spread over 0–100 and another over 0–5, the first decides the result whatever the weights.
Tools: QGIS Field calculator (Tool - QGIS).
Rank
Operator Schema: the position of each feature when all features are sorted by a value: 1 for the highest, n for the lowest. Selecting rank ≤ k keeps the top k.
Choices to record: the direction of the sort, and how ties are treated (in sorted order they get consecutive ranks, so which of two equal features comes first is arbitrary).
Tools: QGIS Add autoincremental field (Tool - QGIS) with a sort expression.
Map algebra (per cell)
Operator Schema: a new raster computed cell by cell from one or more rasters on the same grid: arithmetic between bands (a vegetation index such as NDVI), a condition that keeps or removes cells (a mask: if(cloud = 0, value, nodata)), a rescaling (reflectance × 10,000 to reflectance).
Choices to record: the formula and the meaning and unit of the result; the grid (cell size, extent, alignment) the inputs share or are resampled to; the data type the calculation uses (integers can overflow or be divided as integers); what happens to NoData and to division by zero.
Tools: QGIS Raster calculator (Tool - QGIS).

operators/conversion-and-data-management.title: Conversion and data management (Operator family)
operators/conversion-and-data-management.content:
These Operators change the form, extent or storage of data without changing what it says: from vector to raster and back, from codes to classes, from the whole country to the study area. They are rarely the point of an analysis, but every analysis needs them, and each one involves a choice that can change the result.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Distance to habitat (Task), Network gaps and stepping stones (Task), Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Task).
Rasterize
Operator Schema: vector features become raster cells, with a fixed value or a value from a field.
Choices to record: cell size; which cells count as covered (by default a cell is burned when its centre is inside the polygon, so features narrower than a cell can disappear); extent.
Tools: QGIS Rasterize (Tool - QGIS).
Polygonize
Operator Schema: connected cells with the same value become polygons.
Tools: QGIS Polygonize (raster to vector) (Raster conversion).
Reclassify
Operator Schema: cell values are replaced according to a table of ranges or values: land-use codes to “farmland yes/no”, distances to distance classes.
Choices to record: the class boundaries, and whether a boundary value belongs to the class below or above.
Tools: QGIS Reclassify by table (Raster analysis).
Clip to extent
Operator Schema: keep only the part of a layer inside a rectangle, typically the study area plus a margin.
Choices to record: the margin. An analysis that stops exactly at the study area boundary treats everything outside as missing: a patch just outside the area is still part of the network.
Tools: QGIS Clip raster by extent (Raster extraction); for vector layers Clip (Tool - QGIS) with a rectangle, or Package layers (Tool - QGIS).
Reproject
Operator Schema: coordinates are transformed to another coordinate reference system. Danish data belong in ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N (EPSG:25832), where distances and areas are in metres.
Tools: QGIS Reproject layer; Package layers (Tool - QGIS) can reproject while saving.
Save
Operator Schema: write a layer to a file, usually a GeoPackage.
Tools: QGIS Export › Save Features As…, or Package layers (Tool - QGIS), which saves several layers into one GeoPackage with a common clip extent and their styles.

operators/geometry-generation-(operator-.title: Geometry generation (Operator family)
operators/geometry-generation-(operator-.content:
Geometry generation Operators create new geometry by a rule, not from observed data: a grid of cells, a regular set of sample points. The result is a frame for other data, so its rule — size, shape, origin — is a choice that shapes every result built on it.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Aggregating points to zones (Task).
Generate grid
Operator Schema: cells of equal size and shape covering an extent: squares or hexagons (polygons), or their centre points or edges.
Choices to record:

Predefined or ad hoc. If an official grid exists for the purpose — the Danish Kvadratnet or the European statistical grid, see Statistical Units — use it, or generate cells that coincide with it exactly. An ad hoc grid is for questions no official grid serves, and its results cannot be compared with others’.
Shape: square or hexagon; see Square and hexagonal grids.
Size: the cell size sets the scale of the result.
Origin and CRS: a square grid aligned with an official grid starts at its corner values in its CRS (for the Danish grid, round kilometres in EPSG:25832; the European grid is in EPSG:3035, so the two do not coincide).

Tools: QGIS Create grid (Tool - QGIS).

operators/geometry-restructuring-(operat.title: Geometry restructuring (Operator family)
operators/geometry-restructuring-(operat.content:
These Operators change how geometry is divided into features, not where it is. The same area can be one feature, many features, or one feature made of many parts, and each choice answers a different question: “how much nature is there?” needs one dissolved area; “how many patches are there?” needs one feature per patch.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Nature content layer (Task), Habitat network (Task).
Merge
Operator Schema: puts the features of several layers into one layer, unchanged. Overlapping features stay separate and keep overlapping.
Choices to record: which field says where each feature came from (QGIS adds layer and path automatically).
Note: the layers must have the same geometry type. Lines (hedges, streams) must first become polygons with a dilation.
Tools: QGIS Merge vector layers (Tool - QGIS).
Dissolve
Operator Schema: joins features into one, optionally per value of a field. Shared borders and overlaps disappear. Without a field, everything becomes one (multipart) feature.
Choices to record: dissolve all, or per category; whether separate pieces stay one multipart feature or become separate features (that is explode).
Tools: QGIS Dissolve (Tool - QGIS), or Buffer (Tool - QGIS) with Dissolve result.
Explode
Operator Schema: splits every multipart feature into one feature per part. After a dissolve, each separate piece becomes its own feature: one feature per cluster.
Note: each new feature keeps its parent’s attributes, including its id. In a GeoPackage two features cannot share a fid, and saving fails. Renumber the ids: Renumber feature ids (Tool - QGIS).
Tools: QGIS Multipart to singleparts (Tool - QGIS), or the Keep disjoint … separate option of Dissolve (Tool - QGIS) and Buffer (Tool - QGIS).

operators/index.title: Operators
operators/index.content:
An Operator is one tool-agnostic transformation of spatial data: buffer, clip, dissolve, zonal statistics. Operators are kept simple: each does one thing. A Tool is what a software Stack bundles into one dialog, and one Tool can realise several Operators through its options (see Terminology Glossary, §9).
Operators are grouped in families: Operators that do the same kind of work. The families are the index to search when a new problem comes up. They are domain-neutral: the same Proximity Operators measure walking distance to a park in urban design and link habitats into a network in landscape ecology. What differs is the domain that uses them.


















































FamilyWhat it doesOperatorsSelectionKeeps some features or cells, drops the restby attribute, by locationOverlayCombines two layers as setsintersection, union, difference, symmetric difference, clipProximityWorks with distancedilation, erosion, fringe, margin, distance surface, shortest lineGeometry restructuringChanges how geometry is split into featuresmerge, dissolve, explodeGeometry generationCreates new geometry by a rule, as a frame for other datagenerate gridAggregationSummarises many values into one per zone or groupsummary by location, zonal statistics, tabulate area, group-by statisticsAttribute calculationDerives new values per feature or per raster cellrecode, indicator (0/1), ratio, aggregate over a group, rescale, weighted sum, rank, map algebraConversion and data managementChanges the form or extent of data, without changing what it saysrasterize, polygonize, reclassify, clip to extent, reproject, save
From problem to Operators to Tools

Write the problem as a Task (for example Habitat network (Task)): the decisions it needs and the Operators that carry it out (see C - Authoring the Recipe).
Find each Operator in its family and read its choices: they are the decisions the Task must record.
Only then look up the Tool that realises the Operator in your Stack, for QGIS in the Tool notes (Buffer (Tool - QGIS) and the others linked from each family).

Asking an AI assistant
A question about a whole problem (“how do I find connected habitats in QGIS?”) gets a general answer that is hard to check. A question about one step of a Task gets a precise one:

I am doing step 3 of my Task: dilate all nature patches by 50 m and dissolve them into clusters, keeping separate clusters as separate features. Which QGIS 4.2 tool does this, with which parameters, and what can go wrong?

The assistant then works on the Extent (which tool, which settings), and you keep the Intent (what the step is for and why 50 m). Check its answer against the Tool notes here, and against the tool’s own help text in QGIS.

operators/overlay-(operator-family).title: Overlay (Operator family)
operators/overlay-(operator-family).content:
Overlay Operators combine two layers as sets of areas. They are the spatial form of and, or and not, and they turn a list of conditions into areas that meet them.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Network gaps and stepping stones (Task), Nature content layer (Task), Site screening by criteria (Task).



































OperatorSet logicTypical useIntersectionA and Bareas that meet two conditionsUnionA or Bareas that meet at least one condition, or alternativesDifferenceA not Bremove what is excluded (a negative constraint)Symmetric differenceA or B, not bothone of two conditions is acceptable, both together is notClipA, cut to the outline of Bintersection that keeps only A’s attributes
Intersection
Operator Schema: the parts of A that are also in B. The result carries the attributes of both layers.
Tools: QGIS Intersection (Tool - QGIS).
Union
Operator Schema: all parts of A and of B, split where they overlap, so every piece knows whether it belongs to A, B or both. The attributes of both layers are kept.
Tools: QGIS Union (Tool - QGIS). To merge layers without splitting them, use merge instead.
Difference
Operator Schema: the parts of A that are not in B. Order matters: A minus B is not B minus A.
Tools: QGIS Difference (Tool - QGIS).
Symmetric difference
Operator Schema: the parts in A or B but not in both. Used for “either condition is acceptable, both together are not”.
Tools: QGIS Symmetrical difference (Vector overlay).
Clip
Operator Schema: the parts of A inside B, keeping only A’s attributes. It looks like an intersection on the map; the difference is in the attribute table.
Tools: QGIS Clip (Tool - QGIS). Clipping to a rectangle (a study area) is also part of clip to extent.
From a text to Overlay Operators
A description such as “within 100 m of existing nature, on farmland, but not on roads or in towns” breaks down into:

positive constraints, combined with intersection (and) or union (or): within 100 m of nature, on farmland;
negative constraints, combined with union and then removed with difference: roads, towns.

The result is positive constraints minus negative constraints.

operators/proximity-(operator-family).title: Proximity (Operator family)
operators/proximity-(operator-family).content:
Proximity Operators work with distance: they grow or shrink shapes, describe how far every place is from something, or find the shortest connection between things. Most location questions (“close to”, “within walking distance”, “not too near”) end up here.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Distance to habitat (Task), Habitat network (Task), Network gaps and stepping stones (Task), Nature content layer (Task), Site screening by criteria (Task).
Dilation (the ordinary buffer)
Operator Schema: every shape grows outward by a distance d. A point becomes a circle, a line a strip, a polygon a larger polygon that includes the original.
Choices to record: the distance and why; whether overlapping results are merged (that is a second Operator, dissolve); the shape of line ends (round or flat).
Note: a dilated lake includes the lake. “Close to the lake” usually means the fringe, not the dilation.
Tools: QGIS Buffer (Tool - QGIS) with a positive distance.
Erosion (negative buffer)
Operator Schema: every polygon shrinks inward by d. Parts narrower than 2 × d disappear.
Choices to record: the distance; what it means that thin parts vanish (a narrow woodland strip has no “core”).
Tools: QGIS Buffer (Tool - QGIS) with a negative distance.
Fringe (outer edge)
Operator Schema: the zone outside a shape up to distance d, without the shape itself: dilation, then the difference with the original. “Near the lake, but not in it.”
Tools: no single QGIS Tool. Buffer (Tool - QGIS) followed by Difference (Tool - QGIS).
Margin (inner edge)
Operator Schema: the zone inside a shape within distance d of its edge: the original minus its erosion. The forest edge, as opposed to the forest core.
Tools: Buffer (Tool - QGIS) with a negative distance, then Difference (Tool - QGIS) (original minus eroded).
Distance surface
Operator Schema: a raster where every cell holds the distance to the nearest target cell. Unlike a buffer it answers “how far” for every place at once, not just “within d or not”.
Choices to record: cell size (it sets the precision: 10 m cells give distances in 10 m steps); straight-line distance or distance along a network or across a cost surface (this family covers straight-line distance only).
Tools: QGIS Rasterize (Tool - QGIS) to make the targets a raster, then Proximity (Tool - QGIS).
Shortest line
Operator Schema: for each feature in one layer, the shortest straight line to the nearest feature in another layer. It shows where a gap is narrowest.
Choices to record: to the nearest point on the target or to its centroid (nearest point is almost always what is meant); how many neighbours; a maximum distance.
Tools: QGIS Shortest line between features (Tool - QGIS).
Kernel density
Operator Schema: each point is spread over a circle of radius r, weighted towards the centre, and the circles are added into a raster surface: a density without zones.
Choices to record: the radius (it plays the role zones play in an aggregation: a small radius shows streets, a large one districts); the cell size; the kernel shape; raw or scaled values.
Tools: QGIS Heatmap (Tool - QGIS).

operators/selection-(operator-family).title: Selection (Operator family)
operators/selection-(operator-family).content:
Selection Operators keep some features and drop the rest. They are where definitions become data: “larger woodlands” becomes woodland polygons of at least 5 ha, “hedges” becomes GeoDanmark hedges of type Levende.
Part of the Operators families. Used in: Nature content layer (Task), Network gaps and stepping stones (Task), Site screening by criteria (Task), Multi-criteria suitability (Task).
Selection by attribute
Operator Schema: keeps the features whose attributes (or computed values such as area or length) meet a condition.
Choices to record: the condition and the reason for it; what the condition leaves out (features with an empty or unknown value are a data-quality question, not a detail).
Tools: QGIS Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS). Interactive Select by expression does the same on screen, without a new layer.
Selection by location
Operator Schema: keeps the features of one layer that stand in a spatial relation to another layer: intersect, are within, contain, touch, are disjoint.
Choices to record: the relation, and its direction. Intersect includes features that only touch the edge; are within does not. See Spatial relations.
Tools: QGIS Extract by location (Vector selection).

supporting-concepts/basemap.title: Basemap
supporting-concepts/basemap.content: A basemap is a data layer used to provide a backdrop of reference information for other layers in a GIS. It can either provide a geographical context for data visualisation or function as the basis for a visual interpretation for creating new data layers. Basemaps, typically Topographical maps including geographical features such as coastlines, major roads, and political boundaries, are areal(Orthophoto)/satellite imagery.

supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/c.title: Classification for maps
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/c.content:
A choropleth map divides a range of values into classes and gives each class a colour. The class boundaries decide what the map shows as different and what it shows as the same, so they are an analytical choice, not a matter of style. Classifying for a map changes only how data are drawn; turning the data themselves into classes is the reclassify Operator (Conversion and data management).
Used in: Comparable choropleth maps (Task), Distance to habitat (Task).









































MethodHow the boundaries are setGood forWatch outEqual intervalthe range cut into equal stepsvalues spread evenly; easy to readone extreme value leaves most classes emptyQuantile (equal count)the same number of areas in each classranking areasvery different values can share a class; boundaries change with the dataNatural breaks (Jenks)boundaries in the gaps of the datashowing clusters in one datasetboundaries are specific to the dataset, so two maps get different classesStandard deviationsteps of one standard deviation from the meanshowing above and below averagereaders must know what the mean isManual (fixed)boundaries you set, e.g. round numberscomparing maps, or meaningful thresholdsyou must justify them
Classes shared between maps
Two or more maps of the same variable use the same class boundaries, so the same colour means the same value on every map.
Choices to record: how the shared boundaries were found, e.g. round numbers covering the range of all maps together, or quantiles of the pooled values. A method computed separately for each map (quantiles or natural breaks per map) makes the maps look alike even where the values differ.
Tools: QGIS Graduated symbology (Tool - QGIS) with Mode set and classes edited by hand, then the same style loaded on the other layers.
Missing and unreliable values
Areas without a value (no points) or with too few points to trust get their own class, shown in a neutral colour and named in the legend, e.g. “fewer than 20 dwellings”.
Tools: QGIS Rule-based or Categorized symbology on an expression; see Comparable choropleth maps (Recipe - QGIS).

supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/m.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data Visualisation/Map design and concepts/Map Types/General-purpose Map.md
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/m.title: General-purpose Map
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/m.content:
A general-purpose map, also known as a reference map, provides a broad overview of geographical features and is designed to give users a sense of the spatial context of an area. These maps serve as a foundational layer, often used as a Basemap in a GIS project to support more specific geographic data or thematic maps. By providing essential information like roads, water bodies, terrain, and place names, general-purpose maps help users understand the geographic framework within which other spatial information is analysed.
Common Uses of General-Purpose Maps
General-purpose maps are widely used in GIS and cartography as basemaps for various purposes:

Setting Context: These maps provide the necessary spatial context for overlaying thematic data, such as population density, land use, or environmental conditions.
Navigation and Location: In urban areas, they serve as a reference for navigating through cities, understanding infrastructure, and visualizing proximity between features.
Complementing Thematic Maps: They serve as the background for more specific or detailed thematic maps that focus on particular variables, like flood risks or demographic data.

Types of General-Purpose Maps by Area Type


Urban Areas:

In densely populated areas, it is common to use OpenStreetMap (OSM) as the general-purpose map. OSM offers detailed information on streets, buildings, and services, making it ideal for urban navigation, infrastructure planning, and service location analysis.
Google Maps and other proprietary maps also function in this role, often including business information, transportation networks, and real-time data, which enhance urban mapping.



Rural Areas and Countryside:

In more rural or natural settings, a Topographical maps is often a more appropriate general-purpose map. Topographic maps focus on elevation, natural landforms, water bodies, and terrain features, making them invaluable in areas where natural geography is more relevant than man-made structures.
These maps are widely used for hiking, rural planning, and land management, where detailed terrain understanding is crucial.



Small Areas or Large-Scale Maps:

When working with small areas at a large scale, such as individual plots of land, it is common to use an orthophoto as a reference. While orthophotos (geometrically corrected aerial or satellite imagery) are not strictly considered maps, they provide an accurate visual representation of the landscape and built environment. This makes them particularly useful in fields like environmental monitoring, urban development, or detailed site analysis.
Orthophotos allow users to see actual structures, vegetation, and natural features as they appear in the real world, providing a more realistic background than abstracted maps.



Choosing the Right Basemap
The choice of a general-purpose map or reference map depends on several factors:

Scale: In large-scale maps (small geographic areas with high detail), orthophotos or detailed vector data from sources like OSM may be more appropriate. In small-scale maps (large geographic areas with less detail), topographical maps or simpler vector maps are more useful.
Purpose: For navigation, urban planning, or infrastructure analysis, OSM or other urban-focused maps are typically better. For environmental analysis or rural planning, topographical maps are more relevant.
Clarity and Precision: General-purpose maps are typically abstracted to some degree to make information clearer. However, when precise real-world representation is needed, orthophotos may provide more valuable information.

Orthophotos as a Special Case
While orthophotos are not traditional maps, they are frequently used as basemaps because they provide a photographic representation of the area. They combine the visual accuracy of aerial photography with the geometric accuracy of maps, making them especially useful for high-detail work where precise visualization is required. In situations like land surveying or urban development, an orthophoto may be the best way to visually represent the real-world environment.
Conclusion
General-purpose maps, whether they are detailed urban street maps like OpenStreetMap, topographical maps for rural areas, or orthophotos for precise visualization, play a critical role in providing the geographical context necessary for deeper geographic analysis. They serve as foundational layers in many GIS projects, helping users situate their data within a known and understandable spatial framework. Choosing the right general-purpose map depends on the specific needs of the project, including the area of interest, the scale, and the purpose of the analysis.

supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/m.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data Visualisation/Map design and concepts/Projection.md
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/m.title: Projection
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/m.content:
Projections are a fundamental component of a Coordinate Reference System (CRS) and play a crucial role in the design and interpretation of maps. When we represent the curved surface of the Earth on a flat map, we use a projection to transform geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) into Cartesian coordinates (x and y) on a plane. This transformation is necessary for creating maps, but it also introduces distortions that must be carefully managed depending on the purpose of the map.
What is a Projection?
A projection is a mathematical operation that converts the three-dimensional surface of the Earth (or any other celestial body) into a two-dimensional plane. This process allows us to represent the curved surface of the Earth on flat maps, which can be used in various applications, from navigation to thematic mapping.
The Role of Projections in a Coordinate Reference System
A Coordinate Reference System (CRS) consists of two main components:

Datum: A model of the Earth that defines the origin and orientation of latitude and longitude lines. It includes the shape and size of the Earth, as well as the position of the coordinate system’s origin.
Projection: The method used to translate geographic coordinates from the Earth’s surface (defined by the datum) onto a flat map.

The projection is essential because the Earth is not flat, and any flat representation of it involves some distortion. These distortions can affect area, shape, distance, and direction. Different projections are designed to minimize these distortions for specific purposes.
Types of Projections
Projections are generally categorized based on what they preserve and what they distort:


Conformal Projections: Preserve local shapes and angles, making them useful for navigational charts and topographic maps. However, they distort area, especially near the poles.

Example: Mercator Projection



Equal-Area Projections: Preserve area, making them suitable for thematic maps where comparing the size of different regions is important. However, they distort shape and distance.

Example: Albers Equal-Area Projection



Equidistant Projections: Preserve distance from a central point or along certain lines. These projections are useful for distance measurements but distort area and shape.

Example: Equirectangular Projection



Azimuthal Projections: Preserve direction from a central point, often used for polar maps and radio signal mapping.

Example: Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area Projection



Compromise Projections: Attempt to minimize distortion in all aspects (area, shape, distance, and direction) but do not fully preserve any one property. These are often used for world maps.

Example: Robinson Projection



Choosing a Projection for Map Design
The choice of projection is a major element in the design of a map and depends on the map’s purpose:

Thematic Maps: If your map’s purpose is to compare areas (e.g., population density, land use), you might choose an equal-area projection.
Navigational Maps: If your map is for navigation, you would typically choose a conformal projection, such as Mercator, which preserves angles and direction.
World Maps: For general world maps, a compromise projection like Robinson or Winkel Tripel is often used to provide a visually pleasing balance of distortions.

Distortion and Trade-offs
Every projection distorts the Earth’s surface in some way. Understanding these distortions is crucial for interpreting the map correctly:

Area Distortion: A map projection may exaggerate the size of regions near the poles or equator.
Shape Distortion: Some projections preserve shapes locally but distort them globally.
Distance Distortion: Distances may be accurate along certain lines (e.g., equator, meridians) but distorted elsewhere.
Direction Distortion: Some projections preserve true directions from a central point, while others distort direction as you move away from this point.

supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/g.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data Visualisation/geometries for spatial data.md
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/g.title: Geometries for Spatial Data
supporting-concepts/data-visualisation/g.content:
When explicitly referencing a location relative to the Earth using coordinates, these coordinates represent simple geometry, such as points, lines, and polygons in 2 (x,y) or 3 (x,y,z) dimensions. While it is also possible to work with time as a dimension, this is typically nor part of the geometry but rather that entities can be represented by different geometries at different times (x,y,z, time).
Before diving deeper into this, it is important to remember that coordinates alone are not enough to explicitly refer to a Location Relative to the Earth; we also need to specify the Coordinate Reference System (CRS).
For a Python-based demonstration of how points, lines, and polygons can be used to represent spatial data, see github.com/Esbern/GIS_demo/blob/main/simplegeodata_plot.ipynb
While the Python demonstration illustrates the essence of geometries for spatial data, Desktop GIS and their underlying data structures add an additional layer of complexity to the set of geometries. The GeoPackage format operates with not less than 10 different geometry types. Geometry types in geopackage database
While the (X,Y,Z) coordinate is the basis for 3D visualisation, the application domains of 3D visualisation and analysis use somewhat different terms from traditional GIS.

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Coordinate reference systems/Coordinate Reference System (CRS).md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: Coordinate Reference System (CRS)
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
Coordinate reference systems define how a given coordinate reference is related to a Location on the Earth. Because of the Earth’s complex shape, continental drift, and long history of mapping, there are literally thousands of different coordinate reference systems (CRS). Fortunately, you will normally only need to deal with a small number of CRSs depending on where and at what scale you are working (Shortlist of Danish, European and Global CRS).
It is common to distinguish between two families of coordinate reference systems (CRS), namely:

Geographic
Projected
Some typical CRSs are:

If you are creating maps over larger areas, one aspect of the CRS that needs to be taken into account is the projection
When working with z data (3D), the CRS also needs to define the baseline (sea level) for this. In this case, we talk about vertical datum.

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Coordinate reference systems/ESPG code.md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: ESPG code
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
A EPSG code is a unique identifier of a Coordinate Reference System (CRS). The reason it is named a ESPG code is that the system of codes was originally developed and maintained by the organisation “European Petroleum Survey Group” (ESPG). This responsibility now rests with the  “International Association of Oil & Gas Producers” (IOGP). While there are some Coordinate Reference Systems with commonly used names such as WGS84, most  Coordinate Reference Systems have long, complex names and it has become common to reference them by their ESPG code. In QGIS, you can, for instance, change the  Coordinate Reference Systems of the map display in the bottom left corner of the user interface

You can explore a Shortlist of Danish, European and Global CRS

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Coordinate reference systems/Shortlist of Danish, European and Global CRS.md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: Shortlist of Danish, European and Global CRS
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
Danish CRS
Almost all public geospatial data is delivered in the CRS named ERTS89 / UTM zone 32. The ESPG code for this CRS is 25832. This is a 2D coordinate system but is also used in most Danish 3D, assuming a vertical datum such as DVR90. For 3D data it is therefor more correct to also specify the vertical datum using a compound CRS such as ESPG 7416, which is ERTS89 / UTM zone 32 + DVR90.

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Coordinate reference systems/vertical datum.md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: vertical datum
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
A vertical datum is a reference surface used as a baseline to measure elevations or depths on the Earth’s surface. It defines zero elevation and serves as a standard for measuring height (elevations) or depth (such as underwater depths). There are two main types of vertical datums:


Tidal Datum
Dansk Normal Nul (DNN): A vertical datum used in Denmark based on mean sea level. It was historically used before being replaced by newer datums.


Geodetic Datum
DVR90 (Danish Vertical Reference 1990): The current official vertical datum in Denmark, based on a precise geoid model.

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Data Formats and Standards/Data Formats and Standards.md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: Data Formats and Standards
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
Note: Data Formats and Standards in Geospatial Data
In the world of geospatial data, data formats and standards play a crucial role in ensuring that data can be stored, shared, and used effectively across different platforms and applications. Understanding the distinction between data formats and standards—and recognizing their importance—is key to working successfully in geospatial domains.
Data Formats vs. Standards


Data Formats:

Definition: A data format refers to the specific way in which data is encoded for storage or transmission. It determines how data is structured and how it can be read by software applications.
Examples:

Shapefile: A widely-used data format developed by Esri for storing vector data (e.g., points, lines, polygons). Although it is a de facto standard due to its widespread use, it is not an open standard.
GeoJSON: An open format based on JSON for encoding a variety of geographic data structures. It is widely supported in web mapping and is an example of an open standard data format.
GeoPackage: An open, compact format based on SQLite that can store raster and vector data in a single file. It is both a data format and an open standard, widely used in GIS applications like QGIS.





Standards:

Definition: A standard is a formalized guideline that defines how data should be structured, accessed, or communicated. Standards ensure interoperability between different systems and software by providing a common framework.
Examples:

ESPG Codes: These codes define coordinate reference systems (CRS) and projections, ensuring that spatial data is aligned correctly when overlaid from different sources.
OGC Standards: Developed by the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) these include data format standards like GML and GeoPackage, as well as service standards like WMS (Web Map Service) and WFS (Web Feature Service).
ISO Standards: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) develops standards that ensure consistency in processes, including geospatial data management. For example, ISO 19115 defines metadata standards for describing geospatial datasets.
Timetable Standards: Standards like GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) and NeTEx (Network Timetable Exchange) provide structured formats for exchanging public transportation schedules, enabling the integration of transit data across different platforms.





The Importance of Standards in Geospatial Data
Standards are essential in the geospatial domain for several reasons:


Interoperability: Standards ensure that data created in one system can be read and used in another, facilitating the seamless exchange of geospatial information. For example, OGC standards like WMS and WFS allow different mapping applications to access and display the same geospatial data over the web.


Data Integrity: By adhering to standards, data producers and users can ensure that their data is accurate, consistent, and trustworthy. This is particularly important for geospatial data, where even small errors can lead to significant misinterpretations.


Scalability: Standards provide a foundation for scaling geospatial systems and applications. As organisations grow and their data needs become more complex, standardised formats and protocols allow them to integrate new data sources and technologies without starting from scratch.


Compliance: Many industries and governments require compliance with specific standards as part of regulatory or operational requirements. For example, adhering to ISO standards for metadata ensures that geospatial data meets international data documentation and quality guidelines.


Examples of Standards and Their Applications


ESPG Codes: Used to specify coordinate reference systems, ensuring that spatial data is accurately projected and aligned when combined from different sources.


OGC Standards:

GML (Geography Markup Language): An XML-based format for encoding geographic information, used for data exchange between different geospatial systems.
GeoPackage: A versatile format that can store both raster and vector data, often used in mobile and desktop GIS applications.
WMS/WFS/WCS: Standards for web services that allow the distribution and access of geospatial data over the internet.



ISO Standards:

ISO 19115: Defines how to document geospatial data, ensuring that datasets are accompanied by clear, standardised metadata.



Timetable Standards:

GTFS: Provides a common format for public transportation schedules and related geographic information, widely used in transit applications.
NeTEx: A more comprehensive standard for exchanging public transportation schedules and related data, used in Europe and beyond.



Conclusion
Understanding the difference between data formats and standards is fundamental for anyone working with geospatial data. While data formats dictate how data is stored and structured, standards provide the necessary guidelines for ensuring that this data can be shared and used effectively across different platforms and applications. Whether you’re dealing with ESPG codes, OGC standards, or ISO guidelines, adhering to these principles is key to maintaining data integrity, ensuring interoperability, and supporting the efficient management of geospatial information. As the geospatial field continues to evolve, the role of standards will only become more critical, especially with the increasing complexity of data and the growing importance of 3D and real-time applications.

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Data Formats and Standards/GTFS.md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification)
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) is a widely adopted data format designed to represent public transportation schedules and associated geographic information. Originally developed by Google in collaboration with the City of Portland’s TriMet agency, GTFS has become the de facto standard for public transit data worldwide, particularly in North America. Its simplicity and ease of use have made it a popular choice for transit agencies, application developers, and GIS professionals.
Key Features of GTFS


Standardized Data Format:
GTFS is a standardised format that uses a series of plain text files (usually in CSV format) to represent various aspects of public transit systems. These files include:

Agency Information: Basic details about the transit agency, including name, URL, and contact information.
Routes: Information about the transit routes, including route names, types (bus, rail, etc.), and descriptions.
Trips: Detailed information on individual trips made along routes, including service schedules and directions.
Stops: Locations where passengers can board or disembark, including coordinates, names, and accessibility information.
Stop Times: The specific times when vehicles are expected to arrive at and depart from each stop.
Calendar: Information on the days and times when services are active, including exceptions for holidays and special events.
Fare Information (Optional): Basic fare details, including ticket prices and payment options.



Simplicity and Accessibility:
One of GTFS’s key strengths is its simplicity. The format is straightforward to implement and use, making it accessible to transit agencies of all sizes, from small local systems to large metropolitan networks. The plain text files can be easily created, edited, and shared, which has led to widespread adoption.


Wide Adoption and Community Support:
GTFS has a large and active community of developers, transit agencies, and organizations that contribute to its ongoing development and support. This community has produced a wealth of tools, libraries, and documentation, making it easier for new users to get started with GTFS.


Integration with Other Tools:
GTFS is supported by a wide range of transit applications, including trip planners, schedule viewers, and mapping services. Major platforms like Google Maps, Apple Maps, and OpenTripPlanner utilize GTFS data to provide public transit information to millions of users worldwide.


Advantages of Using GTFS

Ease of Implementation: GTFS is relatively easy to implement, requiring only a basic understanding of how to structure data in CSV files. This makes it an attractive option for transit agencies looking to share their data without significant technical overhead.
Interoperability: Because GTFS is widely used, it ensures that transit data can be easily integrated into a variety of applications and platforms. This interoperability is crucial for providing consistent and reliable transit information across different services.
Community and Tooling: The strong community support behind GTFS means that users have access to a rich ecosystem of tools and resources, from validation tools that check GTFS feeds for errors to open-source libraries that simplify working with GTFS data.

Challenges and Considerations

Limited Complexity: While GTFS is excellent for basic transit data, it has limitations when it comes to more complex scenarios. For example, GTFS’s handling of fare structures is relatively basic compared to more sophisticated formats like NeTEx.
Static Nature: Traditional GTFS is designed for static schedules and does not natively support real-time updates (although a related specification, GTFS-realtime, addresses this). This can be a limitation for agencies that operate dynamic services or need to provide real-time information to users.
Geographical Limitations: Although GTFS is widely adopted in North America and many other parts of the world, it is less prevalent in Europe, where NeTEx and other standards are more commonly used.

GTFS vs. NeTEx
Compared to NeTEx (Network Timetable Exchange), GTFS is simpler and easier to use, making it suitable for agencies that need to publish basic schedules and route information quickly. NeTEx, on the other hand, is a more complex and feature-rich format that supports advanced features such as detailed fare modelling and flexible service areas. While NeTEx is often used in Europe, GTFS remains the preferred standard in many other parts of the world due to its simplicity and widespread support.

supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.filePath: Supporting concepts/Data and representations/Data Formats and Standards/GeoJSON.md
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.title: GeoJSON
supporting-concepts/data-and-representat.content:
GeoJSON is a widely-used format for encoding a variety of geographic data structures using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON). It is designed to represent simple geospatial features and their non-spatial attributes, making it a popular choice for web services, data exchange, and lightweight geospatial applications.
Key Features of GeoJSON


GeoJSON Structure:

Geometry: GeoJSON supports several geometry types as defined by the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) in the Simple Feature Access (SFA) standard, including Point, Line String, Polygon, MultiPoint, Multiline String, and MultiPolygon`. Each geometry type is represented as a JSON object with specific coordinate data.
Feature: A GeoJSON Feature object represents a spatially bounded entity with a geometry and associated properties (attributes). Each feature is a combination of a geometry and properties stored in a dictionary-like structure.
FeatureCollection: This is a collection of Feature objects, allowing multiple features to be grouped together in a single GeoJSON file.

Example:
{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [
    {
      "type": "Feature",
      "geometry": {
        "type": "Point",
        "coordinates": [12.4924, 41.8902]
      },
      "properties": {
        "name": "Colosseum"
      }
    }
  ]
}


GeoJSON Creation and Editing:

Online Creation: You can create and edit GeoJSON files directly in your web browser using tools like geojson.io. This online tool provides a simple interface for drawing points, lines, and polygons, and it allows you to export the resulting GeoJSON file.
Using QGIS: QGIS, a popular open-source GIS platform, also supports the creation and editing of GeoJSON files. You can import data into QGIS, edit it, and then export it as a GeoJSON file, making it a versatile tool for managing geospatial data.



GitHub and GeoJSON:

Native Support: GitHub natively supports GeoJSON files. When you upload a GeoJSON file to a GitHub repository, it will automatically render the data as an interactive map, allowing viewers to visualize the geospatial data directly within the GitHub interface.



GeoJSON in Web Services:

Exchange Format: GeoJSON is frequently used as an exchange format for simple geospatial data in web services. It is lightweight, easy to parse, and well-suited for web applications.
Example Web Service Call: A typical example of a GeoJSON response from a web service is the following API call:
api.dataforsyningen.dk/adresser

This URL requests all addresses for the municipality of Lolland (code 0360) in Denmark, returning the data in GeoJSON format. This demonstrates how GeoJSON is often used to provide spatial data in a web-friendly format, making it ideal for web mapping applications.



Advantages of GeoJSON

Human-Readable: Like JSON, GeoJSON is human-readable, making it easy to understand and debug.
Lightweight: It is a lightweight format, which is beneficial for web applications where data transfer efficiency is crucial.
Interoperability: GeoJSON is supported by many GIS software packages and web mapping platforms, making it an excellent format for data exchange.
Flexibility: With support for a variety of geometries and the ability to store properties, GeoJSON is versatile for different types of geospatial data.

Conclusion
GeoJSON is a powerful and flexible format for representing simple geospatial data. Its integration with web services, native support in platforms like GitHub, and ease of creation through tools like QGIS and geojson.io make it a go-to format for many geospatial applications. Whether you’re sharing geospatial data on the web or integrating it into a mapping application, GeoJSON provides a straightforward and effective solution.
For more information on the underlying structure, you can refer to the   JSON note that provides a foundational understanding of the JSON format on which GeoJSON is based.
