Datasets: The foundational data that drives the project. This can include geographic features, satellite imagery, demographic information, environmental measurements, and infrastructure details.


Analytical Operations: The processes and methods applied to the datasets to extract meaningful insights. This involves spatial analysis, modeling, data transformation, and other techniques that help address the project’s core questions or objectives.


Visualizations: The creation of maps, charts, and other visual tools that represent the results of the analysis. These visualizations are crucial for communicating findings to stakeholders and supporting decision-making.


Organizational Framework: The structure within which the project operates, defining the project’s scope, resources, and constraints. This framework includes:

Resources: The available resources for the project, such as man-hours, software, hardware, and other necessary tools.
Legislation and Compliance: Legal constraints must be adhered to, such as privacy regulations, data protection laws, and other relevant legislation.
Design and Branding: Constraints on visualisations, often dictated by a design manual to maintain corporate identity and ensure consistency in presentation.
Roles and Responsibilities: The allocation of tasks and responsibilities among team members, ensuring everyone understands their role in the project.
Project Management: The workflows and processes that guide the project from start to finish, ensuring that it stays on track and meets its goals.



The purpose of a GIS project is to address a specific problem or goal, whether it be urban planning, environmental management, resource allocation, or any other spatially related issue. Each project is tailored to the unique needs and context of the organisation undertaking it. The organisational framework ensures that all components of the project, including the technical tools, align with the broader goals, resources, and constraints of the organisation.
When working on any GIS project, one of the key tasks is writing and maintaining a clear Design Rationale, especially if you need to present the project to others or hope to receive feedback from peers.

supporting-concepts/gis.title: GIS
supporting-concepts/gis.content:
There are surprisingly many definitions of the term Geographic Information System (GIS). There are even those that take the acronym GIS to mean Geographic Information Science.
I prefer to define GIS as:
“A collection of typically (computer-based) tools focused on collecting, analysing, visualising, storing, editing and managing Geospatial data”
Often, the tools are organised into a coherent desktop processing environment, such as QGIS and ArcGIS pro. But a GIS can also consist of a programming environment such as JupyterLab, typically in the programming language Python, using a series of common Geospatial Libraries
There are many GISs out there, and Choosing the right processing environment is often a hard job
Closely related to the term GIS are the terms GIS project, which is a project that uses GIS to solve Geospatial problems and Geoinformatics, which is the science of geospatial processing and its application

supporting-concepts/geoinformatics.title: Geoinformatics
supporting-concepts/geoinformatics.content:
Geoinformatics is a term commonly used in Europe to describe the interdisciplinary field that encompasses the collection, analysis, and interpretation of geographic data. While similar to the American term Geographic Information Science (GIScience), geoinformatics carries a slightly broader connotation. Like informatics, it emphasises not only the technical aspects of managing and analysing spatial data but also the application of these techniques within societal contexts.
Geoinformatics integrates various technologies, including GIS, Remote Sensing, and GPS, with computer science and data management to solve real-world problems. It is particularly focused on the practical application of these tools in areas such as urban planning, environmental management, and disaster response, ensuring that geospatial data and analysis contribute directly to decision-making and policy development.

supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.title: Bounding Box
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.content:
A Bounding Box, often abbreviated (BBox), is a fundamental concept in geospatial analysis, commonly used to define the rectangular extent of a geographic area. It is typically aligned with the coordinate axes, making it a convenient tool for tasks like clipping, extracting, and querying spatial data efficiently. The bounding box is the simplest form of what we might call Envelope Geometries—a family of geometric shapes that enclose a set of points or features in space.
Bounding Box: The Default Case
When we refer to a bounding box, we usually mean the axis-aligned bounding box . This is a rectangle (or rectangular prism in 3D) that is defined by the minimum and maximum coordinates along each axis of the coordinate system:

Minimum X (min_x): The smallest x-coordinate (longitude).
Minimum Y (min_y): The smallest y-coordinate (latitude).
Maximum X (max_x): The largest x-coordinate (longitude).
Maximum Y (max_y): The largest y-coordinate (latitude).

This box is parallel to the coordinate system axes, which makes operations like clipping and spatial indexing straightforward and computationally efficient.

The hatched area is the axis-aligned bounding box containing all addresses of the municipality of Lolland, Denmark calculate using the Coordinate Reference System (CRS) WGS84 ESPG code 4326
Coordinate System Dependency
It’s important to note that an axis-aligned bounding box is dependent on the Coordinate Reference System (CRS) in which it is calculated. A bounding box defined in one CRS will not align with a bounding box calculated in a different CRS. If you reproject your spatial data to another CRS, the bounding box must be recalculated to align with the new coordinate axes. This dependency is crucial to consider when working with geospatial data that spans different coordinate systems.
**Envelope Geometries
While the bounding box is the simplest and most commonly used envelope geometry, it is part of a broader set of geometric operations designed to enclose spatial features. These include:


Convex Hull: The smallest convex shape that can contain all points in a dataset. Unlike the bounding box, the convex hull can take on a variety of shapes that conform more closely to the actual distribution of the points.


Minimum Bounding Circle: The smallest circle that can encompass all points in a dataset. This is useful in cases where a circular or radial boundary is more appropriate.


Minimum Bounding Rectangle (Rotating Rectangle): A bounding box that is not necessarily aligned with the coordinate axes but instead rotates to fit the data more tightly, minimizing the area of the rectangle.


Each of these envelope geometries has its own applications and advantages depending on the spatial analysis task at hand. The axis-aligned bounding box, however, remains the most commonly used due to its simplicity and efficiency in geospatial processing.
Application of Bounding Boxes
Bounding boxes are widely used in GIS for a variety of tasks, including:

Clipping: Restricting data to a specific area by clipping features to the bounding box’s extents.
Spatial Queries: Efficiently querying whether features fall within a given bounding box.
Map View Extents: Defining the visible area on a map, often described by the bounding box coordinates.

Further Notes and Software-Specific Implementations
This note serves as an introduction to the concept of bounding boxes. For specific implementations and calculations, you can explore the linked notes in the note graph, such as:

Calculating Bounding Box in Python (GeoPandas)
Calculating Bounding Box in QGIS
Calculating Bounding Box in PostGIS

Conclusion
A bounding box is the simplest and most widely used form of envelope geometry, crucial for efficient geospatial analysis and operations. While it is often the default choice for tasks like clipping and querying, understanding it as part of a broader family of envelope geometries opens up a range of possibilities for more sophisticated spatial analysis. By recognizing the bounding box as a special case within this family, GIS professionals can better choose the appropriate geometry for their specific needs. Additionally, always consider the coordinate system dependency when working with bounding boxes across different CRS, as this can significantly impact your spatial analysis.

supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.filePath: Supporting concepts/Geospatial Analysis/Modifiable areal unit problem.md
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.title: Modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP)
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.content:
When point data are aggregated to areas, the result depends on the areas chosen. The same dwellings, people or observations give different values, different patterns and different conclusions when they are summarised by districts, by neighbourhoods or by a grid. This dependence is the modifiable areal unit problem: modifiable because the areas could have been drawn otherwise, and a problem because the analysis rarely says so.
Related: Aggregating points to zones (Task), Aggregation (Operator family). Worked example: Share of rented dwellings in Copenhagen (Example).
Two effects

The scale effect: smaller areas give a wider spread of values. Large areas average out differences, so a few districts look alike and many small areas do not.
The zoning effect: areas of the same size but with different borders give different results. Moving a grid by half a cell, or redrawing districts, changes the values without changing the data.


In Copenhagen the share of dwellings that are rented is 75.5 % for the city as a whole. Across 10 districts (bydele) it ranges from 65 to 87 %, across 400 roder from 3 to 99 %, and across 250 m grid cells from 0 to 100 %. The standard deviation of the shares rises from 0.07 for bydele to 0.13 for kvarterer, 0.19 for roder and 0.30 for 250 m cells. Moving the 1,000 m grid by 500 m changes the number of cells with at least 50 dwellings from 103 to 99 and the lowest share from 0 to 5 %.
Never average averages upwards
Counts and sums can be added from small areas to a larger area that contains them. Means, shares, medians and densities cannot. A plain mean of the small areas’ values gives every area the same weight, whether it holds 50 dwellings or 2,000.

The roder fit exactly inside the bydele, yet averaging the roder’s shares gives the wrong bydel share in eight of ten bydele, by up to 5 points (Brønshøj-Husum: 59.6 % instead of 64.6 %). For the whole city the mean of the roder shares is 74.2 % against the true 75.5 %.
Do it this way instead:

Shares and means: add up the parts and divide again: share rented in a bydel = the sum of rented dwellings over its roder / the sum of all dwellings over its roder.
Densities: add up the counts and add up the areas, then divide.
Medians and other percentiles: they cannot be built from the parts; aggregate the points again.

The ecological fallacy
An area’s value describes the area, not the people or dwellings in it. A neighbourhood with 50 % rented dwellings can be a mix of rented and owned buildings, or two homogeneous halves. Reading individual behaviour off area averages is the ecological fallacy.
What to do about it

Say which areas a map uses, and why they fit the question.
Try a second set of areas, or a grid, before drawing conclusions; a pattern that survives a change of areas is a stronger finding.
Show areas with too few observations as such, rather than as values.
Treat a kernel density as no escape: its radius plays the role the areas played, and a small radius and a large one give two different cities.

supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.title: Multi-criteria analysis
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.content:
Most planning questions have more than one answer that matters at the same time. A site for new housing should be near transport, spare the heritage, keep green space within reach and use land that has room for more. Multi-criteria analysis (MCA) is the family of methods for combining such criteria into one decision about places: which areas qualify, or how they rank. In GIS it goes back to the overlay maps of landscape planning (McHarg, Design with Nature, 1969), and it was formalised as GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis (Malczewski, GIS and Multicriteria Decision Analysis, 1999).
Related: Scoring criteria (Task), Site screening by criteria (Task), Multi-criteria suitability (Task), Attribute calculation (Operator family). Worked examples: Sites for new housing near stations in Copenhagen (Example), Densification priorities in Copenhagen by multi-criteria analysis (Example).
The parts of an analysis








































PartWhat it isExampleAlternativesthe units being judged: parcels, grid cells, districtsCopenhagen’s 33,818 parcelsConstraintscriteria that rule a unit in or out, with no degreesno listed building on the parcelFactorscriteria that make a unit more or less suitabledistance to a stationScoreseach factor on a common scale, with a direction: high is good100 at the station, 0 beyond 1,200 mWeightshow much each factor counts against the othersstation 0.4, heritage 0.2Decision rulehow scores and weights are combineda weighted sum, then the top 100
Constraints and factors are the same data used in two ways. Distance to a station can be a constraint (within 600 m or out) or a factor (the nearer, the better). The choice between them is the first decision of the analysis.
Decision rules and compensation
The rules differ in how far a good score on one criterion can make up for a bad score on another:

Boolean overlay (sieve mapping, screening): every criterion is a constraint. A unit qualifies only if it passes all of them. Nothing compensates: a unit that fails one criterion is out, however good it is otherwise. See Site screening by criteria (Task).
Weighted linear combination: every criterion is a factor, scored and weighted, and the weighted scores are added. Compensation is full: a very good score can make up for a very bad one. See Multi-criteria suitability (Task).
Ordered weighted averaging (OWA) lies between the two. Besides the weight of each criterion, it weights each unit’s scores by their order, from its worst to its best. With all the order weight on the worst score it behaves like a Boolean AND; with all of it on the best, like an OR; with equal order weights, like the weighted sum.

In practice the rules are combined: constraints first, as a screening, then a weighted sum of the factors on what is left.
Scores
Criteria come in metres, square metres, classes and counts. Before they can be added they must be on one scale, and every way of getting there is a decision: a linear scale, a threshold, a percentile rank, a lookup table for classes. The rescaling also changes how much each criterion counts. A factor spread over 0–100 outweighs one spread over 0–5, whatever their weights say. See Scoring criteria (Task).
Held-out units. Where a criterion has no meaning for a unit (land per address on a parcel that is all road), or its value is unknown, the score is NULL, not 0 or 100. An arbitrary extreme value looks like a real score: it takes the top or the bottom of the ranking, and it moves the maximum, mean and spread that the other units are scaled by. Filling in the mean is no neutral way out either: it shrinks the spread and claims that unknown units are average. Which treatment is right is a policy question the data cannot answer, so it is recorded in the Design Rationale.
Weights
Weights carry the priorities of the analysis, and so its politics. The common ways to set them are:

direct rating: points shared out over the criteria, so that they add up to 1 or 100;
ranking: the criteria put in order, and the weights derived from the order;
pairwise comparison: each pair of criteria compared (“station proximity is moderately more important than green space”), and the weights computed from the comparisons, as in the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP; Saaty, 1980), which also measures how consistent the comparisons are.

Whatever the method, write down whose priorities the weights express. Two sets of weights for two points of view give two scenarios, and the comparison between them is often the most useful result.
Sensitivity
A ranking is only as firm as its least certain choice. Change one weight, one threshold or the rescaling and see how much the top selection changes: units that stay at the top under every variant are robust, and units that appear in one variant only depend on that choice. Report the effective weights next to the nominal ones (see Multi-criteria suitability (Task), step 7), and record every choice in the Design Rationale.
What MCA cannot do
MCA makes a decision explicit; it does not make it right. The criteria are those someone chose and the data could provide. A criterion with no data (soil contamination, noise, ownership, existing plans) has a weight of zero without anyone deciding so. And a high rank says that a unit is better than the others under these criteria, not that it is good.

supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.title: Spatial relations
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.content:
A spatial relation (or spatial predicate) is a yes-or-no question about two geometries: does A contain B? Do they touch? Selection by location, summary by location and every join by location depend on one. The relations are defined in the OGC Simple Features standard, and the same set appears, with nearly the same names, in most GIS software: as tick boxes in QGIS, as functions in spatial SQL (ST_Intersects, ST_Contains, … in PostGIS and in GeoPackage/SpatiaLite), as predicate= in GeoPandas. ArcGIS’s Select Layer By Location uses its own names and adds some, such as have their center in.
Interior, boundary and exterior
Each relation is defined by how the interior, boundary and exterior of A and B meet (the dimensionally extended nine-intersection model, DE-9IM).

























GeometryInteriorBoundaryPointthe point itselfnoneLinethe line without its two end pointsthe two end pointsPolygonthe area inside the outlinethe outline
Everything else is the exterior. The boundary causes most surprises: a point lying exactly on a polygon’s outline is not inside it.
The relations



























































QGISSQL”A … B” is true whenDirectionintersectST_IntersectsA and B have at least one point in common, interior or boundarysymmetricdisjointST_DisjointA and B have no point in common: the opposite of intersectsymmetriccontainST_Containsno part of B lies outside A, and their interiors meetA contains B = B is within Aare withinST_Withinno part of A lies outside B, and their interiors meetA is within B = B contains AequalST_EqualsA and B are the same shape: each lies within the othersymmetrictouchST_TouchesA and B meet only at their boundaries; their interiors do not meetsymmetricoverlapST_OverlapsA and B have the same dimension (two polygons, two lines), share part of their interiors, and each also has a part outside the othersymmetriccrossST_Crossestheir interiors meet, but in something of lower dimension: a line passing in and out of a polygon, two lines crossing at a pointsymmetric
Spatial SQL also has ST_Covers and ST_CoveredBy: like contain and within, but a B lying only on A’s boundary counts too. The QGIS dialogs do not offer them.
Reading the QGIS dialog
QGIS’s location tools read as a sentence: [features in the first layer] [relation] [features in the second layer]. In Join attributes by location (summary):

Join to features in roder — where the features contain — by comparing to boliger

asks for each rode which dwellings it contains. Ticking are within instead asks whether a rode lies within a dwelling point. That is never true, so every rode gets a count of 0, without any warning. Ticking several boxes means or: a feature is matched if any of the ticked relations holds.



































First layerSecond layerRelationzonespointscontain or intersectpointszonesare within or intersectzoneslines (roads, streams)intersect: any part in the zone; contain: the whole line in the zone; cross: passes through the zone’s outlinezonespolygons (buildings, fields)intersect: any part in the zone; contain: wholly in the zone; overlap: partly in the zonepolygonspolygons of the same layertouch: the neighbours
Points on a border
Two square zones, A and B, side by side, and four points: one inside A, one on the border between A and B, one on A’s outer edge and one outside both. In QGIS 4.2.2, Join attributes by location (summary) with the zones as the first layer gives:



































Pointintersectcontaintouchinside AAA—on the border between A and BA and BneitherA and Bon A’s outer edgeAnoneAoutside both———
So intersect counts a point on a shared border in both zones, and contain counts it in none: either way the counts no longer add up to the number of points. Touch finds exactly the points on borders, which makes it a check.
With real coordinates, exact border positions are rare. None of Copenhagen’s 349,743 dwelling address points lies on the border of a rode, kvarter or bydel, and intersect and contain give the same counts (example data). The choice matters when points lie on lines by construction: points snapped to a road centre line or a plot boundary, or coordinates rounded to whole metres counted in a grid whose edges lie on whole metres.
Polygons across zone borders
A building or field that crosses a zone border intersects and overlaps both zones and is within neither. Counted with intersect it is counted twice; with contain it is not counted at all. The choices:

assign it to one zone: the zone it overlaps most (Join attributes by location, one-to-one, largest overlap), or the zone that contains a point placed inside it;
split it at the border and share its values by area (overlay, then area-weighting);
count it in every zone it touches, and say that the totals add up to more than the whole.

Coordinates must match exactly
Equal and touch hold only when coordinates match exactly. Two layers digitised separately rarely share their boundaries exactly. Neighbours that should touch either overlap by a few centimetres or leave a thin gap, so touch finds nothing and overlap finds pairs that are really neighbours. A tolerance helps: in SQL ST_DWithin, in QGIS a small buffer or a distance-based tool.
Related: selection by location, summary by location, Modifiable areal unit problem.

supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.filePath: Supporting concepts/Geospatial Analysis/Square and hexagonal grids.md
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.title: Square and hexagonal grids
supporting-concepts/geospatial-analysis/.content:
A grid divides space into cells of equal size and shape, and is used as a set of zones for aggregating data (see Statistical Units for the predefined grids). Only three regular shapes tile a plane: triangles, squares and hexagons. Squares and hexagons are the two in practical use, and the choice between them matters.
Neighbours
In a square grid a cell has two kinds of neighbour: four that share an edge, and four that touch it only at a corner. The corner neighbours are about 1.41 times as far away, centre to centre, as the edge neighbours. Whether two cells are “next to each other” therefore depends on a rule (rook or queen contiguity), and distances along the grid differ by direction.
In a hexagonal grid all six neighbours share an edge with the cell, and all six are at the same distance, centre to centre. There is only one kind of neighbour, so analyses of neighbourhood, movement, connectivity and spatial clustering treat every direction alike.
Shape and edges
A hexagon is closer to a circle than a square is: for the same area it has a shorter boundary, and every point in it is nearer its centre. A cell’s value is then less influenced by what lies in its corners, and fewer points fall near a cell edge. Patterns that do not follow a north–south and east–west direction, such as coastlines, roads and valleys, look less blocky on a hexagonal map.
Why squares are still the standard

They nest. Four 500 m squares make a 1 km square, and a hundred 1 km squares a 10 km square. Statistics can be published at several resolutions that add up exactly. Hexagons do not nest: a large hexagon cannot be made of small ones.
They are the official grids. Danmarks Statistik’s grid statistics use the Danish square grid (Det Danske Kvadratnet), and Eurostat’s use the European square grid. Data published on those grids can only be compared with data on the same squares.
They match rasters. A raster is a square grid; square zones line up with raster cells, hexagons never do.
A cell can be named from a coordinate. In the Danish grid a cell’s name is its lower-left corner, truncated to the cell size, so any coordinate gives its cell without an overlay.

Choosing





























QuestionGridResults to compare with official statistics or other studiesthe predefined square grid (Danish or European), aligned exactlySeveral resolutions that must add upsquare, nestedCombining with raster datasquare, on the raster’s gridNeighbourhood, movement, connectivity, clusteringhexagonA map whose pattern should not be shaped by the cellshexagon
Whichever shape is chosen, its size and origin are choices too: moving the same grid half a cell gives different values (the zoning effect of the Modifiable areal unit problem).

supporting-concepts/geospatial-data.title: Geospatial data
supporting-concepts/geospatial-data.content:
According to the ISO standard 19109:2015, Geographic (geospatial) data is defined as data with implicit or explicit reference to a location relative to the Earth.
In this context, we can think of the “data” as the “what” and the reference to a location relative to the Earth as the where. The when is also generally considered to be part of the data.
Implicit Reference to a Location Relative to the Earth.
While this formulation seems strange, it is rather simple. Implicit reference means that the data refers to a location on Earth using some name or code that refers to a location that is explicitly defined somewhere else.
For instance, on the website of the Danish Statistical Office, we can find data describing the number of Contacts with a doctor covered by public health insurance by sex, region and time.  In this data set, the location relative to the Earth is given implicitly by the name of the municipality while the data is the columns Male, female and Year.





























MinicipalityMalefemaleYearCompehagen223674336934622023Frederiksberg3936036811492023…
For implicit referencing to work, there must be some standards for how different typical geometries, such as countries, municipalities, etc., are referenced. This is done through national and international  spatial coding standards.
Explicit Reference to a Location Relative to the Earth
The following text is a geojson specification of the location of my office at the campus.
{
“type”: “Feature”, “properties”: { “What”: “Office” }, “geometry”: { “type”: “Point”, “coordinates”: [ 12.1413, 55.652] }
}`
In this geojson text, the location relative to the Earth is given explicitly by the coordinates (Longitude and Latitude ). To ensure a correct reference relative to the Earth the coordinates alone, we also need to specify the coordinate system used for the coordinates. In the context of geospatial data, such a coordinate system is named a Coordinate Reference System (CRS).
In the above example, the coordinates represent a point in 2D, but more complex geometry types (lines and polygons) and higher dimensions can be used.  While terms like Point, Line(Sting) and [Polygon] seem well-defined, you quickly run into more exotic terms such as “MultiCurve” or “MultiPoint”. In order to ensure the Interoperability and Reusability of data (the I and R of Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC)‘s FAIR principles)
While Geospatial data typically consist of 0, 1 and 2-dimensional objects (Points, lines and polygons), 3D objects are beginning to appear, especially in geospatial data for urban planning (for more, see the note on CityGML) it is, however,, important to be clear that there is a distinction between the dimensions of the space and the dimension of the objects. The official Danish infrastructure data (GeoDanmark)is 0, 1 and 2D objects but represented in a 3D space, i.e. using XYZ coordinates. For more information on this topic, see   Dimensions in Geospatial Data.
When it comes to working with more than 2D geometries, there are especially three use cases to take note of, namely:

Surface  and Terrain models
Buildings
Buildings and tunnels

A emerging area is the incorporation of real-time sensor dat in a geospatial context combining real-time data and 3D geospatial data comes close to the concept of a Digital Twin

supporting-concepts/photogrammetry.title: Photogrammetry
supporting-concepts/photogrammetry.content:
Photogrammetry is the science and technology of obtaining reliable information about physical objects and the environment through the process of recording, measuring, and interpreting photographic images. It involves the use of photographs (often taken from the air or ground) to create maps, 3D models, and other representations of objects or spaces.
Photogrammetry has evolved from simple photo interpretation to advanced techniques involving digital images and software algorithms. There are two primary methods of photogrammetry:
Stereoscopic Photogrammetry
Stereoscopic Photogrammetry or Stereoimage Interpretation involves capturing two or more images of the same object or area from different angles. By analysing these images simultaneously, usually with the aid of stereoscopes, a 3D model or map of the area can be created. This technique leverages the principle of stereopsis (the perception of depth) and is widely used in topographic mapping, architecture, and archaeology.
Structure from Motion (SfM):
Structure from Motion is a more modern approach that uses multiple overlapping images taken from different viewpoints. Unlike traditional stereoscopic methods, SfM does not require precise camera positions or angles. The images are processed using computer algorithms to automatically identify and match features across images, allowing the generation of 3D models and point clouds. This method is particularly popular in digital photogrammetry for creating detailed 3D reconstructions of landscapes, objects, and buildings.

supporting-concepts/relational-database-.title: Relational Database (Concept)
supporting-concepts/relational-database-.content:
A relational database is a type of database that organizes data into tables, also known as relations. Each table consists of rows and columns, where:

Tuples (or rows) represent individual records in the table.
Attributes (or columns) define the properties or fields of the data stored in the table.

Tables (Relations)
A table is the primary structure within a relational database where data is stored. Each table contains a set of attributes, and each tuple in the table represents a single data entry or record.
For example, a table representing a collection of users might look like this:























UserIDFirstNameLastNameEmail1AliceSmithalice@email.com2BobJohnsonbob@email.com
In this example:

The attributes are UserID, FirstName, LastName, and Email.
Each tuple corresponds to a single user, containing information across those attributes.

Primary Keys
A primary key is an attribute (or a set of attributes) that uniquely identifies each tuple in a table. This ensures that no two rows in the table have the same primary key, making each record unique. In the example above, the UserID attribute is the primary key because it uniquely identifies each user.
Foreign Keys
A foreign key is an attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, establishing a relationship between the two tables. Foreign keys help maintain referential integrity between related data stored in different tables.
For instance, if we have another table called Orders, which tracks orders placed by users, it might look like this:























OrderIDUserIDProductQuantity1011Laptop11022Smartphone2
In this table:

OrderID is the primary key for the Orders table.
UserID is a foreign key that refers to the UserID primary key in the Users table, establishing a link between the two tables. This link allows us to associate orders with the users who placed them.

Relationships Between Tables
Tables in a relational database can be related in various ways, including:

One-to-one relationships: Each tuple in one table corresponds to one tuple in another.
One-to-many relationships: A single tuple in one table relates to multiple tuples in another (e.g., a user placing multiple orders).
Many-to-many relationships: Tuples in one table can relate to multiple tuples in another and vice versa. This usually requires an intermediary table.

Database Management Systems (DBMS)
A Database Management System (DBMS) is the software that manages the creation, storage, and querying of relational databases. DBMSs offer various features that enhance data management, including:

User Management: Most DBMSs include user management features, allowing administrators to control access to the database. This involves assigning roles and permissions, enabling multi-user collaboration, and maintaining data security.
Scalability: Relational databases are designed to handle increasing amounts of data efficiently. Some DBMSs are optimized for large-scale, multi-user applications, while others are suited for smaller, single-user projects.

Server-based vs. Serverless Databases
Relational databases come in two main types based on how they are deployed and accessed:


Server-based Databases: These databases require a dedicated server to host the DBMS. They are designed for multi-user environments and can handle large amounts of data with high availability, performance, and security. Examples include:

PostgreSQL: A powerful, open-source, server-based relational database that supports advanced features such as geospatial data processing (with the PostGIS extension).
MySQL and Microsoft SQL Server: Other examples of server-based relational DBMSs that offer enterprise-level features, including user management and scalability.

Server-based databases are ideal for large applications, such as web platforms, multi-user systems, or any scenario where scalability, performance, and concurrency are critical.


Serverless (Embedded) Databases: These databases do not require a dedicated server to run. They are typically embedded within an application and are designed for local, single-user environments. A key example is:

SQLite: A serverless, lightweight database that is embedded in applications. It is commonly used in mobile apps and local desktop applications. SQLite is also the foundation for the GeoPackage format, widely used in GIS applications like QGIS to store geospatial data in a portable, self-contained file.

Serverless databases are often used in scenarios where simplicity and portability are more important than scalability. They are easy to deploy and ideal for local data storage.


SQL
The structure of relational databases is managed and queried through Structured Query Language (SQL). SQL is the standard language for interacting with relational databases, allowing users to insert, query, update, and manage data. While this note focuses on the core concepts of relational databases, a more detailed exploration of SQL, especially in the context of geospatial processing, will be provided in a separate note. That note will also discuss how standard SQL can be extended with spatial operators for handling geographic data.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/digit.filePath: Supporting concepts/Remote sensing/Digital images and reflectance.md
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/digit.title: Digital images and reflectance
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/digit.content:
Chapter 3 of Remote sensing.
Pixels
A digital image is a raster: a grid of pixels (picture elements) in rows and columns. Each pixel covers an area on the ground and has a value and an address, its row and column. The value is the average for the whole area the pixel covers.
The geographic position of each pixel follows from its row and column, given the imaging geometry and the satellite’s orbit. Making that link is geometric correction and georeferencing: the image is corrected for distortions (from the Earth’s rotation, or a sensor not looking straight down) and fitted to a map projection, often with ground control points whose true coordinates are known. Satellite images are normally delivered already corrected and projected: Sentinel-2 in UTM, for Denmark zone 32N (EPSG:32632).
Digital numbers and radiometric resolution
The sensor records the radiation as a digital number (DN), an integer stored with a fixed number of bits. The number of bits is the radiometric resolution: 8 bits give values from 0 to 255 (2⁸ − 1), 12 bits from 0 to 4095. The measured radiation is scaled to fit that range.
From digital numbers to reflectance
A DN only means something together with the sensor’s calibration. In a radiometrically calibrated image the DN is converted to radiance with coefficients specific to the sensor:

Lλ = a × DN + b

where Lλ is the spectral radiance in W m⁻² sr⁻¹ µm⁻¹ (sr, the steradian, is the unit of solid angle: it is to the surface of a sphere what the radian is to the circumference of a circle).
Radiance depends on how much light there was. To compare images taken under different light, radiance is turned into reflectance, the fraction of the incoming sunlight that is reflected (as with a handheld spectrometer). That needs the sun’s irradiance in the band, Eλ (W m⁻² µm⁻¹), the sun’s zenith angle θs, and the Earth–sun distance d in astronomical units (close to 1, varying over the year):

r = π × Lλ × d² / (Eλ × cos θs)

Top-of-atmosphere and surface reflectance

Top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance uses only the sun’s position and the Earth–sun distance, from the image’s metadata. It still contains the atmosphere’s effects: haze, and absorption by gases. Sentinel-2 Level-1C products are TOA reflectance.
Surface reflectance, also called bottom-of-atmosphere (BOA) reflectance or atmospherically corrected images, also removes the atmosphere’s effects, estimated from the image itself, weather data and terrain. It is the best estimate of what the surface reflects, and the right choice for comparing places and dates and for indices. Sentinel-2 Level-2A products are surface reflectance.

How reflectance is stored
Sentinel-2 stores reflectance as 16-bit integers, reflectance × 10,000, so 0.0323 is stored as 323. Since processing baseline 04.00 (January 2022) the products from ESA have an offset of 1000 added, so negative values from the correction can be stored:

reflectance = (DN − 1000) / 10,000

Where the data come from decides what has been done already:

From the Copernicus Browser’s analytical download the values are already harmonised: as 32-bit floats they are reflectance (0–1), as 16-bit integers reflectance × 10,000, with no offset.
From the original product (.SAFE), the offset must be subtracted.
Other archives differ, and their metadata do not always match the values. Look at the values: summer vegetation has a red reflectance of about 0.02–0.05 and a NIR reflectance of about 0.3–0.5.

A wrong offset makes a vegetation index impossible: NDVI comes out above 1 (see Vegetation index from Sentinel-2 (Recipe - QGIS)).
Multispectral images
A multispectral radiometer measures in several wavelength bands (the name comes from bands of the spectrum). Each band is an image of its own, and together they form a multispectral image with one layer per band.
Sentinel-2 bands







































































































BandNameCentre (nm)PixelUseful forB1Coastal aerosol44360 maerosols, coastal waterB2Blue49010 mwater, soil and vegetation; true colourB3Green56010 mthe green peak of vegetation; true colourB4Red66510 mchlorophyll absorption; true colour; NDVIB5Red edge 170520 mthe steep rise from red to NIR in vegetation: chlorophyll, stressB6Red edge 274020 mas B5B7Red edge 378320 mas B5B8NIR84210 mbiomass, leaf structure; NDVIB8ANarrow NIR86520 mas B8, narrower bandB9Water vapour94560 matmospheric correctionB10SWIR cirrus137560 mthin cirrus clouds (Level-1C only)B11SWIR 1161020 mmoisture of soil and vegetation; snow and cloudB12SWIR 2219020 mmoisture; minerals; burnt areas
Level-2A products also contain a scene classification layer (SCL, 20 m), with a class per pixel from the atmospheric correction: 0 no data, 1 saturated or defective, 2 dark area, 3 cloud shadow, 4 vegetation, 5 not vegetated, 6 water, 7 unclassified, 8 cloud (medium probability), 9 cloud (high probability), 10 thin cirrus, 11 snow or ice. It is the simplest cloud mask.
Landsat 8 and 9 bands
Landsat’s OLI has bands 1 coastal aerosol, 2 blue, 3 green, 4 red, 5 NIR, 6 SWIR 1, 7 SWIR 2 (all 30 m), 8 panchromatic (15 m) and 9 cirrus; TIRS adds 10 and 11, thermal infrared (100 m). Band combinations written for Landsat translate to Sentinel-2 as 2→B2, 3→B3, 4→B4, 5→B8 (or B8A), 6→B11, 7→B12.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/earth.filePath: Supporting concepts/Remote sensing/Earth observation platforms and sensors.md
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/earth.title: Earth observation platforms and sensors
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/earth.content:
Chapter 2 of Remote sensing.
Earth observation satellites
Earth observation satellites monitor land, sea, ocean currents, clouds and much else from space. Compared with other platforms they offer:

coverage of large areas;
frequent, repeated coverage of the same place;
quantitative measurements, from radiometrically calibrated sensors;
processing and analysis that can largely be automated;
a low cost per area covered.

Each satellite and sensor is described by four kinds of resolution: spectral (which wavelength bands it measures), spatial (the ground size of a pixel), temporal (how often it images the same place) and radiometric (how finely it records brightness, see digital numbers).









































Satellite (sensor)Pixel sizeRevisitAccessSentinel-2 A/B/C (MSI)10, 20, 60 m; 13 bandsabout 5 days with two satellites, more often at Danish latitudesfree, Copernicus Browser / Copernicus Data Space EcosystemSentinel-1 (C-band radar)about 10 mabout 6–12 daysfree, as aboveLandsat 8 and 9 (OLI, TIRS)30 m (15 m panchromatic, 100 m thermal)16 days each, 8 days togetherfree, USGS EarthExplorerMODIS (Terra, Aqua)250–1000 mdailyfree, NASACommercial (e.g. Pléiades, WorldView, PlanetScope)about 0.3–5 mdaily or on requestpaid, some free for research
Free imagery can be downloaded from the archives (the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem for Sentinel, which replaced the Copernicus Open Access Hub in 2023; USGS EarthExplorer for Landsat) or processed in the cloud without downloading it (Google Earth Engine, the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem’s own processing services).
Satellite orbits
A satellite follows an elliptical orbit around the Earth. The time one revolution takes is its orbital period. The path it traces on the ground is its ground track; as the Earth rotates beneath it, each revolution traces a different track. Earth observation satellites are usually placed in orbits that repeat their tracks after a fixed interval, the repeat cycle.

Geostationary orbit. A satellite circling above the equator in the direction of the Earth’s rotation, with a period of 24 hours, stays above the same point. It must be about 36,000 km up. It always views the same, very large area, which suits weather satellites.
Near-polar orbit. The orbit is tilted only slightly from the Earth’s axis, so the satellite passes close to the poles and covers nearly the whole Earth in one repeat cycle.
Sun-synchronous orbit. A near-polar orbit at a height chosen so the satellite passes any given latitude at the same local solar time. Images of a place are then taken under the same light, apart from the seasons. Most Earth observation satellites, Sentinel-2 and Landsat among them, use one (Sentinel-2 passes Denmark late in the morning).

Airborne sensors
Sensors mounted on aircraft and drones, looking down or to the side, give images of very high spatial resolution (0.2 m or less). Their coverage is small and their cost per area high, so they are flown for one-time campaigns, whereas satellites monitor continuously. The Danish orthophotos are taken from aircraft.
Handheld spectrometers
Handheld spectrometers such as the FieldSpec measure the reflectance of a surface in the field, for instance from 325 to 1075 nm in 512 channels about 3 nm wide. The instrument measures radiation, which changes with the light conditions, so it is calibrated against a white reference, a surface that reflects (almost) 100 % at all wavelengths:

reflectance = radiation from the target / radiation from the white reference

A dark current measurement removes the signal the instrument produces by itself. Field measurements like these are used to understand satellite images and to develop new indices.
Radar (microwave) sensors
Radar satellites, such as Sentinel-1, work with microwaves, from about a centimetre to a metre. These long waves pass through clouds, whose droplets are far smaller than the wavelength, so radar sees the surface in any weather, day and night.
A radar is an active sensor: it sends out its own pulse and measures what returns, the backscatter. It usually works at a single wavelength, and it locates what it sees from the time the signal takes to return, which is why such satellites are called radar or SAR satellites. Synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) builds up, from the satellite’s movement, the effect of the very long antenna it would otherwise need.
The strength of the backscatter depends on the target:

Surface roughness: a smooth surface (calm water, a road) reflects the pulse away from the sensor and looks dark; a rough surface scatters part of it back.
Volume scattering: a tree canopy or dry soil scatters the pulse within its volume. Objects smaller than the wavelength are almost invisible to the radar.
Water content: wet surfaces reflect more strongly.

Radar also sends and receives in different polarisations (horizontal or vertical). The difference between them shows the orientation of structures, such as upright stems in a field.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/elect.title: Electromagnetic radiation and the atmosphere
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/elect.content:
Chapter 1 of Remote sensing.
Radiation measured by a satellite has travelled a long way: from its source (the sun, or the Earth itself), down through the atmosphere, to a surface that absorbs part of it and reflects the rest, and up through the atmosphere again to the sensor. This chapter follows that path. It ends with the atmosphere, which is a problem when you want to see the surface and the subject when you want to measure the air.
Electromagnetic waves
Remote sensing needs energy that the target reflects or emits: electromagnetic radiation. It consists of an electrical field, which varies in strength perpendicular to the direction the radiation travels, and a magnetic field at right angles to the electrical field. Both travel at the speed of light, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s.
Two properties matter most for remote sensing: the wavelength λ (in metres) and the frequency f (cycles per second). They are related by

c = f × λ

so a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency. Radiation also comes in packets, photons, and the energy of each photon grows with the frequency:

E = h × f = h × c / λ  (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, Planck’s constant)

A photon of blue light carries more energy than one of red light, and much more than one of thermal infrared. That decides what radiation can do when it meets matter: ultraviolet photons can break molecules apart, visible photons can drive photosynthesis, and infrared photons can only make molecules vibrate and rotate, that is, warm them.
The electromagnetic spectrum
The whole range of wavelengths is the electromagnetic spectrum, from gamma rays shorter than an atom to radio waves longer than a building. It is divided into regions by wavelength; the boundaries are approximate, and neighbouring regions overlap.

The electromagnetic spectrum, from long waves on the left to short on the right: whether the radiation gets through the atmosphere (top), its type and wavelength compared with familiar objects, its frequency, and the temperature of a body whose emission peaks at that wavelength. Figure: Inductiveload, NASA, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
The top row shows why only part of the spectrum is useful for observing the Earth: the atmosphere lets through visible light, some infrared and radio waves, and blocks the rest. The bottom row links wavelength to temperature: hot bodies emit short waves, cold bodies long waves (see the next section).
The regions used in remote sensing:








































RegionWavelengthIn remote sensingGamma rays, X-rays< 0.01 µmabsorbed high in the atmosphere; not used for Earth observationUltraviolet (UV)0.01–0.4 µmmostly absorbed by ozone; used to measure ozone and other gasesVisible0.4–0.7 µmreflected sunlight: colour, water, vegetationNear and short-wave infrared (NIR, SWIR)0.7–3 µmreflected sunlight: vegetation, moisture, minerals, and the absorption bands of CO₂ and CH₄Mid- and long-wave infrared3–15 µmradiation emitted by the surface: temperatureMicrowaves1 mm–1 mradar, which sends its own signal and sees through clouds (see radar sensors); also weak natural emission, for soil moisture and sea ice
Units: 1 µm = 0.001 mm = 1,000 nm.
Visible light, about 0.4–0.7 µm, is the narrow band the human eye sees:





































ColourWavelength (µm)Violet0.40–0.43Indigo0.43–0.45Blue0.45–0.50Green0.50–0.57Yellow0.57–0.59Orange0.59–0.61Red0.61–0.70
Infrared, 0.7–300 µm, is divided further:



































RegionWavelength (µm)Near infrared (NIR)0.7–1.5reflected infrared: the infrared part of sunlight reflected by the surfaceShort-wave infrared (SWIR)1.5–3reflected infraredMid-wave infrared (MWIR)3–8thermal infrared: radiation emitted by the surface, from which surface temperature is calculatedLong-wave infrared (LWIR)8–15thermal infraredFar infrared (FIR)> 15
Sources: the sun and the Earth as black bodies
Every body warmer than absolute zero emits radiation. A black body is the ideal case: it absorbs all radiation that falls on it and emits the most a body of its temperature can. Its spectrum depends only on its temperature, as described by Planck’s law:

The spectrum of a black body at 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 K. The black curve is the classical (Rayleigh–Jeans) theory that Planck’s law replaced. Figure: Darth Kule, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
Two rules follow from Planck’s law:

Wien’s displacement law: the wavelength of the peak is inversely proportional to the temperature, λ_max ≈ 2,898 µm K / T. The hotter the body, the shorter the wavelength at which it emits most. A stove plate goes from dark to red to orange as it heats.
Stefan–Boltzmann law: the total energy emitted grows with the fourth power of the temperature, M = σT⁴ (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴). Twice the temperature gives sixteen times the energy.

The sun and the Earth are close enough to black bodies for these laws to explain why remote sensing has two kinds of passive sensor:

Sunlight arriving at the top of the atmosphere (a 5,778 K black body, diluted by the distance to the sun) and radiation emitted by the Earth’s surface (a 288 K black body), calculated from Planck’s law. Both axes are logarithmic.

The sun, at about 5,800 K, peaks at about 0.5 µm, in visible green light. At the top of the atmosphere it delivers about 1,361 W/m², the solar constant.
The Earth, at about 288 K (15 °C), peaks at about 10 µm, in the thermal infrared, and emits about 390 W/m².
The two curves cross at about 4–5 µm. Below that, a sensor sees reflected sunlight; above it, radiation emitted by the surface itself. That is why optical sensors measure reflectance and thermal sensors measure temperature, and why thermal images can be taken at night.

Solar radiation at the surface
The sunlight that reaches the ground is not a smooth black-body curve. On its way down, the atmosphere has absorbed and scattered part of it, and some wavelengths are almost gone:

Sunlight at the top of the atmosphere (yellow) and at sea level (red), with a 5,778 K black body for comparison. The gaps in the red area are absorption bands of ozone, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide. Figure: Robert A. Rohde, Global Warming Art, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
At noon on a clear summer day about 1,000 W/m² reaches the ground; over a year in Denmark, about 1,000 kWh/m². The incoming solar radiation is itself a mapped quantity. It is estimated from geostationary weather satellites, which see the clouds every 15 minutes, and used to plan solar energy (for example the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service’s solar radiation data and the EU’s PVGIS), to model evaporation and crop growth, and to study urban heat.
Spectral reflectance
Radiation that reaches a surface is transmitted, absorbed or reflected. Optical remote sensing is concerned with the reflected part, because that is what the sensor measures. How much is reflected depends on the material and on the wavelength. The reflectance of a material is the fraction of the incoming radiation that it reflects, from 0 (nothing) to 1 (everything). Reflectance across many wavelengths is the material’s spectral signature (see Spectral signatures and vegetation indices).
Reflectance is a ratio: dividing what the surface reflects by what reaches it removes the shape of the solar spectrum, so a surface has the same reflectance in the morning and at noon, in Denmark and in Spain. That is why images are converted to reflectance before they are compared (see Digital images and reflectance).
Radiation and plants: photosynthesis and the red edge
The most important thing radiation does at the Earth’s surface is drive photosynthesis. Plants use light between 0.4 and 0.7 µm, the same band the eye sees, called photosynthetically active radiation (PAR). Its photons have the right energy to excite chlorophyll: ultraviolet photons carry so much energy that they damage cells, and infrared photons carry too little to drive the reaction.
Each part of the leaf’s spectral signature has a physical cause (the absorption spectra of the chlorophylls are shown in the NDVI note):

Blue and red are absorbed. Chlorophyll a and b absorb most strongly around 0.43–0.45 µm (blue) and 0.64–0.68 µm (red). A healthy leaf reflects only a few percent of red light.
Green is absorbed less and partly reflected, which is why leaves look green.
Near infrared is reflected. The photons are of no use for photosynthesis, and absorbing them would only heat the leaf. Instead they are scattered at the boundaries between cell walls and air spaces inside the leaf, the mesophyll, and about half is reflected. Several layers of leaves reflect even more.
The red edge is the steep rise between the two, from about 0.68 to 0.75 µm, where chlorophyll’s absorption stops and the leaf’s scattering takes over.

The red edge is sensitive to the plant’s condition. Its steepest point, the red-edge position, lies at about 0.70–0.73 µm and moves to longer wavelengths as the chlorophyll content rises: in a dense, well-fertilised crop the absorption band is broader and the edge shifts towards the infrared. In stressed, diseased or senescent vegetation, chlorophyll declines, red reflectance rises, near-infrared reflectance falls, and the edge flattens and shifts towards shorter wavelengths. These changes can show up before the plant looks different to the eye.
Sensors and the red edge. A sensor with one red and one near-infrared band, like most older ones, measures on either side of the edge but not on it. Sentinel-2 has three narrow bands on the edge itself: B5 (705 nm), B6 (740 nm) and B7 (783 nm), at 20 m resolution, between red (B4, 665 nm) and near infrared (B8, 842 nm, and B8A, 865 nm). They are used for red-edge indices of chlorophyll and nitrogen (see red-edge indices), which stay sensitive in dense vegetation where NDVI saturates.
Fluorescence. A small part of the light chlorophyll absorbs, about 1–2%, is given off again as a faint red and far-red glow, peaking at about 0.685 and 0.74 µm. This solar-induced fluorescence (SIF) comes from photosynthesis itself rather than from the leaf’s structure, so it says more directly how actively plants are working. It is far weaker than the reflected sunlight and can be measured only in narrow wavelengths where there is almost no sunlight to drown it: absorption lines of the sun’s own atmosphere, and oxygen’s band at 0.76 µm. It is measured by the greenhouse-gas satellites described below, and ESA’s FLEX mission is built for it.
The atmosphere between source and sensor
What the sensor receives
A satellite sensor looking down records a sum of several kinds of radiation:

Sunlight reflected by the surface in the pixel, weakened by the atmosphere twice, on the way down and on the way up. This is usually what we want.
Path radiance: sunlight scattered towards the sensor by the atmosphere before it ever reached the ground. It adds brightness, most in blue, and makes images look hazy.
Light from neighbouring surfaces, scattered into the pixel’s line of sight: a dark lake next to bright fields looks brighter at its edges than it is (the adjacency effect).

To study the surface, the atmosphere’s contribution has to be estimated and removed: atmospheric correction, the step from top-of-atmosphere to surface reflectance (see top-of-atmosphere and surface reflectance). To study the atmosphere, the same physics is used the other way round: the surface is the background, and what the atmosphere has taken out or added is the measurement. Either way, the atmosphere’s two effects, scattering and absorption, have to be told apart from the surface.
Scattering
On its way through the atmosphere radiation is absorbed or scattered by gases and particles. Absorption turns the radiation’s energy into energy of the molecules; scattering sends it off in all directions. Both take energy out of the beam.

Rayleigh scattering is caused by gas molecules and particles much smaller than the wavelength. It depends strongly on wavelength, roughly as 1/λ⁴: blue light at 0.45 µm is scattered about four times as much as red at 0.65 µm. It is why the sky is blue, and why sunsets are red: with the sun low, light travels a longer path through the atmosphere, the blue is scattered away, and more of the red reaches the ground.
Mie scattering is caused by aerosols, such as pollen, dust, smoke, sea salt and water droplets in the lower atmosphere, that are about as large as the wavelength or larger. It varies from day to day and place to place, and is the hardest part of atmospheric correction to estimate.
Non-selective scattering is caused by particles much larger than the wavelength, such as cloud droplets. It affects all wavelengths alike, which is why clouds are white.

Absorption by gases
Each gas absorbs radiation in its own wavelength bands, set by how its molecules vibrate and rotate. The bands are the gas’s fingerprint:








































GasMain absorption bandsConsequenceOzone (O₃)below 0.32 µm; 9.6 µmblocks most ultraviolet; measured in the UVOxygen (O₂)0.69 and 0.76 µm (the A-band)its amount is known, so the depth of the band gives the length of the light’s path, and the height of cloudsWater vapour (H₂O)0.94, 1.13, 1.38, 1.87 and 2.7 µm; 6.3 µm; much of the far infraredthe largest and most variable absorber; the gaps in the solar spectrum aboveCarbon dioxide (CO₂)1.6, 2.0, 4.3 and 15 µmthe 15 µm band absorbs the Earth’s own emission: the greenhouse effectMethane (CH₄)1.65, 2.3, 3.3 and 7.7 µmmeasured from space in the SWIRNitrogen dioxide (NO₂)0.4–0.5 µma marker of combustion: traffic, industry, shipping
Atmospheric windows
Only the regions between the main absorption bands can be used to observe the Earth’s surface. These atmospheric transmission windows lie in the visible, the near infrared, parts of the short-wave infrared (around 1.6 and 2.2 µm), the thermal infrared between about 8 and 14 µm, and the microwave region. Sensors built to observe the land place their bands inside them.
The thermal window is also part of the climate system. The atmosphere lets most sunlight through but absorbs much of the Earth’s own thermal radiation outside the 8–14 µm window, and sends part of it back down: the greenhouse effect. More CO₂ and CH₄ absorb more of the Earth’s emission at the edges of the window, which is why their concentrations are monitored so closely.
Effects on images

Absorption weakens both the incoming sunlight and the reflected radiation, by an amount that varies with wavelength and with the amount of water vapour, and so alters the measured spectral signature of the target.
Scattering matters most in the visible and near infrared. It adds path radiance and lowers contrast. The effect is strongest in blue light.

Sentinel-2 carries three bands that are there to measure the atmosphere rather than the surface, so that it can be corrected:

























BandWavelengthMeasuresB1443 nmaerosols, where scattering is strongB9945 nmwater vapour, inside its absorption bandB101,375 nmcirrus: the water vapour band is so deep that the surface is invisible, and only high, thin ice clouds above most of the vapour show up
The bands in the windows see the surface; the bands in the absorption bands see the atmosphere. Comparing the two is the basis both of atmospheric correction and of measuring gases.
Measuring the atmosphere itself
Turned around, the absorption bands become the measurement. A sensor that splits sunlight reflected from the surface into thousands of narrow wavelengths, a spectrometer, can see how deep each gas’s bands are, and from that how much of the gas lies along the path from the sun to the ground and up to the satellite. Oxygen, whose amount is known, gives the length of that path, so the measurement can be expressed as a concentration.

Air quality. Sentinel-5 Precursor, with the TROPOMI instrument (launched 2017), maps NO₂, ozone, SO₂, CO, formaldehyde and aerosols every day, worldwide, at about 5.5 × 3.5 km. It shows the NO₂ from traffic in cities and from shipping lanes in the North Sea, and its drop during the 2020 lockdowns. Sentinel-4, in geostationary orbit over Europe, and Sentinel-5, on the MetOp-SG weather satellites, continue the work.
Methane (CH₄). TROPOMI maps methane worldwide in the 2.3 µm band. Large single sources, such as leaking gas installations, landfills and coal mines, can be found as plumes. Even Sentinel-2, built for land, can see the largest plumes: methane absorbs much more in band B12 (2,190 nm) than in B11 (1,610 nm), so a plume appears as a local dip in B12 relative to B11.
Carbon dioxide (CO₂). CO₂ is harder: it is already about 420 parts per million everywhere, and a power plant or a city adds less than one percent to the column above it. Satellites built for it, Japan’s GOSAT (2009) and NASA’s OCO-2 (2014), use the 1.6 and 2.0 µm bands and the oxygen A-band, with a precision of about 1 ppm. The Copernicus CO2M mission is planned to map emissions from cities and power plants.

These are atmosphere products, not images of the surface: their pixels are kilometres wide, and clouds hide what is below. Like surface reflectance, they are delivered as calibrated, corrected products, and the work is in choosing the right one and understanding what its pixels mean.
The sections on waves, the spectrum, reflectance and scattering draw on the tutorial Fundamentals of Remote Sensing by the Canada Centre for Mapping and Earth Observation (Natural Resources Canada). Figures from Wikimedia Commons as credited; the sun-and-Earth figure is calculated from Planck’s law.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/image.title: Image interpretation and classification
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/image.content:
Chapter 6 of Remote sensing.
Visual interpretation
Three kinds of information in an optical image are used to interpret it:

Radiometric information: the values in each band, read as colour and brightness, and as spectral signatures.
Texture: the pattern of variation between neighbouring pixels, especially in high-resolution images. In an image of a plantation, mature trees in rows, closed canopy and open grass can have the same colour but different texture. Texture can also be measured numerically and used in automatic classification.
Geometric and contextual information: shape, size, pattern, location and association with neighbouring features. Using it requires some prior knowledge of the area. Fields and city blocks can both be rectangular, but blocks are smaller, lie in a regular grid and have a different colour; fields follow the terrain.

Interpretation can be wrong. The only certainty is ground truth: going to the place and seeing what is there.
Ground truth
Positional and thematic field observations are a precondition for most image interpretation. Field measurements of reflectance with a handheld spectrometer link what is on the ground to what the sensor measures, and are used to develop new methods, such as vegetation indices, that quantify surface properties from reflectance.
Image classification
An image classification assigns each pixel to one category, a land cover class, from its values in the bands used. The bands need not be the original ones: they can be an index such as NDVI, the result of a statistical transformation, data from another sensor, or the same bands from another season (seven bands from a summer image and seven from a winter image).
Each pixel is a point in a space with one dimension per band: with six bands, a six-dimensional spectral space. Ideally, pixels of the same land cover form clusters in that space, separate from the others. In practice the clusters overlap: a scatter plot of a NIR band against a red band shows clouds of points with no clear borders.
Unsupervised classification
An algorithm finds the k most distinct clusters in the spectral space, and the analyst then names them. Nothing guarantees that the clusters match useful land cover classes; they are only spectrally different. The most common algorithm is k-means:

Place k cluster seeds in the spectral space at random.
Assign every pixel to the nearest seed, forming clusters.
Move each seed to the mean of the pixels in its cluster.
If any seed moved, go back to step 2; otherwise the clusters are the result.

Supervised classification
The analyst first marks training areas, pixels or polygons known to be of each class, and an algorithm assigns the remaining pixels to the classes they resemble. Nothing guarantees that the classes can be told apart in the spectral space. A class that varies a lot is often better split into homogeneous subclasses (sea and lakes, or deep and shallow water) and merged afterwards.

Minimum distance: computes the mean of each class’s training pixels and assigns each pixel to the class whose mean is nearest in the spectral space.
Classification and regression tree (CART): a decision tree that splits the spectral space step by step at the band value that best separates the classes (“B8 below 0.029”), until a stopping rule is met. Trees are very sensitive to the training data.
Random forest: many trees, each trained on a random subsample of the training data (often 50–60 %). Each pixel goes to the class most trees vote for. Even a small forest is more robust than a single tree.

A classifier can in principle be applied to any image with the same bands. Applying it to another date than it was trained on works best with surface reflectance, so that differences in light between, say, summer and winter do not look like differences in land cover.
Evaluating a classification
The ground truth is split in two: one part trains the classifier, the other (often about 30 %) is kept for validation. The validation pixels give a confusion matrix: the true class along one axis, the class assigned along the other. In this example, of 112 pixels that are truly class 4, 97 were classified as 4, 1 as 1, 13 as 2 and 1 as 3:




































































True class→ 0→ 1→ 2→ 3→ 4Producer’s accuracy0281800001.0010750001.00210173030.98304022420.97401131970.87User’s accuracy1.000.940.930.990.95
Three measures follow from it:

Overall accuracy: the share of all validation pixels classified correctly.
Producer’s accuracy, per class: the share of the pixels truly in the class that were classified as it (row by row; errors of omission).
User’s accuracy, per class: the share of the pixels classified as the class that truly belong to it (column by column; errors of commission). It tells a map user how far to trust the class on the map.

A large class that is easy to classify, like class 0 here, lifts the overall accuracy; the per-class accuracies show where the classification fails.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/ndvi.title: Normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI)
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/ndvi.content:
Part of Remote sensing. Background: photosynthesis and the red edge and Spectral signatures and vegetation indices. In practice: Vegetation index from satellite imagery (Task).
The normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI) is the most used number in remote sensing of vegetation. It compares how much red light and how much near-infrared light a surface reflects:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)

The result lies between −1 and 1. Green vegetation gives high values, bare soil and built surfaces values near 0, and water negative values. The index was introduced in the 1970s for the early Landsat satellites (Rouse et al., 1974; Tucker, 1979). It has been calculated for the whole Earth almost every day since the 1980s, which makes it one of the longest records of the state of the planet’s vegetation.
Why it works: chlorophyll and photosynthesis
NDVI measures the contrast that photosynthesis creates. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light to drive photosynthesis, and the leaf’s inner structure reflects near-infrared light, which it cannot use:

Top: how much light chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and carotenoids absorb at each wavelength. Bottom: the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. Figure: John Whitmarsh and Govindjee, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
The figure shows the two absorption peaks of chlorophyll, in blue (about 430–480 nm) and red (about 640–680 nm), and the low absorption in green between them. Photosynthesis follows the absorption: it is fastest in blue and red light, slower in green, and drops to almost nothing above 700 nm. The red band used for NDVI lies on chlorophyll a’s red peak; the near-infrared band lies beyond 700 nm, where nothing is absorbed. The more green, healthy leaves there are in a pixel, the darker it is in red and the brighter in near infrared, and the higher the NDVI.
Using a normalised difference rather than the bands themselves has two advantages. The index has a fixed range, so values from different places and dates can be compared. And because it is a ratio, much of what affects both bands equally cancels out: differences in illumination from slope or sun angle, and the scale factor with which reflectance is stored.
The bands of common sensors








































SensorRedNear infraredNDVIPixel sizeSentinel-2 MSIB4 (665 nm)B8 (842 nm)(B8 − B4) / (B8 + B4)10 mLandsat 8 and 9 OLIB4 (655 nm)B5 (865 nm)(B5 − B4) / (B5 + B4)30 mLandsat 4–7 TM, ETM+B3 (660 nm)B4 (835 nm)(B4 − B3) / (B4 + B3)30 mMODIS (Terra, Aqua)band 1 (645 nm)band 2 (858 nm)(b2 − b1) / (b2 + b1)250 m
The band numbers differ between sensors, and so do the exact wavelengths, so NDVI from two sensors is close but not identical. Compare values from the same sensor, or harmonise them first.
A year of NDVI in Denmark

NDVI over Denmark and southern Sweden in 2022, one frame per 16 days, from light brown (low NDVI) to dark green (high NDVI). Water is masked in black. Animation: Esbern Holmes, calculated in Google Earth Engine (script).
The animation shows the phenology of the landscape, the yearly rhythm of the vegetation:

Winter (January–February): NDVI is low, but Denmark is not brown. Grass, winter cereals and winter rape stay green through the mild winter. In southern Sweden the lowest values of the year come in mid-January, most likely from snow.
Spring (March–May): the fields green up and the deciduous forests come into leaf. NDVI rises fast through April and May.
Early summer (late May–June): the whole landscape reaches its maximum. Fields, forests and grassland look almost alike: NDVI has saturated (see below).
Late summer (late July–August): Denmark turns lighter and patchy while the Swedish forests stay dark. The cereals ripen and are harvested, and the fields go from green to yellow to stubble. Most of Denmark is farmland, most of southern Sweden forest, and NDVI shows the difference without any map of land use.
Autumn (September–November): new growth on harvested fields, winter crops coming up and grass keep NDVI moderate until the leaves fall and the light fades.

Two technical points lie behind such an animation:

Compositing. Clouds reflect red and near infrared about equally, so cloudy pixels have an NDVI near 0. A single image of Denmark is rarely cloud-free. Each frame is therefore a composite of all images within a period, here 16 days, keeping for each pixel a clear observation, often the one with the highest NDVI (the maximum value composite). The price is that a frame is not a single date, and the value of a pixel may come from any day in the period.
Scale. At the scale of a country the pixels are large, and each frame shows regions rather than fields. At 10 m (Sentinel-2) the same rhythm can be followed field by field, see Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example).

What NDVI measures, and what it does not
NDVI measures greenness: how much green, chlorophyll-bearing leaf area there is in a pixel. It is closely related to quantities like leaf area, the fraction of light absorbed by plants, and photosynthesis, but it is none of them:

Saturation. Above an NDVI of about 0.8, more leaves hardly change the value. Dense forests and closed crops look alike, as in the June frames of the animation. Red-edge indices and the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) stay sensitive longer.
Soil and background. In sparse vegetation the soil shows through, and its colour and moisture change the value.
Green is not healthy, and not productive. A lawn and a forest can have the same NDVI. Water stress may show only after some delay, when the leaves have already lost chlorophyll.
Atmosphere. Haze adds most to the red band and lowers NDVI. Use surface reflectance (see top-of-atmosphere and surface reflectance), and mask clouds and their shadows.
Time. NDVI follows the season. Two images are only comparable if they are from the same time of year, as the animation shows; a change between April and June is not a change in land use.

References

Rouse, J. W., Haas, R. H., Schell, J. A. and Deering, D. W. (1974). Monitoring vegetation systems in the Great Plains with ERTS. Third ERTS Symposium, NASA SP-351, 309–317.
Tucker, C. J. (1979). Red and photographic infrared linear combinations for monitoring vegetation. Remote Sensing of Environment, 8(2), 127–150.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/index.title: Remote sensing
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/index.content:
Remote sensing is, in the U.S. Geological Survey’s definition, “the process of detecting and monitoring the physical characteristics of an area by measuring its reflected and emitted radiation at a distance”. Two terms recur throughout:

The sensor (instrument) measures the radiation, the electromagnetic radiation (EMR). The most common sensor is a multispectral radiometer, which measures EMR at several wavelengths at the same time.
The platform carries the sensor over the target: a drone, an aircraft or a satellite.

These notes deal mainly with multispectral radiometers on satellites, and with how their measurements of the Earth’s surface are used to understand the physical environment. Data from them are free and plentiful: Sentinel-2 alone images every place in Denmark every few days at 10 m resolution. Handling that amount of data is part of the work. These notes use the Copernicus Browser to find an image and cut out the study area, and QGIS to analyse it.
Three kinds of sensor

Reflected sunlight. Most sensors measure sunlight reflected by the surface, in visible and infrared wavelengths. Sentinel-2’s MultiSpectral Instrument (MSI) and Landsat 8’s Operational Land Imager (OLI) are of this kind.
Emitted radiation. Some measure radiation emitted by the surface itself: thermal infrared, from which surface temperature can be calculated (Landsat 8’s Thermal Infrared Sensor, TIRS), or the light of cities at night (VIIRS on the Suomi NPP satellite).
Active sensors send out their own radiation and measure what comes back: radar from satellites (Sentinel-1), lidar from aircraft and drones.

The seven elements of remote sensing

Energy source or illumination: the sun, or the radar or lidar on the platform.
The atmosphere: the radiation passes through it on its way to the target, and again on its way from the target to a satellite sensor.
Interaction with the target: part of the radiation is absorbed, a little is transmitted, and part is reflected, depending on both the surface and the wavelength.
Recording by the sensor: the sensor records the reflected or emitted radiation.
Transmission, reception and processing: the recording is sent to a ground station and processed into images, often together with derived products that make analysis easier.
Interpretation and analysis: the image is interpreted, visually or digitally, to extract information about the target.
Application: the information is used to understand the target better, reveal something new, or help solve a problem.

Chapters

Electromagnetic radiation and the atmosphere: wavelengths, the spectrum, the sun and the Earth as black bodies, photosynthesis and the red edge, the atmosphere as noise (atmospheric correction) and as signal (CO₂, CH₄ and air quality).
Earth observation platforms and sensors: satellites and their orbits, aircraft, handheld spectrometers, radar.
Digital images and reflectance: pixels, digital numbers, calibration, top-of-atmosphere and surface reflectance, bands.
Visualising multispectral images: grey-scale and colour composites, contrast stretch.
Spectral signatures and vegetation indices: how water, soil and vegetation reflect, and NDVI.

NDVI: why the index works, the bands of common sensors, and a year of NDVI in Denmark.


Image interpretation and classification: visual interpretation, ground truth, classification and its accuracy.
