In practice: Vegetation index from satellite imagery (Task), with the Recipe Vegetation index from Sentinel-2 (Recipe - QGIS) and the worked example Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example).
These notes are a revision of the compendium “Earth System Science & Remote Sensing” (Esbern Holmes, 2021), written for Google Earth Engine. The chapters on radiation, the atmosphere, orbits and images draw on the tutorial Fundamentals of Remote Sensing by the Canada Centre for Mapping and Earth Observation (Natural Resources Canada), free for non-commercial use.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/spect.filePath: Supporting concepts/Remote sensing/Spectral signatures and vegetation indices.md
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/spect.title: Spectral signatures and vegetation indices
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/spect.content:
Chapter 5 of Remote sensing.
Spectral reflectance signatures
The reflectance of a material across a range of wavelengths is its spectral reflectance signature. In principle a material can be recognised and mapped from its signature, if the sensor measures enough bands to tell it from other materials’ signatures. That is the basis of multispectral remote sensing.

Clear water reflects little at all wavelengths, most in blue, less and less towards the infrared, and almost nothing in the near infrared. It looks dark blue.
Turbid water, with suspended sediment, reflects more in red (about 0.65 µm) and looks brownish.
Bare soil reflects more and more from blue to short-wave infrared. How much depends on its composition, colour, structure and moisture: wet soil is darker than dry.
Vegetation has a signature of its own, which makes it easy to tell from other surfaces:

low in blue and red, where chlorophyll absorbs the light it uses for photosynthesis;
a peak in green, which makes plants look green;
a steep rise from red to near infrared around 0.7 µm, the red edge (why leaves absorb red and reflect near infrared is explained in photosynthesis and the red edge);
high in the near infrared, reflected by the cell structure inside the leaves; the arrangement of leaves in the canopy affects it too, which helps tell vegetation types apart;
in the short-wave infrared, lower and varying with the water content of the leaves, with absorption bands of water at about 1.45, 1.95 and 2.5 µm. Between those bands, reflectance rises as leaves dry out, which is why SWIR bands help detect drought stress and burnt areas.



The signature also depends on the plant’s condition. Stressed or senescent vegetation reflects less in the near infrared and more in red: the red edge flattens.
Vegetation indices
Bands can be combined to bring out vegetation. Because vegetation reflects much in the near infrared and little in red, the ratio of the two is high for vegetation and low for everything else: the ratio vegetation index,

RVI = NIR / Red

A ratio has no upper limit. A fixed range, from −1 to 1, is often more useful, and is reached with a normalised difference of two bands, (V1 − V2) / (V1 + V2). With near infrared and red it is the normalised difference vegetation index:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)

For Sentinel-2, NDVI = (B8 − B4) / (B8 + B4); the bands of other sensors, the index’s history and a year of NDVI in Denmark are in the NDVI note. Typical values:

























SurfaceNDVIWaterbelow 0Bare soil, rock, built surfacesabout 0–0.2Sparse or dry vegetationabout 0.2–0.5Dense, green vegetationabout 0.6–0.9
Because NDVI is a ratio of reflectances, a common scale factor cancels out: the result is the same whether the bands are stored as reflectance (0–1) or as reflectance × 10,000. An offset does not cancel; it must be removed first (see how reflectance is stored).
What NDVI does not show

Saturation. Above an NDVI of about 0.8 the index hardly changes as vegetation gets denser. In June, forest and a closed cereal crop have nearly the same NDVI, although a colour-infrared image tells them apart (Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example)).
Soil background. Where vegetation is sparse, the colour and moisture of the soil beneath change the value.
Mixed pixels. A 10 m pixel on a road with grass verges, or on a pond edged by trees, averages them. Small or narrow features take the value of their surroundings.
Date. NDVI follows the growing season. A field is bare in April and green in June, and a harvested field is bare again in August. Values are only comparable between images from the same time of year, and preferably the same sensor.

Red-edge indices
Sentinel-2’s three red-edge bands (B5 at 705 nm, B6 at 740 nm and B7 at 783 nm, all 20 m) measure on the slope between red and near infrared, where the leaf’s chlorophyll content shows. Indices built on them stay sensitive in dense vegetation, where NDVI saturates:

























IndexSentinel-2 bandsShowsNDRE (normalised difference red edge)(B8A − B5) / (B8A + B5)like NDVI, with a red-edge band in place of red; chlorophyll and nitrogen in dense cropsCIre (chlorophyll index, red edge; Gitelson et al., 2003)B7 / B5 − 1canopy chlorophyll contentS2REP (Sentinel-2 red-edge position; Frampton et al., 2013)705 + 35 × ((B4 + B7) / 2 − B5) / (B6 − B5)the wavelength, in nm, of the red edge’s steepest point; higher with more chlorophyll
The band choices vary between authors; record the formula used. The results have the 20 m resolution of the red-edge bands.
Other normalised differences
The same form with other bands gives other indices, for example the normalised difference water index (green and NIR, for open water) and the normalised difference moisture index (NIR and SWIR, for the water content of vegetation).
The NDVI layer can also be combined with other bands in a colour composite, to help distinguish types of vegetation.

supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/visua.title: Visualising multispectral images
supporting-concepts/remote-sensing/visua.content:
Chapter 4 of Remote sensing.
Grey-scale images
A single band is usually shown in shades of grey: the brighter the pixel, the higher its value, and the more radiation the surface reflected in that band. Beyond brightness, a grey-scale image can be read from shape, texture and context (see Image interpretation and classification).
Colour composites
A screen mixes every colour from red, green and blue light. Any three bands can be shown together by assigning one to each of the three colours: an RGB colour composite.
True colour
If the red, green and blue bands are shown in red, green and blue, the image looks roughly as the eye would see it. For Sentinel-2: R = B4, G = B3, B = B2.

False colour
Any other assignment is a false colour composite. The most common shows near infrared in red, red in green and green in blue, R = B8, G = B4, B = B3, called colour infrared (CIR). Growing vegetation reflects strongly in the near infrared, so it shows in shades of red that differ with type and condition. Clear water is dark; turbid water, with sediment that reflects red light, is cyan. Bare soil, roads and buildings show as blue, grey or brownish, depending on their material.

In the colour-infrared image of Ledreborg (14 June 2025) the forests are dark, textured red, the fields smooth red or pink depending on the crop, bare and dry surfaces, roads and buildings cyan to white, and the lakes black. In the true-colour image of the same date nearly all of it is a similar green.
Common band combinations
A composite with a short-wave infrared band, such as R = B12, G = B8A, B = B4, separates moisture and bare soil better. Common combinations, with the Landsat 8 bands they were defined for:




























































PurposeSentinel-2 (R, G, B)Landsat 8True colourB4, B3, B24, 3, 2Colour infrared (vegetation)B8, B4, B35, 4, 3False colour (urban)B12, B11, B47, 6, 4AgricultureB11, B8, B26, 5, 2Atmospheric penetrationB12, B11, B8A7, 6, 5Healthy vegetationB8, B11, B25, 6, 2Land and waterB8, B11, B45, 6, 4Natural with atmospheric removalB12, B8, B37, 5, 3Short-wave infraredB12, B8, B47, 5, 4Vegetation analysisB11, B8, B46, 5, 4
A combination is chosen to bring out a contrast that matters for the question: between crops, between wet and dry, between built and bare. It is also a first step towards change detection and classification.
Contrast stretch
A screen shows each colour with values from 0 to 255. Surface reflectance runs from 0 to 1 (0 to 10,000 as stored), but most pixels of a scene use only a small part of that range: vegetation reflects 0.02–0.05 in red. Mapping the full range to 0–255 gives a dark, flat image. A contrast stretch maps only the range that holds most of the values:

Minimum–maximum: from the lowest to the highest value; a few extreme pixels (clouds, roofs) make the rest dull.
Cumulative count cut: from, say, the 2nd to the 98th percentile, ignoring the extremes. QGIS uses this by default.
Mean ± standard deviations: from the mean minus n standard deviations to the mean plus n.
Gamma: bends the stretch away from a straight line. A gamma below 1 brightens the image, above 1 darkens it.

The histogram of a band, the number of pixels at each value, shows where the values lie before you choose. A dark image has its histogram squeezed into the low end. A stretch only changes the display, never the values used in calculations. Two images stretched separately cannot be compared by their colours.

tasks/aggregating-a-categorical-raster-t.filePath: Tasks/Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Task).md
tasks/aggregating-a-categorical-raster-t.title: Land-use composition per zone (Task)
tasks/aggregating-a-categorical-raster-t.content:
Implementation: Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS).
Land-use composition per zone is the Task of measuring how much of each land-use class lies in each zone — each landscape, municipality or grid cell — from a categorical land-use raster. The result is a table of areas or shares, one row per zone and one column per class, ready for a chart.
Used in examples: Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Choose the land-use source and its classes (decision point) — e.g. Basemap04’s aggregated classes (lu_agg_2021), with names from its legend.
Choose the zones — e.g. the landscapes from landscape delineation.
Count the cells of each class in each zone (Operator: tabulate area) — as area or as percentage.
Group zones of the same type (decision point) — add up the areas of polygons of the same landscape type, then compute the shares.
Group classes for presentation (decision point) — e.g. all built-up classes as “Built-up”; 30 classes do not fit in one chart.

Output: a table of land-use area and share per zone (or zone type), and a 100 % stacked bar chart.
Epistemic Choices to record

Classification: Basemap04 combines several sources; its classes are not those of field observation. “Agriculture, extensive” is a land-use class, not a habitat type.
Cell-centre rule: a cell counts in the zone that contains its centre; small zones get edge effects.
Shares of what: of all cells, or only of cells with a class? Unmapped cells and water change the denominator.
Grouping: combine areas, never average shares: the share for a landscape type with two polygons is the summed area of each class divided by the summed total.

tasks/aggregating-a-continuous-raster-to.filePath: Tasks/Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task).md
tasks/aggregating-a-continuous-raster-to.title: Zonal summary of a surface (Task)
tasks/aggregating-a-continuous-raster-to.content:
Implementation: Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS).
Zonal summary of a surface is the Task of describing a continuous raster — soil organic carbon, elevation, a vegetation index — inside each zone with a few numbers: mean, median, a high percentile. It is how a map of values becomes a comparison between landscapes.
Used in examples: Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Know the surface (decision point) — what the value means, its unit, depth or date, and how it was made (measured, interpolated from samples, modelled from satellite data).
Bring surface and zones to the same reference (Operator: reproject if needed) — same coordinate system; the study area plus a margin.
Compute statistics per zone (Operator: zonal statistics) — count, sum, mean, median, a high percentile.
Combine zones of the same type (decision point) — from sums and counts, not from the zones’ means.
Optionally, split by a category (Operator: zonal statistics with a categorical raster as zones) — e.g. the mean value per land-use class.

Output: a table of statistics per zone or zone type, ready to set beside other zonal results (such as land-use composition).
Epistemic Choices to record

Concentration or stock: soil organic carbon in percent is a concentration; tonnes of carbon per hectare would also need bulk density and depth. Say which the analysis is about.
Mean or median: a few extreme cells (peat in a valley) pull the mean far above the median. Report both when they differ.
What the surface covers: a soil model predicts values under lakes and buildings too; leave such cells out or say why they stay.
Model uncertainty: a modelled surface is an estimate with its own error; differences between zones smaller than that error are not findings.

tasks/aggregating-points-to-zones-(task).title: Aggregating points to zones (Task)
tasks/aggregating-points-to-zones-(task).content:
Implementation: Aggregating points to zones (Recipe - QGIS).
Aggregating points to zones is the Task of summarising point data — dwellings, buildings, people at their addresses — within a set of zones: districts, statistical areas or a grid. It is how almost all Danish statistics reach a map, both because a map of points hides the pattern and because points can identify individuals.
Used in examples: Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)


Prepare the points — Point data is often primary data, e.g., from a register of dwellings, data points from loggers of agricultural machines, crime incident reports, and therefore they often need a thorough cleaning process before they can be used with any confidence; see categories from register codes.


Choose the zones (decision point) — zones differ in two ways: their form, regular cells or irregular areas, and their origin, predefined by someone else or built for this study.




















PredefinedPurpose-builtRegular (grids)national and European statistical grids: the Danish Kvadratnet, the GISCO grid (Statistical Units)a grid made for the question, e.g. hexagons or 250 m squares (Operator: generate grid); see Square and hexagonal gridsIrregular (areas)existing administrative and statistical units: municipalities, bydele, kvarterer, roder, NUTSzones drawn to capture a characteristic of the data: areas of high or low concentration, areas of a specific composition
Predefined zones make the result comparable with official statistics and other studies; prefer them, or a grid aligned with a predefined grid, unless the question needs otherwise. Purpose-built zones fit the question but cannot be compared, and irregular ones drawn from the data itself can make almost any pattern appear — the same freedom that makes gerrymandering possible. Whatever the choice, the zones are part of the result, not a neutral container.


Summarise the points in each zone (Operator: summary by location) — choose the statistics by the role they play, and by the level of measurement of the field:



































RoleStatisticsFieldsAmountcount, sumcount: any; sum: ratioCentral tendency — the typical valuemode; median; meanmode: nominal; median: ordinal and up; mean: interval and ratio. The mean of a 0/1 indicator is a share.Dispersion — the spread around itrange, interquartile range; variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variationinterquartile range: ordinal and up; the others: interval and ratio (the coefficient of variation: ratio only)Shape of the distributionskewness (the Fisher–Pearson moment coefficient), kurtosisinterval and ratioSpecialised measuresinequality: the Gini coefficient; diversity of categories: e.g. the Shannon indexGini: ratio; Shannon: nominal
A central value alone hides how different the points in a zone are: two zones with the same mean dwelling size can hold one kind of dwelling or a mix of very small and very large. Report a measure of dispersion with it. Not every operator computes shape and specialised measures; they can be computed from the points grouped by zone (Operator: group-by statistics).


Check the sums — the counts over all zones against the number of points; points on borders or outside every zone explain differences.


Set a minimum count (decision point) — zones with too few points get no value (and are shown as such), because a mean of a handful of points is unreliable and can reveal individuals.


Derive what the map needs (Operator: attribute calculation) — e.g. a density from a count and the zone’s area.


Output: the zones with counts and summaries, and a flag for zones below the minimum count.
Epistemic Choices to record

Which zones and why: a different set of zones gives a different map of the same points (the modifiable areal unit problem: the scale effect of zone size and the zoning effect of where the borders run). Try a second set before concluding.
Mean or median: a few very large or very small units pull the mean; report the median where it differs.
Minimum count: 20? 50? Name it and show the zones it hides.
Never average averages upwards: a value for a larger zone is computed from the points again, or from sums and counts, never as the mean of smaller zones’ means.
Which point: a dwelling placed on its building’s point or on its entrance’s address point can fall in different zones near a border.
Ecological fallacy: a zone’s average describes the zone, not the people or dwellings in it.

tasks/backdrop-digitalisation.title: Backdrop Digitalisation (Task)
tasks/backdrop-digitalisation.content:
Related: 2.2 Establishing the Data Framework (Part 2) and Primary Data Collection: Field Work (Part 3) — this is the data-entry step that follows fieldwork. Depends on Georeferencing (Task) as a prerequisite. Implementation: Backdrop digitalisation (Recipe - QGIS).

Editorial note: the digitising mechanics this Task’s Recipe describes are grounded in the transcript of your “basic GIS operations in QGIS” video, supplied manually. That video covers general digitising over an OpenStreetMap basemap — it does not itself demonstrate reconciling hand-drawn field notes against an aerial photo, so the field-note-reconciliation material below (decision point 3) is still a general reconstruction, not verified against a source specific to backdrop digitalisation. Correct it once you have that material to hand.

Backdrop digitalisation is the Task of translating a Pilot Fieldwork session — hand-drawn sketch maps and paper notes, recorded with deliberately unstructured tools — into a structured spatial table, by tracing over a georeferenced aerial photograph. Where the field session produced a rough, expressive record of what was observed and where, backdrop digitalisation is the Final Registration step: applying the (by now refined) Domain of Discourse consistently, to produce clean, precisely located data.
It sits, in workflow terms, at the boundary between Confronting the Sensoric Manifold and Executing the Analytical Schema — the Realisation exists first as a sketch, and only becomes a Realisation an Analytical Schema can act on once it has been digitised against the Attribute Framework and geometry.
Flow
flowchart TD
    A[Obtain a georeferenced backdrop] --> B{Source is a paper map<br/>not yet georeferenced?}
    B -- yes --> C["Georeferencing (Task)"]
    B -- no, already a live basemap --> D[Load basemap]
    C --> E{Digitised data goes into...}
    D --> E
    E -- a new table --> F[Create geospatial table]
    E -- existing data needing an update --> G[Enable editing]
    F --> H[Digitise features against backdrop]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Reconcile against field notes]
    I --> J[Enforce shared-boundary topology]
    J --> K[QA pass against field notes]

Nodes in this flow:

Obtain a georeferenced backdrop
Source is a paper map not yet georeferenced?

yes → Georeferencing (Task)
no → Load basemap (not yet its own Task note)


Digitised data goes into…

a new table → Create geospatial table (not yet its own Task note)
existing data needing an update → Enable editing (not yet its own Task note)


Digitise features against backdrop
Reconcile against field notes
Enforce shared-boundary topology
QA pass against field notes

Only Georeferencing (Task) is a real click-through link — the other nodes are steps internal to this Task, not separate notes (yet). This list exists because Mermaid’s own click links don’t resolve reliably in both Obsidian and the published site (see discussion in the vault’s working notes); an ordinary markdown/wikilink list under the diagram does resolve reliably in both, so this is the actual navigation — the diagram is the overview.
This is also a first pass at sketching the Task as a flow rather than a numbered list — the two decision points above (georeference-or-load-basemap; new-table-or-enable-editing) aren’t both reflected in the numbered Schema below yet. The Schema currently only covers the new-table branch (step 1); the “existing data needing an update → enable editing” branch is new, surfaced by drawing this out, and still needs its own paragraph — see open item below step 1.
Prerequisites

A georeferenced aerial photograph of the study area — see Georeferencing (Task) if it isn’t already one. Most student work will start from an already-referenced orthophoto (e.g., in Denmark, Dataforsyningen’s WMS/WMTS service) and can skip straight to digitising.
Your hand-drawn field maps and notes from the Pilot Fieldwork session, ideally photographed or scanned so they can be viewed alongside the digitising software.
A finalised Attribute Framework — the NOIR-typed table from your (refined) Domain of Discourse — so that the fields you create match a specification you have already committed to, rather than being improvised feature by feature.

Task Schema (tool-agnostic)


Obtain the backdrop, and prepare the target table (decision point + Operation) — first: if the backdrop source is a paper map or otherwise un-referenced image, it must go through Georeferencing (Task) first; otherwise, load an already-georeferenced basemap directly. Second: instantiate an empty spatial table per entity — matching the geometry type your thematic specification already settled on for that Cognised Existence (point, line, or polygon), the target CRS, and the Attribute Framework’s fields exactly (a nominal field as text with an appropriate maximum length, a ratio or interval field as a numeric type) — or, where the digitised data is an update to existing data rather than a new capture, enable editing on the existing table instead of creating a new one. Building the schema before digitising a single feature — rather than adding fields as you go — is what keeps this step a Recipe rather than an improvisation.
Open item: the “existing data needing an update → enable editing” branch needs its own worked-through paragraph, parallel to the “new table” case above — what changes about steps 2–5 below when you’re editing an existing Realisation rather than creating a fresh one (e.g., does reconciliation against field notes work the same way against pre-existing attribute values)?


Digitise each feature against the backdrop (Operation, with an embedded decision point) — place each feature’s geometry using the aerial photo for precise, metrically accurate placement, and the hand-drawn notes as the record of what was observed and where it should belong — the sketch tells you which bench, path, or zone boundary you are looking at; the orthophoto tells you exactly where its geometry belongs. Populate attributes directly from the field notes as each feature is completed.
Decision point: where a Cognised Existence has an interior exclusion — a courtyard cut out of a building footprint, a paved-over patch excluded from a wider polygon — it must be represented as a hole in that same feature, never as a second, separately-owned polygon placed on top. A separate overlapping polygon will not behave as an exclusion in later spatial operations, however visually similar it looks on screen.


Reconcile deliberately, and log the reconciliation (decision point) — a hand-drawn sketch is never as precise as an aerial photo, and reconciling the two is an interpretive act, not a mechanical one: deciding exactly where a sketched “picnic area” boundary falls against the orthophoto’s actual tree lines and paths is the same kind of judgement call as the GeoDanmark specification’s skønnes (“is assessed”), discussed under thematic specification in Part 2. Where the reconciliation is not obvious, note the decision in your Design Rationale rather than letting it pass silently.


Enforce shared-boundary topology while digitising, not after (decision point) — for any Domain of Discourse rule that depends on two features meeting exactly (no gap or overlap between adjacent zone polygons; a path endpoint that must land precisely on a boundary), the adjacency must be enforced at the moment the second feature is drawn. Correcting a near-miss afterwards is far more error-prone than preventing it as you draw. This addresses adjacency/shared-boundary constraints only — a containment rule (e.g., “must fall entirely within Tivoli’s boundary”) or a connectivity rule (e.g., a harbour-front severance test) still needs a separate manual check or follow-up geoprocessing step; neither is something boundary-snapping alone can catch.


Close out with a QA pass against the original field notes (Operation) — not to re-decide anything, but to catch anything transcribed incorrectly or left out. This closes the loop from Observation, through Recording, to a spatial table ready to enter the Analytical Schema.


Output: a populated spatial table, faithful to the Attribute Framework and the field observations, ready to enter the Analytical Schema.
Task Recipes (tool-bound)

QGIS: Backdrop digitalisation (Recipe - QGIS)
ArcGIS: (not yet written)

tasks/building-heights-from-elevation-mo.title: Building heights from elevation models (Task)
tasks/building-heights-from-elevation-mo.content:
Used in: Urban Design Visualisation (Example). Implementation: Building heights from DHM (Recipe - QGIS).
Building heights from elevation models is the Task of giving each building footprint a height above ground — and, where needed, an eave height and a roof type — by comparing a surface model (DSM, the top of everything) with a terrain model (DTM, the bare ground). Footprint registers rarely carry reliable heights; elevation models carry heights, but not buildings. This Task joins the two.
In workflow terms it sits at Recording the Domain of Discourse: it produces an attribute of an already-accepted Cognised Existence from primary data, rather than analysing anything.
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Choose the source models (decision point) — a DSM and a DTM of the same date, resolution and vertical datum. Mismatched dates (a building built between the two) give nonsense heights.
Compute height above ground (Operator: local map algebra) — nDSM = DSM − DTM.
Restrict to the building interior (Operator: inward buffer) — shrink each footprint, typically by about 0.5 m, so wall-edge and street pixels are excluded.
Remove outliers (Operator: filter) — discard pixels far above the typical roof level (chimneys, antennas, overhanging trees).
Summarise the remaining pixels (Operator: zonal statistics) —

height: a high percentile (e.g., the 95th) — the ridge, without the outliers
eave: a low percentile (e.g., the 10th)
ground: the terrain elevation under the building, from the DTM


Derive the roof (Operator: arithmetic + reclassify) — roof_rise = height − eave; roof_type = flat below a threshold (e.g., 1.0 m), else pitched.
Flag problems (Operator + decision point) — mark buildings with too few pixels, no data or negative heights, and check unusually large roof_rise values by hand: they usually mean a lower wing inside the same footprint.

Output: building footprints with height, eave, roof_rise, roof_type, ground and a quality flag — ready for Context massing (Task).
Epistemic Choices to record
The percentiles, buffer distance, outlier rule and flat-roof threshold are all judgements. The defaults suit Danish town centres at 0.4 m resolution; record any change, and any height corrected by hand, in the Design Rationale.
Task Recipes (tool-bound)

QGIS: Building heights from DHM (Recipe - QGIS)
Python: (not yet written — rasterio + rasterstats would implement the same Schema)

tasks/categories-from-register-codes-(ta.title: Categories from register codes (Task)
tasks/categories-from-register-codes-(ta.content:
Implementation: Categories from register codes (Recipe - QGIS).
Categories from register codes is the Task of turning the codes of an administrative register (BBR, CVR, CPR-based statistics) into the categories an analysis needs: construction period from a construction year, tenure from a rental code, ordinary dwelling from a use code. Registers are made for administration, not for research, so their categories rarely match a research question one to one. This Task is where a concept is operationalised, and where most of the analysis’s assumptions are made.
Used in examples: Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

State the concept (decision point) — what the analysis is about, in words, before looking at the data (e.g. “dwellings built before the Second World War”).
Find the codes and read the code list (decision point) — which fields can express the concept, and what each code means according to the register’s own documentation (for BBR: teknik.bbr.dk/kodelister).
Count the codes (Operator: aggregate per value) — how many units have each code, including empty values, before deciding anything.
Decide the mapping (decision point) — which codes go into which category, and what happens to codes that fit none (left out, or a category of their own).
Select the population (Operator: selection by attribute) — the units the analysis is about (e.g. standing dwellings, without student housing).
Write the category or indicator (Operator: indicator or recode).
Check the counts again — every unit should be in exactly one category, or deliberately left out.

Output: the units with a new category or indicator field, and a table of how many units each code and each category holds.
Epistemic Choices to record

The code’s real meaning: read the definition, not only the label. A construction year (opførelsesår) belongs to the building, so a dwelling converted from an old warehouse carries the warehouse’s year.
What the code list cannot say: a register has the categories its administration needs. If the category your concept needs is not in the list, it is hidden inside another category; find out which, and say what that does to the result.
Empty and residual codes: “unknown”, “not in use” or an empty field are decisions too: in the denominator, or out.
Who reports the codes: who registers a code, when it is updated, and whether anyone has a reason to keep it correct. A code nobody uses administratively can stay wrong for decades.
Date: registers change; give the date of the extract.

tasks/comparable-choropleth-maps-(task).title: Comparable choropleth maps (Task)
tasks/comparable-choropleth-maps-(task).content:
Implementation: Comparable choropleth maps (Recipe - QGIS).
Comparable choropleth maps is the Task of mapping two or more groups (two periods, two tenures, two years) so that a reader can compare them: the same zones, the same classes, the same colours, and the same treatment of zones without a reliable value. Without that, two maps that look alike can show different values, and two that look different can show the same.
Used in examples: Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Start from aggregated zones — one layer per group, from aggregating points to zones, with the same zones and the same minimum count.
Look at the values of all maps together — their combined range and distribution.
Choose one set of classes for all maps (decision point; Operator: classes shared between maps) — e.g. round boundaries that cover the combined range.
Give zones without a reliable value their own class (Operator: missing and unreliable values) — a neutral colour, named in the legend.
Apply the same style to every map — same colours, same order, same legend text.
Compose each map — title naming the group, legend, scale bar, north arrow, source; same extent and scale on every map.

Output: two or more maps that can be laid side by side and read with one legend.
Epistemic Choices to record

Class method: round manual boundaries make maps comparable and readable; quantiles or natural breaks computed per map do not.
Number of classes: five to seven is about what a reader can tell apart.
Colours: one sequential colour scheme for a quantity that only goes up; a diverging scheme only if there is a meaningful middle (e.g. the city average).
What the colour does not show: the number of points behind each zone. A zone with 25 dwellings and one with 2,500 get the same weight on the map; consider printing counts, or a second map of counts.
Large, empty zones dominate: a big zone with few dwellings draws the eye more than a small dense one with many.

tasks/context-massing-(task).title: Context massing (Task)
tasks/context-massing-(task).content:
Used in: Urban Design Visualisation (Example). Depends on: Building heights from elevation models (Task). Implementation: Context massing (Recipe - Blender).
Context massing is the Task of turning 2D building footprints with height attributes into a simple 3D model of the surrounding city: a 2.5D-to-3D extrusion (see 2.5D geometries, 3D geometries) at a deliberately chosen Level of Detail:

LOD1 — each footprint extruded to its height as a flat-topped block.
LOD2 — each footprint extruded to its eave height, with a roof form added on top.

Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Decide the Level of Detail per building (decision point) — typically LOD2 only for the buildings that frame the subject and appear in close views, and LOD1 for the rest. Record the choice as an ordinal lod attribute.
Place the terrain (Operator, optional) — import the DTM as a surface, so the buildings stand on real ground. Worth it wherever the site slopes.
Extrude (Operator) — LOD1 buildings to height; LOD2 buildings to eave; each standing at ground.
Model the roof forms (decision point + Operator) — for each LOD2 building, choose the roof form (gable, hipped, pyramid, mansard, flat with parapet) from photographs or the site visit, and raise the ridge by roof_rise. About half a metre of accuracy is enough.
Apply one neutral material (decision point) — the context is the ground of the image, not the figure; see Visual hierarchy and figure-ground.
Clean the geometry (Operator) — merge duplicate vertices and make all faces point outwards, so the model survives export.

Output: a 3D context model, georeferenced, with the LOD of every building known.
Task Recipes (tool-bound)

Blender + BlenderGIS: Context massing (Recipe - Blender)
QGIS 3D view (LOD1 only, for a quick check): extrude the footprints by the height field in the layer’s 3D View properties.

tasks/georeferencing-(task).title: Georeferencing (Task)
tasks/georeferencing-(task).content:
See also: Backdrop digitalisation (The technology stack/QGIS) — a walkthrough that assumes this Task’s output as a prerequisite. Implementation: Georeferencing (Recipe - QGIS).
Georeferencing is the Task of assigning a Coordinate Reference System to an image (a scanned map, an aerial photograph, a satellite image) that does not yet carry one, so that it can be used as a Realisation-bearing source alongside other spatial data. It is tool-agnostic: every Stack that offers georeferencing implements the same underlying Task Schema below, with different interfaces and defaults.
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)
The Task decomposes into decision points and Operations. The order below is fixed; the content of each step is not.


Identify control points (decision point) — locate a set of points on the image being georeferenced that are also identifiable in a reference source (Ground Control Points, GCPs). This is a human judgement call, not an Operation: it requires recognising the same real-world feature in two representations — a road intersection, a building corner, a natural landmark — and is not mechanically executable. The number and spatial distribution of control points needed depends on the transformation chosen in step 3.


Obtain corresponding coordinates (decision point + acquisition) — for each control point identified in step 1, obtain its known real-world coordinates from another source. Common sources: an already-georeferenced basemap or orthophoto (visually matching a point on both), a field-surveyed GCP with measured coordinates, or an existing georeferenced dataset. This step may itself be a nested Task (e.g., a field GCP survey has its own decision points and Operators) rather than a single Operator — see the note on Task composition as a graph, not a hierarchy, in the Terminology Glossary (§9, at the vault root).


Choose and apply a transformation (Operation) — with control-point/coordinate pairs established, apply a transformation that warps/rectifies the image into the target CRS. This is the Operation proper: mechanically executable by an Operator (a person following a defined procedure, or software) once its inputs are fixed. Two families:

First-order (affine) transformation — scales, rotates, and translates the image, assuming a flat surface with no lens distortion. Sufficient when the source has no optical distortion to correct — typically a scanned paper map or historical map.
Higher-order (polynomial, second-order and above) transformation — warps the image using polynomial equations to correct non-linear distortion, needed when the image was captured through a lens (an aerial or satellite photograph), where perspective and lens distortion bend the image, especially near its edges. Higher polynomial order corrects more precisely but requires more control points and computation — this is itself a judgement call, not a fixed rule: over-fitting the polynomial to too few control points can warp the image to match noise rather than genuine distortion.

Choice of transformation order is a judgement informed by the source of the image, not a mechanical default — e.g., aerial/satellite imagery and urban-planning overlay work typically warrant higher-order rectification, while a scanned map typically does not.


Output: a georeferenced image, ready to serve as a backdrop/reference for further work — e.g., feeding into Backdrop digitalisation as its step 1 prerequisite, or directly into Recording the Domain of Discourse.
Task Recipes (tool-bound)

QGIS: Georeferencing (Recipe - QGIS)
ArcGIS: (not yet written)


Open item: this is the first Task write-up using the Task/Schema/Recipe template — once a second or third Task exists (e.g., “correct a hydrologically-sound DTM”, “create a table”), revisit this template for consistency rather than treating this file’s exact shape as final.

tasks/history-from-yearly-snapshots-(tas.title: History from yearly snapshots (Task)
tasks/history-from-yearly-snapshots-(tas.content:
Implementation: History from yearly snapshots (Recipe - QGIS).
History from yearly snapshots is the Task of turning a register that is published as a new layer each year (the fields farmers declare, field blocks, environmental schemes) into one layer that says, for every piece of land, what it was in each year of a period, and then summarising that history: a crop sequence, a combination of crops, the number of years with a given crop. Registers like these are made for one year’s administration; each year is digitised anew, the attributes change, and the codes are redefined. The history has to be assembled, and most of the analysis’s choices are made while assembling it.
Used in examples: Crop rotations at Ledreborg (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

State the period, the area and the unit (decision point): which years, which area (with a margin?), and whether the unit is the register’s own feature (a field as declared that year) or a piece of land that keeps its identity over the years.
Fetch every year for the area (Operators: clip to extent, merge) into one layer with a field for the year. Whole features or clipped at the area’s edge is a decision: clipped for area statistics, whole when an attribute refers to the whole feature.
Make the codes comparable (Task: Categories from register codes (Task)): translate each year’s codes into categories that mean the same in every year (a crop class).
Count per category and year (Operator: group-by statistics): area per category and year, before going further.
Flatten (Operator: union, with snapping) (decision point: the tolerance): one layer of pieces, each with one column per year. Boundaries digitised a little differently from year to year must not become thousands of slivers; differences wider than the tolerance are treated as real change.
Summarise each piece’s history (Operator: derive a value per feature) (decision point): the sequence, the unordered combination, the number of years with a category, or the first year of a change.
Map and count the summaries (Operator: group-by statistics): area per summary value; the largest ones on a map.

Output: a layer of pieces with the category in each year and the summary fields, and tables of area per category and year and per summary value.
Epistemic Choices to record

Declared, not observed: a register of applications says what was applied for, not what grew. A satellite image (NDVI) can check it on the ground.
The newest geometry wins: flattening keeps the newest boundaries and moves older ones onto them. State the tolerance, and that strips narrower than it disappear.
Incomplete histories: a piece that is in the register in only some years has a shorter history; say how many years a summary is based on, and whether incomplete pieces are left out.
Unordered or ordered: a combination of crops ignores where in its rotation a field is, which is its strength; it also ignores the order, which matters when one crop prepares for the next (grass ploughed before cereals releases nitrogen).
The categories are the analysis: which codes count as, for example, legumes decides the map. Record the definition.
Preliminary years: the current year of a register is often preliminary and still changing; give the date of the extract.

tasks/multi-criteria-suitability-(task).title: Multi-criteria suitability (Task)
tasks/multi-criteria-suitability-(task).content:
Implementation: Multi-criteria suitability (Recipe - QGIS).
Multi-criteria suitability is the Task of ranking units by several criteria at once, where a weakness in one criterion can be made up by strength in another. Each criterion is turned into a score on a common scale, multiplied by a weight, and the weighted scores are added into one suitability value per unit (a weighted linear combination). Changing the weights gives another scenario from the same data. For the concepts behind it (constraints and factors, compensation, weighting methods, sensitivity), see Multi-criteria analysis.
Used in examples: Densification priorities in Copenhagen by multi-criteria analysis (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Choose the units and the criteria — what is being ranked, and the criteria that matter for the question. For each criterion, write what it stands for and its level of measurement: a distance is a ratio value, a heritage class is ordinal.
Audit each criterion — look at its distribution before it is rescaled: empty values, zeros that mean “unknown”, and extreme values. One extreme value can decide the rescaling of all the others. Where a criterion has no meaning for a unit (land per address on a parcel that is all road), its value is NULL, not a score.
Score each criterion on a common scale (decision point) — by a scoring function chosen for the criterion: a linear scale, a z-score, a percentile rank, thresholds or a lookup table, with NULL for the units the criterion cannot score. See Scoring criteria (Task); the choice also decides how much each criterion counts (step 7).
Set the direction — decide, for each criterion, whether a high score is good or bad for the question. A bad one gets a negative weight, or is reversed (100 − score) before weighting.
Weight and add (decision point; Operator: weighted sum) — write the weights and the argument for them. Weights that add up to 1 (in absolute value) keep the result on the scale of the scores.
Rank and select (Operator: rank) — sort by suitability and keep the top k, or a share.
Check the effective weights — the nominal weight times the criterion’s spread (its standard deviation). If the effective weights differ much from the nominal ones, the rescaling, not the weights, decides the result: go back to step 3.
Make a second scenario — another set of weights for another priority, and compare the two selections: how many units are in both?

Output: a suitability value and a rank per unit for each scenario, the top selections, and the weights and rescaling written down with them.
Epistemic Choices to record

Compensation: a weighted sum lets a very good score make up for a very bad one. Where a criterion must not be compensated (a listed building, a flood zone), screen it out first (Site screening by criteria (Task)) and weigh only what is left.
The rescaling is a weight too: with division by the maximum or min–max, a criterion with a large spread gets more influence than its weight says. Report the effective weights next to the nominal ones.
Ordinal criteria: adding classes 1–9 treats the step from 1 to 2 as equal to the step from 8 to 9. A percentile rank makes that assumption visible instead of hiding it.
Missing values: a unit without a value gets a score by some rule, best, worst or the median, and that rule can move it to the top. Record it.
Ranks are relative: the top 100 are the best of these units under these weights, not good sites in themselves.

tasks/placing-register-units-on-the-map-.filePath: Tasks/Placing register units on the map (Task).md
tasks/placing-register-units-on-the-map-.title: Placing register units on the map (Task)
tasks/placing-register-units-on-the-map-.content:
Implementation: Placing register units on the map (Recipe - QGIS).
Placing register units on the map is the Task of giving units from a register a location: a flat in BBR, a company in CVR, a person in a statistical extract. The unit itself has no coordinates. It has ids that point to other registers, and the location is found by following those ids from table to table. For a dwelling in BBR there are two routes: through the address register (DAR) to the address point at the entrance, or through BBR to the building’s point.
Used in examples: Share of rented dwellings in Copenhagen (Example), Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).

The example building, Eksempelgade 12–14, is made up. One BBR building has two entrances, each a DAR house number; every flat is a BBR unit with its own DAR address. Flats on the same staircase share one address point.
The joins
Every step is a join: a field holding an id in one table matches id_lokalId, the id of a row, in the next table.



































StepFrom (field)To (field)What it gives1BBR_Enhed.adresseIdentificererDAR_Adresse.id_lokalIdthe unit’s full address, with floor and door: adressebetegnelse2DAR_Adresse.husnummerDAR_Husnummer.id_lokalIdthe entrance, also called the access address (adgangsadresse): adgangsadressebetegnelse3DAR_Husnummer.adgangspunktDAR_Adressepunkt.id_lokalIdthe entrance’s coordinates: positionAlternativeBBR_Enhed.bygningBBR_Bygning.id_lokalIdthe building’s coordinates byg404Koordinat, construction year, building use
The old name for a house number is adgangsadresse (from DAWA and the old BBR), which is why the field is called adgangsadressebetegnelse.
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Get each register’s table (Operator: extract to the area) — for Copenhagen the downloads for municipality 0101 where Datafordeleren offers them; DAR’s national tables filtered to the municipality.
Select the units (Operator: selection by attribute) — e.g. standing dwellings.
Choose the route (decision point) — address point or building point.
Join step by step (Operator: join by key) — unit → address → house number → address point; or unit → building.
Make the points (Operator: join onto the point layer, one point per unit).
Count — units in, points out; list the units that found no address or no building.

Output: one point per unit, with the unit’s attributes and its address.
Epistemic Choices to record

Address point or building point: the address point when the staircase matters (a long block on a corner can have entrances on two streets, 50 m or more apart, and in different statistical districts); the building point when one point per building is enough or when a unit has no address. It takes one join instead of three.
Neither point is the unit: every flat on a staircase gets the same point. Floor and door are only in the address text.
Units that do not match: in Copenhagen, 8,590 of 491,935 units have no DAR address, all of them historic, closed or registered in error; 1,672 units have no building point. Say how many were lost and why.
Current or historical: the downloads exist as Current and with history; mixing them gives several versions of the same unit.
Date: each register is extracted on its own date.

tasks/scoring-criteria-(task).title: Scoring criteria (Task)
tasks/scoring-criteria-(task).content:
Implementation: Scoring criteria (Recipe - QGIS).
Scoring criteria is the Task of turning the raw values of a criterion (a distance, an area per address, a heritage class) into a score on a common scale, so that it can be combined with other criteria in a suitability index or a multi-criteria analysis. The score says how good a unit is on this one criterion: by convention 0 is worst and 100 best. The way a score is calculated is as much a decision as the weight it gets later.
Used in: Multi-criteria suitability (Task). Examples: Densification priorities in Copenhagen by multi-criteria analysis (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Say what the criterion stands for — and which direction is good: near a station is good, near a motorway is bad. Note its level of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio.
Audit the raw values — their distribution: empty values, zeros, extreme values, codes that mean “unknown” (−1, 0, 9999). Look at the units behind the extremes before deciding what to do with them.
Decide what is held out (decision point) — the units for which the criterion has no meaning, or no known value, get NULL (see below).
Choose the scoring function (decision point; Operator: rescale) — from the table below, by what the criterion means and how its values are distributed.
Set the direction — so that 100 is always good: reverse a score where high raw values are bad (100 − score), or let a negative weight do it later. Do one or the other, and write down which.
Check the scores — their distribution after scoring: the median, the spread, and how many units share the same score. A score where almost every unit is near 0, or where a quarter of the units share the maximum, will not do what its weight says.

Output: a score field per criterion, 0–100 (or z-scores), with NULL for held-out units, and a note of the function, its parameters and the direction.
Ways of calculating a score



























































FunctionScoreSuitsWatch outDivide by the maximum100 · x / maxratio values that start at 0 and have no outliersone extreme value squeezes all others towards 0Min–max100 · (x − min) / (max − min)interval and ratio values without outliersas above, at both endsz-score(x − mean) / standard deviationinterval and ratio values, roughly symmetricnot 0–100; outliers stay outliers (a z of 175 outweighs everything)Percentile rankthe share of units with a lower value, 0–100skewed values; ordinal valuesthe distances between values are lost; many equal values share one rankLog, then min–maxmin–max of log(x + 1)ratio values with a long right tail (areas, counts, incomes)log(0) is undefined, hence the + 1; the result is harder to explainThresholds (linear between)100 up to a, 0 beyond b, linear betweencriteria with a known good and bad range: 100 within 400 m of a station, 0 beyond 1,200 ma and b are choices to justify, e.g. from a plan or a walking-distance studyDistance decay100 · e^(−x / d)accessibility, where each extra metre matters lessthe decay distance d is a choice; the score never reaches 0Lookup tablea score per classnominal and ordinal criteria (land use, SAVE classes, soil types)the scores of the classes are judgements; write them in a table
The thresholds and lookup functions put knowledge of the domain into the score: what counts as near, what a class is worth. The statistical functions (min–max, z-score, percentile rank) only use the distribution of the data at hand, so the same parcel gets another score if the study area changes.
What each function does to the data
A score is a new distribution, and its shape decides how much the criterion counts in a weighted sum. The figures below score two criteria of Copenhagen’s 33,818 parcels (the data of the densification Example): distance to a station, which has a moderate right tail, and land per address, which has an extreme one. In each figure the left histogram shows the original values and the right one the scores. The scores are shown before the direction is set (step 5): for distance, a high score here still means far.
Divide by the maximum

The shape is kept, but a few parcels 7–8 km from a station set the maximum, so 86% of the parcels score below 15. The criterion uses a sixth of the scale, and in a weighted sum it counts far less than its weight says.
Min–max

Land per address runs from 0 to 3.3 million m² (a large parcel with one address). All but 50 parcels land in the first percent of the scale: practically every parcel scores 0, and the criterion does nothing. Min–max is only as good as the two most extreme units.
z-score

The z-score centres the values on 0 but keeps the outlier: 98% of the parcels lie within ±0.1 of the mean, and one parcel has a z of 175. In a weighted sum that one parcel outweighs everything else.
Percentile rank

Any distribution becomes flat: every score is equally common. The outlier is just the last rank, and every criterion gets the same spread, so the weights mean what they say. The price is that distances between values are lost: a parcel with 2,000 m² per address and one with 20,000 m² are less than 2 points apart (98 and 100), although one has ten times the land of the other.
Log, then min–max

The logarithm pulls in the long tail, and the values spread out across the middle of the scale. The outlier still sets the maximum, so few parcels score above 60.
Thresholds, linear between

Domain knowledge sets the scale: 32% of the parcels are within 400 m of a station and all score 100, and 14% are beyond 1,200 m and all score 0. Differences inside the good and the bad range are deliberately ignored. If almost all units fall on one side of the thresholds, the criterion stops separating them; choose thresholds that cut the actual spread of the data.
Distance decay

The scores fall steeply over the first few hundred metres and then flatten: the difference between 100 and 300 m counts much more than between 1,100 and 1,300 m. With a decay distance of 500 m the median parcel scores 34. No parcel reaches 0.
Lookup table

The nine SAVE classes become three scores. A quarter of the parcels have no assessment; they are not a class, and the table gives them NULL rather than a score (see the next section).
Held-out units: NULL, not 0 and not the mean
Some units cannot be scored on a criterion: land per address on a parcel that is all road, a distance that was never measured, a building no one assessed. What to do with them is the most consequential choice in the scoring, and the easiest to make without noticing. Every tool makes it for you if you don’t make it yourself.
NULL is usually “no data”, and here it means more
In a database, NULL is the normal mark of a missing value, and in rasters a declared NoData value (often −9999 or 0) does the same job. Usually it records an accident: the value was not collected. When a criterion is scored, NULL is used on purpose. It says this unit is held out of this comparison, either because the criterion has no meaning for it or because it can’t be scored fairly. The problem is that the same mark is used both ways: a NULL in the data you were given may be an accident, and a NULL you set may later be read as one. So write down which NULLs you set and why.
The opposite mistake is common in the data you get: a missing value stored as a number. A distance of 0, a SAVE class of 0 or −1, or a score of 100 for “not applicable” will be scored, averaged and ranked as if it were measured.
What filling a gap does
The figure below scores the SAVE assessment of the Copenhagen parcels (SAVE ÷ 9 × 100) and gives the 8,365 parcels that were never assessed four different treatments:


As 0, the unassessed parcels become the largest group, at the bottom of the scale: “not assessed” is now “of the highest preservation value”. The mean drops from 46 to 35, and the standard deviation rises.
As the mean, they pile up in the middle. The mean stays the same, but the standard deviation shrinks from 15 to 13. The criterion separates units less well, and a quarter of the parcels claim to be average without anyone knowing.
As 100, as in the dataset first given to the students, they become the best parcels for densification.
As NULL, the distribution of the assessed parcels is left as it is, and the 8,365 parcels drop out of any ranking that uses the criterion.

The effect on a ranking is larger than on the histogram. Here the scenario that weights heritage highest (weight 0.4) is ranked with the scores from the student exercise, varying only the unassessed parcels:








































Unassessed parcels scored asParcels rankedUnassessed in the top 100in the top 1,000in the bottom 1,000NULL25,437———0 (highest value: protect)33,7010053950 (the middle class)33,70104020100 (lowest value: build)33,701979330
Each row answers a different question. NULL ranks only the parcels we know something about. 0 assumes that unknown buildings must be protected, and 100 that they may go. 50 assumes they are ordinary. None of them is the “correct” answer the data could settle.
Three cases
Distinguish three cases, and record which one applies:

























CaseExampleTreatmentNot applicable: the criterion has no meaning for the unitland per address on a road parcel or a parcel without addressesNULLUnknown: the criterion applies, but the value is missinga building without a SAVE assessmentNULL, or an estimate stated as such: the value of similar units (same period, same street), a field survey, or a deliberately cautious value, with the reasonExcluded: the unit must not be chosen whatever its scoresa listed building, a lakea constraint: screen it out first (Site screening by criteria (Task))
A NULL works without extra steps. Aggregates skip it (count, mean, standard deviation and maximum use only real values), so it does not move the scaling of the other units. A sum with a NULL is NULL, so the unit gets no suitability and drops out of the ranking without a separate filter. The cost is that it drops out: if a quarter of the units are NULL, the result covers three quarters of the city, and the map should show where the gaps are.
Check that NULL stays NULL. Most calculations pass a NULL on, but not all: in QGIS, exp(NULL) returns 1, so a distance-decay score turns a missing distance into the best score, 100. coalesce() and some tools replace NULL with 0 without asking. Test the scoring on a unit with NULL before trusting it.
A wicked problem: record it in the Design Rationale
The treatment of held-out units is a small instance of a wicked problem (Rittel & Webber, 1973). There is no definitive formulation: is an unassessed building worth preserving? is a question of heritage policy, not of data. The answers are not true or false but better or worse for someone: a developer and a heritage officer will prefer different rows of the table above. Each answer changes the result, and there is no stopping rule that tells you when you have chosen right.
So the choice is not for the analyst to settle quietly in a field calculator expression. In SemanticGIS it belongs in the Design Rationale, next to the Analytical Schema, written as an issue with its positions and arguments:

Issue: how are the 8,365 parcels without a SAVE assessment scored?
Positions: NULL (left out of the ranking); 0 (protect until assessed); 50 (assume ordinary); an estimate from buildings of the same period.
Arguments: NULL leaves out a quarter of the city, mostly … ; 0 favours preservation, …
Decision: … , and its consequence for the result: … parcels ranked, … of the top 100 affected.

If the choice matters, run the analysis under two positions and show both: the units that rank high under both are robust to it. See sensitivity.
Epistemic Choices to record

The function and its parameters, and why they fit the criterion: a threshold of 1,200 m because…, a percentile rank because the values are skewed.
The shape of the scores: the histogram before and after scoring, and how much of the scale the criterion actually uses.
The direction of every criterion.
Statistical or domain-based: a statistical score is relative to the units in the study; a domain-based score (thresholds, lookup tables) can be compared between studies.
Held-out units: which units got NULL, how many, under which of the three cases, and where on the map they are. For unknown values, the positions considered and the one chosen, as an issue in the Design Rationale.

tasks/site-screening-by-criteria-(task).title: Site screening by criteria (Task)
tasks/site-screening-by-criteria-(task).content:
Implementation: Site screening by criteria (Recipe - QGIS).
Site screening by criteria is the Task of finding the areas that meet every one of a set of conditions: near a station, not protected, not a park, large enough. Each condition is a filter, and an area is kept only if it passes all of them. The method is old in planning, where it is known as sieve mapping: each criterion is a sheet that blocks out the unsuitable land, and what shows through the stack of sheets is the result. In the terms of multi-criteria analysis, every criterion is a constraint.
Used in examples: Sites for new housing near stations in Copenhagen (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Choose the candidate units (decision point) — what is being screened: parcels, buildings, grid cells or the land itself. Parcels follow ownership and plans; a grid or the land follows the terrain, not the owners.
Write each criterion as a condition — with its threshold and the reason for it, before touching the data: within 600 m of a station, no listed building, at least 1,000 m² left. Name the source of each threshold: a plan, a guideline, a study, or your own judgement.
Sort the criteria by kind — a condition on the unit’s own attributes (Operator: selection by attribute); a relation to another layer, kept or excluded (Operator: selection by location), often after a buffer (Operator: dilation); or a part of the unit to remove, such as the part inside a park (Operator: difference).
Apply the criteria one by one and count what is left after each step. The counts show which criterion does the work, and which hardly changes anything.
Apply size criteria last — a minimum area only makes sense for what is left once parts have been cut away.
Inspect the result — look at the largest and the most surprising areas on a map or an orthophoto. A screening keeps everything the data do not exclude, including lakes, railway land and cemeteries, if no layer says what they are.

Output: the units that pass every criterion, with a table of counts per step, and the map of criteria that led to them.
Epistemic Choices to record

Every criterion is a veto. A unit 601 m from a station is out, however good it is in every other way. If some criteria should be weighed against each other rather than block, the question calls for multi-criteria suitability instead.
Thresholds are borrowed or chosen. Write down where each one comes from, and try one or two others: the result is often more sensitive to a threshold than to the choice of criteria.
Which relation: intersects keeps a parcel that only touches a buffer; within or the parcel’s centre point are stricter. See Spatial relations.
What the data leave out: a criterion can only exclude what a layer contains. Missing layers (water, rail land, contaminated soil, existing plans) let unsuitable areas through.

tasks/slope-and-flow-direction-(task).title: Slope and flow direction (Task)
tasks/slope-and-flow-direction-(task).content:
Implementation: Slope and flow direction from DHM (Recipe - QGIS). Data: the DHM terrain model through the DHM WCS — see WCS for why it must be a coverage, not a WMS picture.
Slope and flow direction is the Task of deriving, from a terrain model, how steep the ground is and which way water on the surface will run. Slope answers questions of accessibility, erosion risk and building suitability; flow direction is the first step of every surface-water analysis (catchments, flow paths, accumulation).
Used in examples: hydrologically corrected terrain models and Hydrological modelling (with the problem of bridges in the terrain model). Domain Examples bring in the domain knowledge (hydrology, planning) that decides which choices below matter; this Task stays domain-neutral.
In workflow terms it produces derived layers from primary elevation data: the results are only as good as the terrain model and the choices made below.
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Choose the elevation source (decision point) — a terrain model (DTM, the bare ground), not a surface model (DSM): water does not flow over tree crowns and roofs. Note its date and vertical datum.
Acquire a local copy (Operator: extract by extent) — the study area plus a margin, at a deliberately chosen resolution (see WCS), in the model’s own coordinate system.
Make the surface hydrologically sound (Operator: fill sinks) — fill closed depressions so every cell can drain to an edge, keeping a minimal downhill gradient across filled areas.
Compute slope (Operator: focal/neighbourhood) — the steepest gradient of each cell against its neighbours, in degrees (or percent).
Compute flow direction (Operator: steepest descent, D8) — for each cell, the one of its eight neighbours that water flows to.
Optionally, accumulate flow (Operator: flow accumulation) — how many cells drain through each cell; high values trace streams and drainage lines.

Output: a slope raster (degrees), a flow direction raster (eight directions) and, optionally, flow accumulation — on the same grid as the local terrain model.
Epistemic Choices to record

Resolution: a finer grid resolves ditches, kerbs and small dikes that steer real water; a coarser grid gives smoother landscape-scale results. The two give different flow paths.
To fill or not to fill: filling removes all depressions. In flat Danish terrain many depressions are real — lakes, wetlands and bluespots where water actually collects. Filling is right for tracing flow paths, wrong for mapping where water stands. Say which question you are answering.
Bridges, culverts and tunnels: a terrain model shows a road embankment as a dam even where a culvert runs under it. Flow paths that stop at embankments may need burning in.
Single (D8) or multiple flow direction: D8 sends all water to one neighbour; multiple-direction methods spread it. D8 is simpler to read and is what this Task produces.
Minimum slope used when filling, and the units of slope (degrees or percent).

Task Recipes (tool-bound)

QGIS: Slope and flow direction from DHM (Recipe - QGIS)
Python: (not yet written — rasterio plus pysheds or richdem would implement the same Schema)

tasks/surface-partitioning-(task).title: Surface partitioning (Task)
tasks/surface-partitioning-(task).content:
Used in: Urban Design Visualisation (Example). Implementation: Surface partitioning (Recipe - QGIS).
Surface partitioning is the Task of turning a collection of edge lines — road edges, kerbs, building outlines — into a planar partition: a set of polygons that covers an area completely, with no gaps and no overlaps, each classified by surface type. Many national datasets record the edges of streets and pavements but not the areas between them; this Task recovers the areas.
The planar partition is itself a topological constraint (the fifth commitment of the Domain of Discourse), and the Task is mostly about satisfying it.
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Select the boundary sources (decision point) — which line layers are real boundaries? Edge lines are; centre lines are not, and must be excluded, or every road is split lengthwise.
Collect and node the edges (Operator) — merge all boundary lines into one layer, snap near-coincident ends within a small tolerance (e.g., 0.3 m) and split lines where they cross.
Find the gaps (Operator) — mark dangles: loose line ends that prevent areas from closing.
Close gaps and add missing boundaries (decision point) — by hand: close each gap, delete overshoots, and draw the boundaries the data lacks (plaza edges, planting beds). This is where the site visit and the orthophoto come in.
Polygonize (Operator) — build polygons from the closed line network. Polygons inside building footprints are classed building.
Classify (Operator + decision point) — a spatial join with the centre lines (and their road type) gives a hint; the practitioner sets the final nominal class: road, cycle path, footpath / pavement, plaza, parking, green, water, building, other.
Iterate — a missing polygon means a remaining gap: return to step 3.

Output: a classified surface layer satisfying the planar-partition constraint. Precision matters where the map will be read closely; elsewhere it can be rough, and that should be stated.
Task Recipes (tool-bound)

QGIS: Surface partitioning (Recipe - QGIS)

tasks/vegetation-index-from-satellite-im.title: Vegetation index from satellite imagery (Task)
tasks/vegetation-index-from-satellite-im.content:
Implementation: Vegetation index from Sentinel-2 (Recipe - QGIS).
Vegetation index from satellite imagery is the Task of turning a multispectral satellite image of a study area into a map of how green, how dense and how active its vegetation is: NDVI, or another index. It is the first quantitative step from an image to a map of the land surface, and the basis for comparing places, seasons and years. Theory: Remote sensing, especially Spectral signatures and vegetation indices.
Used in examples: Vegetation greenness at Ledreborg (Example).
Task Schema (tool-agnostic)

Define the study area — a polygon, with a margin.
Choose the image (decision point; Operator: selection of images by location, date and cloud cover) — a date that fits the question (the season, the stage of the crops), clear over the study area itself, surface reflectance (Level-2A for Sentinel-2).
Get the bands for the area (Operator: clip to extent) — red and near infrared for NDVI; the scene classification for a cloud mask; blue and green for a true-colour image to look at.
Know the values (decision point) — reflectance (0–1) or scaled integers (× 10,000); whether an offset must be removed; the NoData value.
Look at the image — a true-colour and a colour-infrared composite: clouds, haze, shadows, and what the area holds.
Calculate the index (Operator: map algebra) — NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red).
Mask what is not surface (Operator: map algebra with a condition) — cloud, cloud shadow, defective and unclassified pixels.
Check the result — the values lie between −1 and 1, and known surfaces have the values they should: water below 0, roads and roofs near 0, forest and crops in June 0.8–0.9.
Summarise if needed (Operator: zonal statistics) — the index per zone or per land-use class (Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task)).

Output: an index raster of the study area, masked, with a record of the image (satellite, date, product level) and the formula.
Epistemic Choices to record

Date: NDVI follows the growing season. A June image and an August image of the same field can differ from bare soil to dense crop. Comparisons need images from the same time of year.
Product level: surface reflectance makes dates and places comparable; top-of-atmosphere reflectance still contains haze.
Saturation: above about 0.8 NDVI barely separates dense vegetation types; forest and a closed crop look alike. Another date, another index or a colour-infrared image may separate them.
Mixed pixels: at 10 m, narrow and small features (roads, streams, ponds, hedges) take part of their value from their surroundings.
Mask: which classes count as not surface; the scene classification is automatic and misses thin cloud and some shadow.
What NDVI is: an index of greenness, not a measure of biomass, yield or biodiversity. Linking it to those needs field data.

terminology-glossary.title: Terminology Glossary
terminology-glossary.content:
Working reference for internal consistency. Compiled from drafting discussion; verify each entry against the manuscript before treating it as final. Moved to the vault root because it now documents terms that span both the Workflow (Vantage Points, Activities) and the root-level, cross-cutting Tasks/Operators/Tools — it is no longer a Workflow-only reference.

1. Top-Level Terms























































TermDefinitionNotesSemanticGISThe title of the book and name of the methodology/pedagogy it teaches. Full title: SemanticGIS — Designing and Documenting Geospatial Workflows.Never the grammatical subject of verbs like yields, produces, is executed — it teaches, structures, governs. Geospatial Workflows do the producing/executing.GISReserved strictly for the operational technology stack — desktop software (QGIS, ArcGIS) or code ecosystems (Python/R libraries).Deliberately narrowed from Goodchild/Chrisman’s “GI Science.” Framed as a stipulative convention for this book, not a claim about the wider field’s terminology debate.StackSettled. The dedicated term for the computational/technology layer — QGIS, ArcGIS, a Python ecosystem. Interchangeable with GIS in its technology sense.Takes over the computational sense entirely, freeing “Framework” (below) to revert to generic use.Geospatial WorkflowThe specific, documented sequence of semantic reasoning by which a spatial question (from a Domain Project) is answered. Comprises the five Vantage Points and the continuous practice of Workflow Stewardship.This is what SemanticGIS teaches practitioners to design. Stewardship is part of the Workflow, not a parallel track.Domain ProjectThe overarching real-world endeavour (e.g., urban planning, environmental risk management) that sets the brief and human intent.Contains one or more Geospatial Workflows. A single Workflow never spans multiple Projects.Domain ExampleA worked example of a Domain Project (in the vault’s Domain Examples folder): one or more Geospatial Workflows together with the knowledge from outside the strictly geospatial domain that shapes them — urban design, ethnography, landscape ecology, hydrology, energy planning. It is the top level of the chain Domain Example → Geospatial Workflow → Task → Operator → Tool (see §9).⚠️ Added; confirm wording. The domain knowledge is what decides the Spatial Intent and the epistemic choices further down the chain (e.g. in urban design the workflow produces a context for a proposal, not an answer). Tasks and Operators stay domain-neutral and reusable; a Domain Example links to them rather than owning them.FrameworkSettled. Generic term, no longer globally reserved — freed once “Stack” took over the computational sense. Anchors Vantage Point 2’s title (“Establishing the Data Framework”), unchanged from the original draft.Must read unambiguously within its sentence, but no longer needs one fixed meaning book-wide. Manual pass still worthwhile wherever it appears, confirming no stray computational-sense usage remains that should say “Stack” instead.Vantage PointSettled this session. The name for the five main structural positions of the Workflow (Scoping, Establishing the Data Framework, Authoring the Analytical Schema, Designing Spatial Results Communication, Executing the Analytical Schema). See §2.Replaces the earlier, now-retired use of “Activity” for this top level — see next row.ActivitySettled this session. The work performed at a given Vantage Point — what was previously called a “Phase” within Establishing the Data Framework (Activity One–Five, see §3) is the clearest existing example. A Vantage Point can have one or several Activities; the number is not fixed at five the way Vantage Points are.”Phase” is retired in favour of this term. Sits under Workflow, at the same scope as Vantage Point — both are Workflow-internal, unlike Task, which lives at the vault root (see §9).

2. The Five Vantage Points
Five positions the practitioner occupies and revisits over the course of a workflow, each disclosing an aspect of the workflow that no other vantage can. Scoping is always first; Execution is always last. Movement between the three middle Vantage Points is free and expected.



































#Vantage PointWhat it uniquely discloses1Scoping the WorkflowHuman intent and political/ethical/operational constraint. Always entered first.2Establishing the Data FrameworkOntological fit (or gap) between the ideal and the given. See §3 below for its internal Activity structure.3Authoring the Analytical SchemaThe tool-agnostic mathematical/logical structure required to answer the question.4Designing Spatial Results CommunicationLegibility of the result to the Lifeworld it serves. See §5 below.5Executing the Analytical SchemaThe operational/computational reality of a specific Stack. Always entered last.
Workflow Stewardship — not a sixth Vantage Point (it has no partial view of its own); the continuous documentation practice that records movement between vantages, including every Backward Glance and Epistemic Choice. Visually: not a node, but the annotation layer on the edges connecting the nodes.
Backward Glance — a named move within Stewardship: the audit performed at a transition between Vantage Points, checking whether the vantage just departed adequately resolved what the next one requires. Not confined to the immediately preceding vantage — can cascade as far back as the actually unresolved question originates (e.g., a Schema-stage gap tracing all the way back to Scoping).
