Epistemic Choice — the recurring hard decision, surfaced whenever the idealised model cannot be matched to existing/affordable data: compromise the model, or absorb the cost of harvesting new data. Itself a piece of Design Rationale.

3. Vantage Point 2 — Establishing the Data Framework
Now five tightly iterative Activities (revised from four, then five — Recording added; “Phase” retired in favour of “Activity,” see §1), moving from an idealised conception through formalisation and confrontation with observed reality to digital instantiation:









































ActivityNameConcept-level termDefinitionOneIdentifying the Universe of Discourse (Boole, 1854)ConceptThe unconstrained, ideal ontology the workflow would require, independent of what exists or can be observed.TwoAuditing Existing Data (retitled — “Sensoric Manifold” removed from this Activity; see Activity Four)Feature / Feature Class (GIS-technical terms, deliberately introduced here where the semantic and technical layers confront each other)Does the data exist, and how faithfully does it correspond to the ideal ontology? Audit is ontological, not merely one of coverage/resolution — existing (secondary) data carries the categories of whoever collected it; it is already-synthesised, not raw manifold.ThreeFormalising the Domain of DiscourseCognised Existence (mass noun — denotes a kind, not yet a countable instance; grammatically deliberate)The Universe of Discourse, bounded. Five commitments (see below). Functions as a validation gate the Analytical Schema must pass through. Triggers a mandatory Backward Glance to Activity Two, re-validating candidate data against the now-rigorous criteria.FourConfronting the Sensoric Manifold (Kant: Mannigfaltigkeit der Anschauung — the raw, unconceptualised given, prior to any synthesis; not hardware sensor data, and not existing/secondary datasets, which are already synthesised)—Always performed, even where the expected outcome is simple confirmation. Two functions: (1) Validation — does the formalised Domain of Discourse survive direct field contact? (2) Collection — where existing data is insufficient, the manifold is what new data is harvested from; a structured Realisation is extracted per the Domain of Discourse’s criteria. Data collection methodology proper deferred to Chapter [X]; this Activity establishes only its epistemic position.FiveRecording the Domain of DiscourseRealisation (converges here — see below)The digital instantiation of the formalised model: (1) Schema — a spatial table whose geometry type, fields, and field types faithfully carry the Domain of Discourse’s five commitments (Spatial Character, thematic specification, MMU, typing, topology), and whose coordinate reference system is additionally fit for the Analytical Schema’s intended Operators — CRS fitness is Recording’s own distinct concern, not a restatement of Activity Three’s typing (geometry type itself is settled at Activity Three, under Geometric Type; Recording only checks CRS); (2) Population — entering re-evaluated Accept/Transform Realisations from Activity Two, and digitising Collection Realisations from Activity Four, into that same schema. Corrects a stray earlier claim (still to check for remaining instances) that “creating database tables” belongs to Executing the Analytical Schema (Vantage Point 5) — it does not; see the GIS-as-record vs. GIS-as-analysis distinction below.
Activity Three’s five commitments

Spatial Character (name settled — replaces the earlier working label “discrete or continuous”; chosen because it connotes an assigned, decided role — echoing “Cast of Characters” — rather than a discovered, inherent “Nature”) — is the Cognised Existence a bounded, individually identifiable phenomenon (discrete), or a sampled instance of an unbounded continuous field (e.g., a temperature reading)? Settled before anything else because every other commitment depends on the answer: a continuous Cognised Existence has no boundary for thematic specification’s categorical dimension to bound, no MMU to fall below (its analogue is a minimum sampling/interpolation density), and no discrete extent for a topological containment test. Forward-referenced in full to Chapter [X]. (Open item: propagate “Spatial Character” into the actual chapter prose — as of this glossary update, every live use in the manuscript still says “discrete or continuous” without the settled name.)
Thematic specification — an intensional definition (necessary and sufficient conditions) for every Cognised Existence, letting a practitioner decide whether a specific phenomenon in the world is a legitimate instance of that class, given the Spatial Character already settled at (1). Categorical boundary conditions only now — e.g., does a houseboat, permanently moored and used for public events, count as a building? If venue is elsewhere defined as depending on building, the ambiguity propagates. Worked example: houseboat / building / venue (see below).
MMU (Minimum Mapping Unit) / temporal resolution — spatial and temporal resolution below which distinctions are not honoured. Branches on (1): MMU for discrete Cognised Existences; a minimum sampling density for continuous ones. Temporal resolution applies to both alike.
Typing, in two parts — (a) NOIR attribute typing (Nominal/Ordinal/Interval/Ratio — confirm this is the intended acronym, not “NORI”); and (b) Geometric Type — Point/Line/Polygon/Field, an explicit extension this manuscript adds to Stevens (1946) since spatial representation was no part of his problem. States which spatial Operators are legitimate upon a Cognised Existence, exactly as NOIR states which statistical operations are legitimate upon an attribute (e.g., a road typed as Line supports network analysis but not area calculation; typed as Polygon, the reverse). A continuous Cognised Existence is typed as Field automatically, following directly from (1) rather than as a fresh decision here. Geometric Type is an “inadmissible Operator” check, same family as NOIR — distinct from coordinate reference system fitness, which is a “computable but silently wrong” failure and remains Activity Five’s (Recording’s) job, not Activity Three’s.
Topological/spatial-relationship constraints — e.g., roads may not intersect lakes except at bridges; administrative boundaries must not gap or overlap.

Terminology used within thematic specification:

Phenomenon / phenomena — the vernacular, Kantian-justified term for “a specific encountered particular” (this houseboat, this temperature reading) — replaces the earlier, imprecise “thing.” Grammar: phenomenon singular, phenomena plural — check consistently.
“Class” replaced by “Cognised Existence” throughout this passage — mechanical fix, stray leftover from earlier TBox/ABox discussion.

Worked example — houseboat / building / venue: Running example tying Activities One through Four together. A houseboat’s status as building is contested (does the Domain require fixed connection to land?); if venue depends on building, the ambiguity inherits downward. Open consideration: whether to resurface this same example concretely at Activity Four (field-testing the houseboat at the jetty) to close the loop across all four Activities with one continuous case, rather than fresh examples per Activity.
Real-world case study — GeoDanmark building specification: Danish national building-object specification (§4, Representation) used as an authoritative, real-world instance of thematic specification — independently confirms houseboats as a genuine edge case (explicitly included: “husbåd og lignende”), gives real MMU thresholds (25 m² outside, 10 m² inside an Area Polygon, both municipally overridable — a real Epistemic Choice made in production), and is used pedagogically to show that formal precision at the structural level (thresholds to the m²) often coexists with unexamined vernacular terms at the level of meaning — e.g., “permanent” is never defined, despite doing the key classificatory work, and is complicated by the same spec’s separate provision for buildings under construction. The verbs skønnes (“is assessed/judged”) and the phrase “og lignende” (“and similar”) appear repeatedly, each silently delegating judgement back to the practitioner. Ties directly to Epistemic Choice / Backward Glance: this is exactly the kind of undocumented judgement Stewardship should surface, not let pass silently. (Full Danish text and English translation on file from drafting session — translation includes translator’s notes on “Områdepolygon” and “forefindes… ikke” worth checking against full GeoDanmark documentation before quoting in print.)
Realisation — a specific, located, data-backed instance (count noun: “a Realisation,” “these Realisations”). First meaningful appearance at Activity Two (is this feature a valid Realisation of the Activity One Concept?), carrying forward into Activity Three/Four (does it satisfy the formalised Cognised Existence, including its thematic specification?). Not used in Activity One — nothing exists yet to realise. Existing-data Realisations (Activity Two) and manifold-derived Realisations (Activity Four) are two different provenances of the same concept, and converge at Activity Five: both are entered into the same physical schema, and the finished spatial table should not itself reveal which provenance a given row came from.
GIS as instrument of record vs. instrument of analysis — resolves an apparent conflict between Activity Five and Vantage Point 5 (Executing the Analytical Schema), both of which involve GIS software. Activity Five uses GIS to build and populate a spatial table — an instrument of record, committing nothing about how the data will later be analysed. Vantage Point 5 uses GIS to execute the Analytical Schema’s Operators — an instrument of analysis. “GIS enters the workflow only at Vantage Point 5” (Part 1, §1.2) refers to this second sense specifically, not to any use of GIS software whatsoever; both places in the manuscript now say so explicitly.
Open item: Confirm whether your physical copy of Boole is genuinely dated 2005, or if the standard 1958 (Dover) / 2009 (CUP) reprint year applies — verify against your copy before citing.
Open item: A mechanical search-and-check pass is now owed on “thing” and “class” elsewhere in the manuscript (Activity Two, Activity Four, Epistemic Choice paragraph, and beyond) — same treatment as the “framework”/“SemanticGIS” consistency passes.

4. Vantage Point 3 — Authoring the Analytical Schema
The Schema’s only admissible input is the Recorded Domain of Discourse (Activity Five Realisations) — neither Activity One Concepts nor the raw Activity Four Sensoric Manifold qualify, since neither has been typed/geometried/CRS-fitted yet. This makes Authoring strictly downstream of both of Establishing the Data Framework’s gates (the five commitments, and Recording’s CRS-fitness check).
Analytical Schema as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — nodes are individual Operators (buffer, intersect, spatial join, reclassify — see §9 for the full Operator/Tool definition); edges are Realisations flowing from one Operator’s output into the next Operator’s input. Directed: data flows one way, Recorded input → final result, never backward into a completed step. Acyclic: no Operator may depend, even indirectly, on its own output — this is what guarantees the Schema terminates as a finite, well-ordered sequence rather than an undefined circular dependency.
Intermediate/derived Realisations — an Operator’s output is not a return to the Domain of Discourse; it is a new Realisation, often of a Cognised Existence the Domain of Discourse never needed to define because it exists only as an artefact internal to the analysis (e.g., a distance-to-nearest-venue value). The Schema must stay as explicit about these intermediate Realisations’ thematic meaning and typing as the Domain of Discourse was about Recorded ones — an Operator three nodes downstream can fail silently on a poorly-typed intermediate output exactly as the first Operator could on poorly-Recorded input.
Tool-agnosticism secured by the DAG framing — the graph specifies which Operator transforms which input into which output, and in what order, but not which software executes it. See §9 for how each Operator individually carries its own tool-agnostic Schema plus one Tool per Stack — the same duality the DAG as a whole has with its Analytical Recipe (§6).
5. Vantage Point 4 — Designing Spatial Results Communication
“Design” — used throughout in the specific sense of suitability (fitness of a representational choice to its data and its audience), not layout or aesthetic composition. Worth one explicit sentence stating this the first time the Vantage Point is introduced.
Two distinct suitability judgements:

What kind of deliverable — governed by MacEachren’s cartography cube (MacEachren and Taylor, 1994, Visualization in Modern Cartography, Pergamon), three axes: public↔private audience, presenting knowns↔revealing unknowns, low↔high interaction.
How the deliverable represents the data — e.g., classification method (equal interval vs. equal count/quantile vs. natural breaks/Jenks), each suitable to different distributions and audiences, none inherently “correct.”

Open item: exact chapter/page citation for the cartography cube within the 1994 volume — you have the physical book; locate the specific chapter and page range before finalising the citation (do not use the placeholder chapter title suggested during drafting without verifying it against the actual table of contents).
Open item: this Vantage Point’s folder in the vault (Workflow/Part 2.../2.4 Designing Spatial Results Communication/) is currently empty — no explanatory material, protocol, or case example yet exists, unlike every other Vantage Point’s Part 2 folder.

6. Vantage Point 5 — Executing the Analytical Schema
Restates the GIS = Stack convention explicitly at the point it first becomes operationally relevant.
Analytical Schema → Analytical Recipe — the Schema (Vantage Point 3) is tool-agnostic; the Recipe (a Semantic Asset) is the tool-bound, executed translation of it (e.g., a QGIS tool chain or a Python script). The same Schema can yield multiple valid Recipes. Translation is not free — software-specific defaults (interpolation methods, topology tolerances, CRS handling) can reintroduce undocumented decisions, which should be returned to Stewardship as a Design Rationale addendum rather than silently absorbed.
X-Y Problem — the informal term (not “overfitting,” not Dennett’s “competence without comprehension” — both considered and rejected as imprecise fits) for a well-formed-looking request that answers the stated question (X) while the real prior question (Y) goes unasked. Used in the Introduction’s AI-tutor passage: a student may receive a correct procedural answer (e.g., how to buffer) without realising the real prior question was different (e.g., how to reproject first). The comprehension gap sits with the human framing the prompt, not the AI.

7. Semantic Assets (output of the whole Workflow)

Design Rationale — permanent record of every “wicked problem” and how it was resolved. The artifact produced by Stewardship (Stewardship = the ongoing verb; Design Rationale = the resulting noun).
[Formalised] Data Model / Domain of Discourse — the text-indexed bridge between raw data and human intent. (Confirm final preferred term here now that “Domain of Discourse” has superseded “Data Model” as the Activity Three output — check no stray “Data Model” references remain.)
Analytical Recipe — the decoupled, reproducible, tool-bound script (DAG) — see §6.


8. Verification / Citation Checklist









































CitationStatusTomlinson (1969), Journal of Geography (Chigaku Zasshi), 78(1), 45–48✅ Verified directly via J-STAGE.Tomlinson (1968), in Stewart (ed.), Land Evaluation — CSIRO Symposium, Macmillan of Australia, pp. 200–210✅ Verified via the Chigaku Zasshi reprint’s own footnote (secondary-source chain — legitimate, not directly inspected). Recommended citation form: cite 1968 original as primary, note reprint in brackets.Boole, G. (1854), An Investigation of the Laws of Thought✅ Concept and near-exact phrasing verified against primary source. Confirm your copy’s actual reprint year (2005 vs. 1958/2009).MacEachren, A.M. and Taylor, D.R.F. (eds.) (1994), Visualization in Modern Cartography, Pergamon⚠️ Volume-level attribution verified via multiple secondary sources. Chapter/page-level detail not yet verified — locate in your physical copy.NOIR vs. NORI (Stevens, 1946 levels of measurement)⚠️ Confirm intended acronym — standard term is NOIR. Note: manuscript now extends Stevens with a companion Geometric Type dimension (Point/Line/Polygon/Field) not present in the original 1946 framework — flag this extension explicitly wherever Stevens is cited, so it reads as a stated addition rather than a misattribution.”Den Erkendbare Eksistens”Noted as Danish rather than German orthography — confirm intended source language before citing linguistically in-text.GeoDanmark building specification (§4, Representation)Danish source text on file from drafting session, with English working translation. ⚠️ Confirm precise defined meaning of “Områdepolygon” and “forefindes… ikke” against full GeoDanmark documentation before quoting the translation in print; cite the specific document/version and access date.Tomlin, C.D. (1990), Geographic Information Systems and Cartographic Modeling, Prentice Hall⚠️ Added this session as the precedent for “Operator” (§9) — map algebra’s local/focal/zonal/global operators. Verify exact title/year/publisher against your own copy or a library record before citing in print.

9. Task, Operator, Tool
Task — a tool-agnostic, reusable unit of work smaller than a Vantage Point/Activity and possibly smaller than a single Analytical Schema node (e.g., georeferencing, creating a table, correcting a hydrologically-sound DTM, print layout design). Lives at the vault root, not under Workflow — deliberately, because the same Task can be invoked from several different Activities (and, in principle, from more than one Vantage Point), so it isn’t owned by any one place in the Workflow. A Task decomposes into:

one or more human decision points — judgement calls that are not themselves mechanically executable (e.g., deciding which points on an image are usable control points; deciding column names and data types for a new table); and
one or more Operators.

Operator — the tool-agnostic, reusable transformation itself (buffer, intersect, reclassify, CREATE TABLE ...). Precedent: Dana Tomlin’s map algebra classifies exactly this kind of thing as operators (local/focal/zonal/global operators) — see the citation checklist, §8. Formally, “operator” is not restricted to an infix symbol between two operands (the everyday arithmetic sense); the broader mathematical sense — a mapping from one space to another, as in a linear operator or differential operator — is unary or n-ary as needed, and is the sense intended here. “Operation,” used earlier this session for this same concept, is retired — Operator now does that job alone.
Like a Task, an Operator has its own tool-agnostic/tool-bound split, one level further down:

Operator Schema (tool-agnostic): what the Operator does, independent of any Stack — e.g., what buffering means mathematically.
Tool (tool-bound, one per Stack): a specific Stack’s concrete implementation of the Operator — e.g., “the Buffer tool in QGIS’s Processing toolbox,” “the Buffer tool in ArcGIS’s Toolbox” — each exposing its own parameter surface (QGIS and ArcGIS may differ in how end-cap style, join style, or segment count are specified). Deliberately named after the term the software itself already uses (ArcGIS Toolboxes containing Tools; QGIS’s Processing toolbox), so the abstraction maps directly onto vocabulary students already see on screen.

Operators and Tools are many-to-many, and Tools are versioned. (⚠️ Added; confirm wording.) Operators are kept deliberately simple — each does one thing (clip, save, buffer, dissolve) — while a Tool is whatever a Stack happens to bundle into one dialog. One Tool can therefore realise several Operators through its options: QGIS’s Package layers saves many layers with one common clip extent (and can store their symbology with them), so it realises clip and save for a whole set of layers at once; QGIS’s Buffer with Dissolve result and Keep disjoint results separate realises buffer, dissolve and explode in one run. In the other direction, one Operator can need several Tools: the fringe (outer edge) of a buffer is a Buffer followed by a Difference. And the mapping moves between versions of a Stack: Keep disjoint results separate exists in QGIS 4.2 but not in older releases. A Tool note therefore says which Operators it realises, through which options, and from which version — not the other way round.
Operator family — a group of Operators that do the same kind of work, used as the index students search when they meet a new problem: e.g., Overlay (intersection, union, difference, clip), Proximity (buffer, distance surface, nearest feature), Geometry restructuring (dissolve, explode, merge), Zonal (zonal statistics, tabulate area), Surface from samples (interpolation, kernel density). Families are domain-neutral: the same Proximity Operators serve walking distance to a park in urban design and a habitat network in landscape ecology; what differs is the Domain Example that uses them. For the raster Operators, Tomlin’s local, focal, zonal and global classes (see §8) are families in exactly this sense.
A Recipe (§6) is, in these terms, largely a sequence of Tool invocations for one Stack, plus whatever human decision points the Task’s Schema calls for — Recipe is Task-shaped, Tool is Operator-shaped, and they sit at different granularities rather than duplicating each other.
Note on “Schema” overload: the word now does four jobs in this glossary — the Analytical Schema (the whole DAG, §4), Recording’s Schema (the spatial table structure, §3 Activity Five), Task Schema, and Operator Schema. Each is locally clear, but a reader meeting a bare “Schema” without a qualifier may not know which is meant — write “Task Schema” / “Operator Schema” / “the Recording Schema” explicitly rather than relying on context, until this is resolved (if it ever needs to be).
The full chain: Domain Example → Geospatial Workflow → Task → Operator → Tool. (⚠️ Added; confirm wording.) Above the Workflow sits the Domain Example (§1): a worked case that brings in knowledge from outside the strict geospatial domain — urban design, ethnography, hydrology — and so explains why the Workflow is shaped as it is. Read downwards, each level is more tool-bound and more domain-neutral: the Domain Example is specific to a field and a case, the Workflow to a spatial question, the Task and Operator to a kind of work (tool-agnostic), and the Tool and Recipe to one Stack. Read upwards, a Task such as slope and flow direction is reused by several Domain Examples (hydrological modelling, landslide susceptibility, accessibility), linked rather than copied — the same graph principle as below.
Task composition is a graph, not a hierarchy. A larger Task (e.g., building a hydrological model) can be composed of several smaller Tasks and/or Operators (e.g., correct the DTM → flow direction → flow accumulation), but a smaller Task is not “owned” by any one larger Task — the same correct the DTM Task can be referenced from several different larger Tasks (a hydrological model, a viewshed workflow, a landslide-susceptibility workflow) without duplicating its definition. This mirrors the Analytical Schema’s own DAG structure, and mirrors the reuse pattern wanted for the teaching site (one node, linked into multiple context views — see the Canvas/Kumu discussion).
Task write-up template:

Task Schema (tool-agnostic): the decision points + the Operators, in the abstract, with no reference to any specific Stack.
Task Recipe(s) (tool-bound, one per Stack): “This Task is implemented in QGIS by …”, “in ArcGIS by …”. Multiple valid Recipes can exist per Task Schema, exactly as for the Analytical Schema/Recipe pair at §6.

Open item: decide whether the book represents Tasks as a numbered glossary/appendix or as an actual linked graph (network diagram / Canvas), given the graph (not tree) composition structure above.
Open item: fold this Operator/Tool distinction back into the DAG description at §4 wherever a future rewrite touches that section’s prose — the table/glossary form here is settled, but the running prose in the actual manuscript (2.3 Author the Analytical Schema) has not yet been updated to use “Operator” or introduce “Tool.”

Compiled as a working document — treat as a living checklist to run against the full draft once assembled, not a final, print-ready appendix.

the-technology-stack/communication-envir.filePath: The technology stack/Communication Environments/Affinity/Recipes/A0 poster layout (Recipe - Affinity).md
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.title: A0 poster layout (Recipe — Affinity)
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.content:
Used in Urban Design Visualisation (Example) (step 7).
The final output is one A0 poster, laid out in Affinity (free, Windows and Mac, needs a free Canva login). Affinity is also where QGIS plans and diagrams are finished and renders retouched, so everything ends up in one program.
1. Start from the course template





























SettingValuePage sizeA0 portrait, 841 × 1189 mmBleedAs required by the print room (typically 3–5 mm)Margins30 mmGrid6 columns, 15 mm gutterText stylesTitle 160 pt · headings 60 pt · body 28 pt · captions 20 pt
Do not change page size, margins or text styles. One template for the whole class makes the posters read as one exhibition.
2. Structure the poster
The poster has its own visual hierarchy (see Visual hierarchy and figure-ground): one element is read first, and it should carry the main idea.

Title + one sentence stating the main idea of the proposal.
One hero image — the strongest render or the site plan — covering about a third of the poster.
Site plan 1:500 (can be the hero).
Concept diagrams in one row.
2–3 renders and one season variant.
One line drawing (section or perspective, existing vs. proposed).
Short texts: 2–4 sentences per block. The poster is read from 1–2 m away.

3. Bring the material in

Keep all poster files in 06_output/poster/.
File → Place for renders and drawings. Place them linked, not embedded, so a re-render with the same file name updates the poster. The Resource Manager shows missing or changed links.
Plans and diagrams from QGIS: open the exported SVG or PDF in Affinity. Lines, fills and text stay editable vectors: adjust line weights, add textures and people from above, then place the finished file in the poster.
Shadow render: place it above the plan with blend mode Multiply.

4. Image resolution
Aim for 150 ppi at printed size.





















Width on the posterPixels needed (150 ppi)Full width, 841 mmabout 5,000 pxHalf width, 420 mmabout 2,500 pxQuarter width, 210 mmabout 1,250 px
A 4K render (3,840 px) covers up to about 650 mm width; an 8K render (7,680 px) covers the full poster width. Screenshots are never good enough.
5. Export the print PDF

File → Export → PDF, preset PDF/X-4 (or what the print room asks for).
Tick Include bleed, fonts embedded, rasterise Nothing.
Name it groupname_poster_A0.pdf.
Check the PDF at 100% zoom, then make a test print scaled to A3 before sending the A0 to the large-format printer.

the-technology-stack/communication-envir.filePath: The technology stack/Communication Environments/Blender/Introduction to Blender for 3D Urban Modeling.md
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.title: Introduction to Blender for 3D Urban Modeling
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.content:
Blender is a powerful, open-source 3D creation suite that supports the entire 3D pipeline, including modeling, sculpting, animation, rendering, and compositing. While traditionally used in fields such as animation, game design, and visual effects, Blender has also become an invaluable tool for 3D urban modeling due to its flexibility, advanced features, and growing community of users focusing on architectural and city-scale projects.
Blender’s comprehensive toolset makes it an excellent choice for creating detailed, realistic models of urban environments, whether you’re visualizing a single building, an entire cityscape, or simulating urban dynamics.
Why Use Blender for Urban Modeling?


Flexibility and Control: Blender offers a high degree of flexibility and control over 3D models, making it ideal for creating detailed urban scenes. You can model everything from individual buildings to complex city layouts, incorporating both geometric precision and artistic creativity.


Integration with GIS Data: With the help of plugins like BlenderGIS and OSM Import, Blender can integrate real-world geographic data into your 3D models. This allows you to accurately place buildings, roads, and other urban features based on actual geographic coordinates.


Photorealistic Rendering: Blender’s powerful rendering engines, such as Cycles and Eevee, enable the creation of photorealistic images and animations. This is particularly useful for architectural visualization, urban planning presentations, and immersive storytelling.


Open-Source and Community Support: As an open-source tool, Blender is freely available and supported by a vibrant community. This means you have access to a wealth of tutorials, add-ons, and community resources to enhance your urban modeling projects.


Getting Started with Blender for Urban Modeling


Download and Install Blender:

Visit the Blender official website and download the latest version for your operating system. Follow the installation instructions to set up Blender on your computer.



Familiarize Yourself with the Interface:

Blender’s interface can be overwhelming at first, but understanding its layout is crucial. Key areas to focus on include the 3D Viewport, Outliner, Properties Panel, and Timeline.
Explore basic navigation (zoom, pan, rotate) and understand how to use basic tools like the Transform Gizmo for moving, rotating, and scaling objects.



Learn Basic 3D Modeling Techniques:

Start with simple shapes (cubes, cylinders) and practice basic operations like extruding, beveling, and subdividing. These fundamental skills are essential for creating more complex models later.
Experiment with modifiers like Array, Mirror, and Boolean, which are powerful tools for constructing repetitive structures and complex geometries often found in urban modeling.
the YouTube canal The CG Essentials has some really good reviews of Blender 3d modeling



Importing Geographic Data into Blender:

BlenderGIS Plugin: This plugin allows you to import GIS data directly into Blender. You can use it to download elevation data, satellite images, and shapefiles, which serve as the foundation for creating accurate 3D terrains and urban environments.
OSM Import: With the OSM (OpenStreetMap) add-on, you can import building footprints and street networks into Blender. This is particularly useful for creating large-scale urban models based on real-world data.



Importing 3D Photorealistic Tiles:

Integrate Google 3D tiles or similar datasets into Blender to achieve a photorealistic representation of urban areas. This process involves using third-party tools to extract 3D data and importing it into Blender, where it can be refined and enhanced.



Using the GIS and OSM Plugins:

BlenderGIS: This plugin bridges the gap between GIS and Blender, enabling the import and manipulation of real-world geographic data. It supports various formats like GeoTIFFs, shapefiles, and DEMs.
OSM Import: This add-on allows you to import OSM data, including building footprints, roads, and other features. Once imported, you can use Blender’s tools to extrude, texture, and refine the imported geometries.



Creating Detailed Urban Models:

Start by importing GIS data to set up the terrain and base map. Use building footprints from OSM or other sources to extrude basic building shapes.
Add details like windows, doors, and architectural elements using Blender’s modeling tools. Use modifiers and instancing to manage repetitive elements efficiently.



Texturing and Rendering:

Use Blender’s UV mapping tools to apply realistic textures to buildings and landscapes. High-quality textures can significantly enhance the visual appeal of your urban models.
Set up lighting and cameras to showcase your model from the best angles. Use the Cycles or Eevee render engines to produce high-quality images and animations.



Experiment and Learn:

Blender is a versatile tool with a steep learning curve. Experiment with different techniques, follow tutorials, and participate in the Blender community to improve your skills and discover new possibilities for urban modeling.



Next Steps
Now that you have a basic understanding of Blender’s capabilities for 3D urban modeling, you can dive deeper into specific workflows and techniques. Explore the following topics in more detail:

How to import Google 3D tiles into Blender for photorealistic urban modeling.
Using the BlenderGIS and OSM plugins to bring real-world geographic data into your 3D projects.
Advanced techniques for texturing, lighting, and rendering to create stunning visualizations of urban environments.

Blender offers endless possibilities for 3D modeling and visualization in urban contexts. By mastering these tools and techniques, you can create compelling models that not only look impressive but also provide valuable insights for urban planning, architecture, and more.

the-technology-stack/communication-envir.filePath: The technology stack/Communication Environments/Blender/Recipes/Context massing (Recipe - Blender).md
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.title: Context massing (Recipe — Blender)
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Context massing (Task) Schema. Input from Building heights from DHM (Recipe - QGIS). Used in Urban Design Visualisation (Example) (step 4). Budget: one working session.
Before you start
Install BlenderGIS

On github.com/domlysz/BlenderGIS click Code → Download ZIP. Do not unzip it (on Mac, Safari may unzip automatically — re-zip the folder or turn off Open safe files after downloading).
In Blender: Edit → Preferences → Add-ons, click the small arrow ⌄ top right → Install from Disk… and select the zip.
Search for GIS in the add-on list and tick the checkbox.
Check: a GIS menu now appears in the header of the 3D viewport (Object Mode).

Use the same Blender version as everyone else in your group.
Add the Danish coordinate system. BlenderGIS only knows WGS84 and Web Mercator out of the box.

Edit → Preferences → Add-ons → BlenderGIS, expand it, find Spatial Reference Systems and click +.
Definition: EPSG:25832 (include “EPSG:”). Description: ETRS89 / UTM 32N.
Tick Save to addon preferences if shown, then Save Preferences (☰ bottom left).

1. Scene setup

New file, delete the default cube, save as 04_blender/context.blend.
Scene Properties → Units: Metric, Unit Scale 1.0 (1 unit = 1 m).
Press N in the 3D viewport → GIS tab → Geoscene: set the CRS to ETRS89 / UTM 32N.

2. Terrain (optional but recommended)
GIS → Import → Georeferenced raster, select terrain.tif, mode DEM as mesh (or displacement). BlenderGIS moves the scene origin close to your data automatically, so the model stays precise.
3. Import and extrude the buildings
Import the two building files one at a time with GIS → Import → Shapefile:








































Settingcontext_lod1.shpcontext_lod2.shpCRSETRS89 / UTM 32NETRS89 / UTM 32NExtrusion from fieldheighteaveElevationfrom field ground, or from the terrainsameSeparate objectsononObject name from fieldididPut in collectioncontext_LOD1context_LOD2
The LOD2 buildings now stand at their eave height, ready for a roof. Keep the attribute table of context_lod2 open in QGIS: roof_rise tells you how far to raise each ridge.
4. One material for all context

Select all buildings and create one material context_white: Base Color very light grey (about 0.85), Roughness 0.8, no texture.
With all selected, and the one with the material active: Ctrl+L → Link Materials.

That is the whole context material. Do not add brick, glass or facade textures.
5. LOD2 roofs — only where they matter
Roofs are made in Edit Mode by adding a ridge and raising it by roof_rise. Check the roof direction and type against the orthophoto, oblique photos (skråfoto) or your own site photos. Within about half a metre is accurate enough. Note the source you used for each building — it belongs in the Design Rationale.
Controls (also on Mac)

































KeyDoesTabObject Mode ↔ Edit Mode1 / 2 / 3 (top number row)Select vertices / edges / facesAlt+ZX-ray: select through the modelG Z 3 EnterMove 3 m upS X 0.6 EnterScale to 60 % along XN → Item → Median ZType an exact height for the selection
Gable roof (rectangular building)

Tab, press 2, select the two short top edges (Shift-click the second).
Right-click → Subdivide (1 cut) — adds a midpoint on each edge.
Press 1, select the two new midpoints, press J (Connect Vertex Path) — this is the ridge.
G Z, type the building’s roof_rise, Enter.

This keeps the walls clean; a loop cut would add lines down the facades.

Hipped roof: make a gable, then with the ridge still selected press S, the ridge axis (X or Y) and e.g. 0.5, Enter.
Pyramid roof (towers, square buildings): select the top face, right-click → Poke Faces, then G Z and roof_rise.
Mansard roof (common in Danish town centres): select the top face, I (Inset) about 1–1.5 m, then G Z about 2.5 m for the steep lower part. Add a low gable or hip on the inner face if needed.
Flat roof with parapet: select the top face, I 0.3 m, then E and -0.5 so the roof sits inside a 0.5 m edge.
L-shaped and complex footprints: split the top face into rectangles first (select two vertices on opposite edges, J), make a gable on each wing, and join ridge ends with M → At Center.
Faster option: the free Building Tools add-on (N sidebar → Building Tools → Roof) makes flat, gable and hipped roofs from a selected top face with adjustable pitch. Best on simple footprints.

Finish each building: Mesh → Clean Up → Merge by Distance (removes duplicate vertices) and Shift+N (Recalculate Normals, all faces point outwards — needed for Twinmotion and the export back to QGIS).
6. The proposal goes in its own collection
Model the proposal (terrain changes, planting beds, water, furniture, pavilions) in a collection called design. This is where modelling time, materials and detail belong. Trees and people are added later in Twinmotion.
Before exporting: Object → Apply → All Transforms on everything.
7. Export for Twinmotion
Export two files, so the design can be updated without touching the context:




















FileContainsFBX settings03_exchange/context.fbxCollections context_LOD1, context_LOD2, terrainSelected objects, Scale 1.0, Apply Unit and Apply Transform on03_exchange/design.fbxCollection designSame settings; materials named clearly (paving_granite, water, bench_wood)
Optional — back to QGIS as 3D buildings
The edited buildings, including LOD2 roofs, can go back to QGIS at their real coordinates.

Select the buildings, then Object → Apply → All Transforms.
GIS → Export → Shapefile: geometry type PolygonZ, mode Objects to features (one feature per building). BlenderGIS adds the Geoscene offset back and writes the .prj file.
In QGIS, add the Shapefile, open View → 3D Map Views → New 3D Map View, and in the layer’s Properties → 3D View set: Single symbol, altitude clamping Absolute, extrusion 0, culling No culling.
Save as GeoPackage: Export → Save Features As…, geometry type MultiPolygon, tick Include z-dimension.

Don’t use QGIS’s OBJ export of a 3D scene as a base for Blender: it loses the coordinates and building IDs.
Troubleshooting








































ProblemCauseFixNo GIS menu in BlenderAdd-on installed but not enabled, or you are in Edit ModeTick BlenderGIS in Preferences; switch to Object ModeBuildings end up near 0,0 or far from the terrainGeoscene CRS not set, or a different CRS on importSet the Geoscene to ETRS89 / UTM 32N before importing anythingAll buildings have the same heightWrong field in Extrusion from field, or the field is textCheck that height is a decimal field in QGISBuildings float or sinkNo ground elevation usedUse Elevation from field ground, or place on the terrainCtrl+A does nothing on MacMouse not over the viewport, or not in Object ModeUse Object → Apply → All Transforms insteadWalls missing in QGIS 3D viewBack faces culledCulling mode: No culling

the-technology-stack/communication-envir.filePath: The technology stack/Communication Environments/Blender/Recipes/Line drawings and shadow plans (Recipe - Blender).md
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.title: Line drawings and shadow plans (Recipe — Blender)
the-technology-stack/communication-envir.content:
Used in Urban Design Visualisation (Example) (step 5). Input: the model from Context massing (Recipe - Blender).
Blender makes two drawing types Twinmotion cannot: clean line perspectives and sections (like MASU’s 1:50 “existing vs. proposed” drawings), and a top-down shadow render to lay under the QGIS site plan.
1. Line perspective or section perspective

Add a camera (Add → Camera) and frame your view (View → Cameras → Set Active Object as Camera, then N → View → Lock Camera to View).
For a section perspective, stand the camera in the street and raise the camera’s Clip Start (Camera properties) until it cuts through the buildings exactly at your section line.
Render Properties → Freestyle: tick it, line thickness 1–1.5 px. In View Layer → Freestyle Line Set, keep Silhouette, Border and Crease.
Render engine Workbench or EEVEE, World colour white, context material white.
F12 to render, then save as PNG in 06_output/.

Draw the existing and proposed versions from the same camera, so the comparison shows the change of design and not a change of viewpoint. Add people and trees as line drawings afterwards in Affinity.
Vector alternative: Add → Grease Pencil → Scene Line Art makes the lines as strokes, which can be exported to SVG for further editing.
2. Top-down shadow render for the site plan

Add a Sun light. Set a realistic direction with the Sun Position add-on (location Roskilde, e.g. 21 March or 21 June at 15:00), or by hand: sun from the south-west, about 35–45° high.
Add a top-down orthographic camera. BlenderGIS can make one that matches your data (GIS → Camera → Georef cam) and save a world file with the render, so it lands in the right place in QGIS.
Render with EEVEE, white materials only, and save as PNG or TIFF.
Load it in QGIS (or place it in Affinity) under the vector plan, blend mode Multiply, 40–70% opacity.

Unlike a drop shadow, this shadow is a claim — it shows the proposal’s real sun and shade at a stated moment. Label the date and time on the plan, and record them in the Design Rationale.
