the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content: ArcGIS Pro is a commercial desktop GIS that can handle the needs of most Geospatial projects. ArcGIS pro is part of a larger family of geospatial software solutions developed by the firm ESRI that include apps for both web and mobile devices.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/Copernicus Browser/Copernicus Browser.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Copernicus Browser
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
The Copernicus Browser (browser.dataspace.copernicus.eu) is the web application of the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem, the EU’s free access to the data of the Sentinel satellites (and others). In a web browser it finds images, shows them in true colour, false colour or as indices, and downloads the part of an image that covers a study area, already cut out and harmonised. For a small area that saves downloading a whole 100 × 100 km product of about 1 GB.
Account: a free account is needed (Login at the top; register with an e-mail address). Documentation.
Tools

Search (Tool - Copernicus Browser): find the images of an area and a period.
Download image (Tool - Copernicus Browser): download bands for an area of interest as GeoTIFF.

The Browser can also calculate indices such as NDVI on screen (the VISUALIZE tab), which is useful for checking a result made in QGIS.
Licence
Sentinel data are free and open: anyone may use, copy and redistribute them. A map should say Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data [year].

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/Copernicus Browser/Tools/Download image (Tool - Copernicus Browser).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Download image (Tool — Copernicus Browser)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
In the Copernicus Browser: the area-of-interest tool (polygon icon, top right), then Download image in the toolbar on the right, tab Analytical.
Realises:

Clip to extent, reproject and save in one step: the bands cut to the area of interest, resampled to the chosen grid and saved as GeoTIFF.

Settings that matter

Area of interest: draw a rectangle or polygon, or upload or paste one. The Browser takes KML/KMZ, GPX, GeoJSON or WKT, in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) only. From QGIS, the simplest is the SemanticGIS tool Area of interest as WKT (WGS 84) (Processing Toolbox › SemanticGIS › Vector geometry). It gives a rectangle around the layer or its selected features, with an optional buffer in metres. The rectangle is aligned to the layer’s CRS, so a download in UTM is not tilted. The WKT is copied to the clipboard, ready to paste. Without the plugin: Export › Save Features As…, format GeoJSON, CRS EPSG:4326, and upload the file.
Basic gives a picture (JPG or PNG) for a report, not data. Use Analytical:


The Analytical tab set up for NDVI: 16-bit TIFF, a custom resolution of 10 m, UTM 32N, and the raw bands B04 and B08. The size of the image in pixels is shown under the resolution.

Image format: TIFF (16-bit) (reflectance × 10,000) or TIFF (32-bit float) (reflectance, 0–1). Both are GeoTIFFs that QGIS reads with their coordinates. 16-bit files are half the size; for NDVI and other ratios the factor 10,000 cancels out, but for reflectance itself divide by 10,000.
Image resolution: CUSTOM, with Resolution X and Y 10 m/px for B02, B03, B04 and B08; 20 m bands are resampled to it. The size in pixels is shown below: 649 × 669 px at 10 m is about 6.5 × 6.7 km.
Coordinate system: UTM 32N (EPSG:32632) for Denmark, so the pixels are square 10 m cells. It lines up with ETRS89 UTM 32N (EPSG:25832) within a metre.
Add dataMask band to raw layers: adds a band that is 1 where there is data and 0 outside it, for example outside a polygon area of interest. Useful to set NoData in QGIS.
Layers: tick the bands under Raw. The Visualised layers (True color, NDVI, Scene classification map …) are coloured pictures, not measurements: their pixel values are colours.
Download: one ZIP with a TIFF per band.

Watch out

The scene classification (SCL) is not among the raw bands. It is offered only under Visualised, as colours, so a cloud mask from SCL needs another source, such as the original L2A product. Choosing a date without cloud over the study area is the simple way round.
The values are already harmonised: no offset to subtract (see how reflectance is stored).
The bands are resampled to the chosen grid, so values can differ slightly from the original product.
Download a margin around the study area, so that edge effects and later clipping do not cut into it.
Very large areas at 10 m may exceed the download limit; split the area or reduce the resolution.

Written from the Browser and its documentation, November 2026. Labels can change.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/Copernicus Browser/Tools/Search (Tool - Copernicus Browser).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Search (Tool — Copernicus Browser)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
In the Copernicus Browser: the SEARCH tab in the panel on the left.
Realises:

Selection of images by location (the map view or area of interest), by date and by cloud cover.

Settings that matter

Data sources: Sentinel-2 › MSI › L2A (surface reflectance). L1C is top-of-atmosphere reflectance; see TOA and surface reflectance.
Time range: the dates from and to, then Search. The first 50 results are listed; Load more shows the next 50.
Each result shows its date, time, satellite and cloud cover; Visualize shows it on the map.
In the VISUALIZE tab a maximum cloud coverage (30 % by default) limits which dates are offered.

Watch out

Cloud cover is for the whole product, a 100 × 100 km tile. An image with 40 % cloud can be clear over your area, and one with 2 % can have its one cloud right there. Look at the image over the area itself.
Your area may lie in two tiles (Denmark spans tiles of UTM zones 32 and 33) or at the edge of a satellite’s swath, so half the tile may be empty. Pick a result that covers the whole area.
Several results on the same date can be the same overpass in neighbouring tiles.

Written from the Browser and its documentation, November 2026. Labels can change.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/JupyterGIS.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: JupyterGIS
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
JupyterGIS is an extension to JupyterLab that adds a GIS to the notebook environment: a map with layers, symbology and an identify tool, next to the notebooks and files of a project. It is developed by QuantStack and Simula with funding from the European Space Agency, and is open source (GitHub).
Processing or communication?
JupyterGIS has both roles, and which one it plays depends on what you use it for.

As a processing environment, it keeps the analysis and the map together. A notebook loads and processes the data with Python libraries such as GeoPandas and Rasterio, and its Python API adds the result to the map. GDAL tools (rasterize, warp, translate) can also be run from the map itself. Because the code, the result and the text explaining it live in one project, the workflow documents itself.
As a communication environment, it is a shared map. Several people can edit the same map at the same time, “like Google Docs for GIS”, and leave comments tied to places on the map. This makes it useful for discussing a result with others, and less for producing a finished map for print.

On this site JupyterGIS is listed mainly as a processing environment that is easy to share. It is not a replacement for QGIS or the print layout.
Working with QGIS
JupyterGIS can import and export QGIS project files (.qgz), so a project started in QGIS can be opened, discussed and edited in JupyterGIS and taken back. The support covers layers, their data sources and their styles, not everything a QGIS project can contain. Its own maps are saved as .jGIS files.
Data
JupyterGIS reads GeoJSON, GeoPackage, GeoParquet, Shapefile, GeoTIFF and Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF, PMTiles, and WMS and WMTS services. It can also search satellite imagery through STAC.
Python in the browser on this site
Open JupyterGIS in your browser (opens in a new tab): a Python environment that runs entirely in your browser, with nothing to install. Start with the notebook Getting your feet wet:

points, lines and polygons, and what they stand for;
GeoJSON as plain text, and the same file as a table with a geometry column;
the fields farmers declared at Ledreborg in 2026: projecting to metres, area per crop class, a map by crop;
an intersection with the landscapes and a 100 m buffer;
the result on an interactive JupyterGIS map;
saving the results.

Good to know before you start:

The first start takes a while. The browser downloads Python and its libraries (shapely, GeoPandas, pyproj, matplotlib and JupyterGIS), about 120 MB, and keeps them for next time.
Your work stays in this browser. Notebooks and files are saved in the browser’s own storage, not on a server and not on your disk. Use File › Download, or right-click a file and choose Download, to keep it.
Your own data: drag a file into the file browser on the left, then read it with gpd.read_file("my_file.gpkg"). GeoPackage and GeoJSON are simplest; a shapefile needs all its parts.
Saving a GeoPackage must go through /tmp, because the browser’s storage cannot be written to the way a database needs. The notebook shows how; GeoJSON can be written directly.
Data from the web can only be read from servers that allow it from a browser; the course data come with the site.
The libraries are fixed: you cannot install other compiled packages. For more, install JupyterGIS on your own machine (below).

Getting started

Try it in the browser without installing anything: on this site (above), or JupyterGIS’s own online demo in JupyterLite. Real-time editing with others does not work in the browser version.
Install it in a Mamba environment with mamba install -c conda-forge jupytergis, then start jupyter lab. To share a map with others in real time, JupyterLab must run on a server that all of you can reach, for example in a Docker container.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/JupyterLab.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: JupyterLab
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
JupyterLab is an open-source, web-based interactive development environment (IDE) that is widely used in the geospatial data processing community. It is a flexible and powerful tool that allows users to create and share documents that contain live code, equations, visualizations, and narrative text. JupyterLab builds on the success of the classic Jupyter Notebook, offering a more integrated and feature-rich environment that is particularly well-suited for complex geospatial analysis and visualisation tasks.
Key Features of JupyterLab for Geospatial Data Processing


Interactive Notebooks:
JupyterLab provides a highly interactive environment where users can write and execute code in real-time. This is especially useful for geospatial data processing, where analysts and researchers can iteratively develop and test their code, visualise results, and refine their analysis on the fly.

Code Cells: Write and execute code in small, manageable chunks, which is ideal for step-by-step geospatial analysis.
Markdown Cells: Document your workflow with narrative text, equations, and embedded images, making it easier to explain and share your methods.



Integrated Visualisation Tools:
JupyterLab supports a wide range of visualisation libraries, such as Matplotlib, Plotly, and Folium, which are essential for geospatial data analysis. Users can generate interactive maps, charts, and other visualisations directly within the notebook, allowing for immediate feedback and insights.

Interactive Maps: Libraries like Folium and ipyleaflet enable users to create and interact with maps within the JupyterLab environment, making it easy to explore spatial patterns and relationships.
Dynamic Plots: Generate dynamic and interactive plots that allow you to explore your geospatial data in detail, adjusting parameters and filters as needed.



Support for Geospatial Libraries:
JupyterLab integrates seamlessly with popular geospatial libraries such as GeoPandas, Shapely, Fiona, and Rasterio. These libraries provide tools for working with vector and raster data, making it possible to perform a wide range of geospatial tasks, from basic data manipulation to advanced spatial analysis.

GeoPandas: A powerful library for working with geospatial data in Python, enabling easy manipulation and analysis of vector data.
Shapely: A library for geometric operations on spatial data, allowing for advanced spatial analysis and manipulation.
Rasterio: A library for reading and writing raster datasets, making it easy to work with satellite imagery and other raster-based geospatial data.



Reproducibility and Sharing:
One of the major advantages of JupyterLab is its support for reproducibility. Notebooks can be easily shared with others, allowing them to reproduce the analysis and results exactly as you did. This is particularly important in geospatial analysis, where ensuring that others can replicate your workflow is crucial for validation and collaboration.

Export Options: Jupyter notebooks can be exported in various formats, including HTML, PDF, and LaTeX, making it easy to share your work with a wider audience.
Version Control: Integrate with Git for version control, allowing you to track changes to your analysis over time and collaborate with others more effectively.



Scalability and Integration with Other Tools:
JupyterLab can be integrated with cloud computing environments, such as Google Colab, AWS, and Azure, allowing you to scale your geospatial processing tasks as needed. It can also be used in combination with Docker containers or Conda environments to create reproducible and isolated geospatial analysis setups.

Running JupyterLab in Google Colab: Google Colab (colab.research.google.com/) offers a free cloud-based environment where you can run JupyterLab without needing to install any software on your local machine. This is particularly useful for collaborative projects or when you need to leverage cloud computing resources for more demanding geospatial tasks.
Running JupyterLab with Docker: Docker allows you to run JupyterLab in a containerized environment, ensuring consistency and portability. For instance, you can start a JupyterLab instance using a pre-built Docker image by simply running the following command (assuming Docker is installed on your computer):
docker run -p 10000:8888 quay.io/jupyter/scipy-notebook:2024-08-19

This command will launch JupyterLab on your local machine, accessible via your web browser, with all the necessary dependencies pre-installed and isolated from your host system.



Applications of JupyterLab in Geospatial Data Processing


Data Exploration and Cleaning:
JupyterLab is an excellent environment for exploring and cleaning geospatial data. Analysts can load datasets, inspect their contents, and apply cleaning routines, all within a single interactive session.


Spatial Analysis:
With support for geospatial libraries, JupyterLab is well-suited for performing a wide range of spatial analyses, including buffer operations, spatial joins, and raster analysis. The ability to visualise the results immediately helps in refining the analysis and ensuring accuracy.


Modeling and Simulation:
JupyterLab provides an ideal environment for developing and testing geospatial models, such as land use change simulations or transportation models. Users can write and execute model code, visualize the output, and iterate quickly.


Collaboration and Education:
JupyterLab is widely used in educational settings for teaching geospatial concepts and techniques. Its interactive nature makes it easy for students to experiment with code and see the results immediately, while the ability to share notebooks fosters collaboration among researchers and practitioners.


Conclusion
JupyterLab is a versatile and powerful environment for geospatial data processing, offering a rich set of features that support interactive analysis, visualisation, and collaboration. Whether you’re exploring datasets, performing complex spatial analysis, or developing geospatial models, JupyterLab provides the tools and flexibility needed to streamline your workflow and enhance your productivity. Its integration with popular geospatial libraries, support for cloud computing, and ease of deployment via platforms like Google Colab and Docker make it an essential tool for anyone working in the field of geospatial analysis.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/PostGIS.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: PostGIS
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
PostGIS is an extension to the PostgreSQL database that enables advanced geospatial processing by adding support for geographic objects. PostGIS extends the standard SQL language with powerful spatial functions, allowing users to perform complex geographic queries and analysis directly within the database.
This note explores how SQL is extended in PostGIS for geospatial processing and introduces the advanced functions and operations available.
Here’s the revised version of the PostGIS and SQL for Geospatial Processing introduction with the precision added:
Here’s the revised version of the PostGIS and SQL for Geospatial Processing introduction with the precision added:
What is PostGIS?
PostGIS is a spatial extension for PostgreSQL, making it a fully-featured spatial database that supports geographic objects such as points, lines, polygons, and raster data. It follows OGC (Open Geospatial Consortium) Simple Features standards, meaning it works seamlessly with other geospatial tools and formats.
PostGIS adds support for:

Spatial data types: Geometries (2D/3D) and Geography (curved-earth) types.
Spatial indexes: Efficient searching of spatial data using GiST and SP-GiST indexes.
Spatial functions: Over 500 functions for spatial operations, including distance calculations, intersections, buffering, and more.

Extending SQL into the Spatial Domain
PostGIS extends standard SQL into the spatial domain by adding spatial functions that operate on the spatial relationships between the rows (or tuples) of tables. These functions allow you to perform complex spatial queries based on the geographic objects stored in the database.
For instance, in traditional SQL, you might filter rows based on attributes (e.g., Population > 100000). In spatial SQL, you can filter rows based on spatial relationships, such as finding whether a point is within a polygon or if two geometries intersect.
Spatial functions like:

ST_Intersects: to check if geometries overlap,
ST_DWithin: to find geometries within a specified distance of another,
ST_Buffer: to create buffer zones around geometries,

allow users to directly query geographic data and analyze spatial interactions, making PostGIS an essential tool for geospatial processing within a relational database system.
Spatial SQL in PostGIS
PostGIS extends SQL with spatial data types and functions, allowing users to manipulate and query geographic objects directly in SQL. Here are the key concepts and functions for geospatial processing in PostGIS.
Spatial Data Types
PostGIS introduces two key spatial data types:

Geometry: This type is used for flat-Earth (2D Cartesian) projections, such as UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator).
Geography: This type is used for round-Earth (latitude/longitude) calculations, ideal for working with global coordinates.

For example, when creating a table with a spatial column, you can specify the geometry type:
CREATE TABLE Towns (
  TownID SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  TownName VARCHAR(255),
  Population INT,
  geom GEOMETRY(Point, 4326) -- EPSG:4326 for WGS84 (lat/lon)
);
In this example, geom is a spatial column of type GEOMETRY for storing point data in the EPSG:4326 coordinate system (WGS84).
Spatial Functions
PostGIS provides an extensive set of functions that allow users to perform spatial operations. Some of the most commonly used functions include:


ST_Intersects: Returns true if two geometries share any portion of space.
SELECT *
FROM Towns
WHERE ST_Intersects(Towns.geom, ST_GeomFromText('POLYGON((...))'));


ST_Distance: Computes the shortest distance between two geometries.
SELECT ST_Distance(geom, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(12.5683 55.6761)', 4326))
FROM Towns
WHERE TownName = 'Copenhagen';


ST_Buffer: Creates a buffer around a geometry, often used in proximity analysis.
SELECT ST_Buffer(geom, 1000)
FROM Towns
WHERE TownName = 'Copenhagen';


ST_Within: Returns true if one geometry is entirely within another.
SELECT TownName
FROM Towns
WHERE ST_Within(geom, ST_GeomFromText('POLYGON((...))'));


ST_Union: Merges two or more geometries into a single geometry.


Spatial Indexing
To make queries faster, PostGIS uses spatial indexing through GiST (Generalized Search Tree) or SP-GiST indexes. Creating a spatial index on a geometry column improves the performance of spatial queries like ST_Intersects or ST_Within:
CREATE INDEX idx_towns_geom
ON Towns
USING GIST (geom);
This index allows PostGIS to quickly search for spatial relationships, dramatically improving query performance for large datasets.
Example: Finding Nearby Towns
Let’s say you want to find all towns within 50 kilometers of Aarhus. You can use ST_DWithin, which checks whether geometries are within a specified distance:
SELECT TownName
FROM Towns
WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(10.2039 56.1629)', 4326), 50000);
This query finds towns within 50 kilometers of the point representing Aarhus.
Result:














TownNameAarhusOdense
Example: Buffering and Intersection
You can combine spatial functions to perform more complex queries. For instance, you can find all towns that intersect a buffer zone around a specific point:
SELECT TownName
FROM Towns
WHERE ST_Intersects(geom, ST_Buffer(ST_GeomFromText('POINT(12.5683 55.6761)', 4326), 5000));
This query selects towns that intersect a 5-kilometer buffer around a point near Copenhagen.
Example: Spatial Joins
PostGIS allows you to perform spatial joins, where you join two tables based on the spatial relationship between their geometries. For example, if you have a table of LandUsePlans and want to find which towns intersect specific land-use plans:
SELECT Towns.TownName, LandUsePlans.PlanType
FROM Towns
JOIN LandUsePlans ON ST_Intersects(Towns.geom, LandUsePlans.geom);
This query returns the town names and the land-use plans that spatially intersect each other.
Result:

















TownNamePlanTypeCopenhagenResidentialAarhusCommercial
Advanced Spatial Functions
PostGIS supports a wide range of advanced spatial functions that extend beyond simple queries. Here are a few:


ST_Transform: Transforms the geometry into a different coordinate system.
SELECT ST_Transform(geom, 3857)
FROM Towns
WHERE TownName = 'Aarhus';


ST_ConvexHull: Returns the convex hull of a geometry (the smallest polygon that can enclose the geometry).
SELECT ST_ConvexHull(ST_Collect(geom))
FROM Towns;


ST_Rasterize: Converts vector geometries into raster format for analysis.
SELECT ST_AsRaster(geom, 10, 10)
FROM Towns
WHERE TownName = 'Odense';


PostGIS and OGC Simple Features
PostGIS is compliant with the OGC Simple Features specification, which defines how geospatial data should be handled. This ensures that PostGIS can interoperate with other OGC-compliant systems, such as desktop GIS applications (e.g., QGIS) and spatial data formats (e.g., GeoJSON, WKT, and Shapefiles).
Linking to Other Notes
For a broader understanding of how spatial SQL integrates with various geospatial workflows, refer to the following notes:

[Spatial SQL in QGIS and GeoPackage]: Discusses how spatial SQL can be used in QGIS with GeoPackage databases.
[Working with QGIS for Spatial Analysis]: Explores how to leverage QGIS for spatial analysis using both native tools and SQL-based workflows.


This note provides an overview of how PostGIS extends SQL for geospatial processing, with practical examples and advanced functions. Let me know if you need further additions or clarifications!

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/PostgreSQL.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: PostgreSQL
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
PostgreSQL is a highly robust, open-source relational database system that plays a key role in geospatial database management. When combined with the PostGIS extension, it becomes a powerful tool for handling, storing, and querying spatial data. Here’s an expanded look at how PostgreSQL supports geospatial technologies, along with an exploration of its technical features, including its spatial query capabilities, user management, and alignment with OGC standards.
Key Features and Functionality
1. PostGIS: Extending PostgreSQL for Spatial Data
PostGIS is a vital extension that brings geospatial capabilities to PostgreSQL, transforming it into a fully-fledged spatial database. PostGIS allows PostgreSQL to store geographic objects, supporting spatial queries, indexing, and the full range of GIS operations.

Spatial Types: PostGIS supports geometric (2D) and geographic (curved-earth, lat-long) types, such as points, lines, polygons, and multi-geometry collections.
Spatial Functions: It introduces over 500 functions for spatial analysis, including proximity searches, distance calculations, and spatial joins. These functions extend standard SQL, making spatial data as easy to work with as tabular data.

For example, a basic spatial query that finds all points within a certain distance from a given location might look like this:
SELECT name
FROM landmarks
WHERE ST_DWithin(
    geography(landmarks.geom), 
    geography(ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(-75.1652, 39.9526), 4326)), 
    1000
);
In this example:

ST_DWithin is used to find landmarks within 1,000 meters of a given point (in this case, a latitude/longitude coordinate representing Philadelphia).
The geometry is cast to a geography type to enable curved-earth (lat/lon) calculations.

2. OGC Standards Compliance
PostGIS is designed to comply with Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) standards, which ensures that the database follows industry protocols for spatial data. This allows for interoperability with other GIS tools that adhere to these standards, facilitating smooth data exchange between systems. By following OGC standards, PostGIS can store and handle a wide variety of geospatial formats, such as WKT (Well-Known Text), WKB (Well-Known Binary), and GeoJSON.
3. Scalability and Performance
PostgreSQL, with PostGIS, is optimized to handle large-scale geospatial data efficiently. Key performance features include:

Spatial Indexing: PostGIS uses GiST (Generalized Search Tree) and SP-GiST indexes for spatial data, which dramatically increase query performance by allowing fast spatial searches. For instance, a spatial index on a geometry column would significantly speed up queries like “find all features within this polygon.”
Tiling and Raster Data: PostGIS also supports raster data, enabling the handling of continuous spatial data like satellite imagery or elevation data. It supports tiling strategies for large datasets and integrates raster-vector analysis in the database.

4. Multi-user Support and Fine-grained Permissions
PostgreSQL is a multiuser system, providing excellent user and permission management features. This is especially important in collaborative environments where multiple users may need access to the database at different levels of control.


Role-based Access Control (RBAC): PostgreSQL allows for the creation of roles and fine-grained access control. You can create roles for different types of users (e.g., GIS analysts, database administrators, or data entry clerks) and assign them varying levels of permissions over specific tables, views, or functions.
For example, you might want to allow one group to only query spatial data, while another can modify or update geometry features:
-- Create a role for read-only users
CREATE ROLE readonly;
 
-- Grant read-only access to the spatial data
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE landmarks TO readonly;
 
-- Create a GIS analyst role with more permissions
CREATE ROLE gis_analyst;
 
-- Grant the ability to insert, update, and delete records
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLE landmarks TO gis_analyst;


User and Group Management: PostgreSQL allows for detailed user and group management, letting administrators control who can create spatial indexes, execute spatial functions, or access specific datasets. This allows for tight control over spatial data security and integrity.


5. Integration with QGIS
PostGIS is well-integrated with QGIS, an open-source GIS platform that can directly connect to PostgreSQL/PostGIS databases. QGIS allows for visualization, spatial analysis, and editing of PostGIS data through a graphical interface, enabling users to interact with the data without needing to write SQL queries. This makes PostgreSQL a common choice for back-end spatial databases in QGIS projects, particularly for larger datasets or multi-user environments.
6. Example Spatial Query Use Cases
Here are some common spatial queries and functions made possible with PostgreSQL and PostGIS:


Find Points Within a Polygon: Querying points that fall inside a specific geographic area.
SELECT name
FROM landmarks
WHERE ST_Within(landmarks.geom, ST_MakePolygon(...));


Buffering: Creating buffer zones around points, lines, or polygons. For example, generating a 500-meter buffer around all roads:
SELECT ST_Buffer(roads.geom, 500)
FROM roads;


Intersection: Finding where two geographic features overlap, such as roads intersecting a specific region:
SELECT name
FROM roads
WHERE ST_Intersects(roads.geom, ST_MakePolygon(...));


Distance Calculations: Calculating the distance between two geographic objects:
SELECT ST_Distance(
    ST_MakePoint(-75.1652, 39.9526),
    ST_MakePoint(-77.0369, 38.9072)
) AS distance;


This query calculates the distance between Philadelphia and Washington, D.C.
Conclusion
PostgreSQL, with its PostGIS extension, forms the backbone of many modern geospatial applications. It not only supports a wide variety of geospatial data and formats, but it also enables sophisticated spatial queries, high-performance indexing, and fine-grained user control. Its alignment with OGC standards ensures compatibility with other GIS tools like QGIS, making it an ideal choice for organizations and projects that require robust, multi-user, and scalable spatial data management solutions. Whether you’re performing complex spatial analysis, managing massive datasets, or ensuring secure, role-based access to geospatial data, PostgreSQL with PostGIS provides a powerful, flexible, and open-source solution.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Changing the UI language.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Changing the UI language
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
By default, the UI language of GIS is that of your OS, so if your OS is Danish, then QGIS UI is also Danish. However, if you want the UI to be in some other language, for instance, English, so it fits with the documentation, this is how to do it.
For demonstration purposes, I will here change the user interface from English to Danish.
From the Settings menu (instillinger in Danish) Choose options (instillinger in Danish)
In the general tab (Generelt in Dabsih), tick the box Override System Local and in the “User Interface translation”, choose the language you wish to use. 
NB ! The changes first take effect after restarting QGIS.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Managing QGIS plugins.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Managing QGIS plugins
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Plugins are a powerful feature in QGIS that allow you to extend the functionality of the software. Most plugins are available from the official QGIS Plugin Repository—the “app store” for QGIS. This guide will walk you through installing, updating, deactivating, and uninstalling plugins to enhance your QGIS experience.
Installing Plugins


Open the Plugin Manager:
Go to the Plugins menu and select Manage and Install Plugins… This will open the Plugin Manager window.



Understand the Plugin Manager Interface:

• The Plugin Manager has several key sections:

Tabs/Filters: Options like All, Installed, Not Installed, Upgradable, and New help you filter plugins based on their status.
Search Bar: Use this to find plugins by entering keywords related to their name or functionality.
Plugin List: Displays plugins based on your selected filter and search terms.
Plugin Information: Provides details about the selected plugin, including its description, version, author, and more.
Action Buttons: Allows you to Install, Uninstall, Upgrade, Activate, or Deactivate plugins.



Search for a Plugin:
In the All or Not Installed tab, type a keyword (e.g., “geocoding” or “Plot”) into the search bar to find relevant plugins.



Install the Plugin:
Select the desired plugin from the list.
Click the Install Plugin button at the bottom of the window.

Once installed, the plugin may add new menus, panels, or toolbars to QGIS.


Updating Plugins
Plugins are regularly updated to add new features or fix bugs. By default, you will be notified about updates at startup. You can also “manually” check for updates by opening the plugin manager. If the “Upgrade all” button is active, there are updates. In the “Installed” tab, you can update the plugins individually.
Hiding/unhiding installed plugins, including the Processing menu
A problem I often come across is that the processing menu is missing from QGIS, and the typical reason is that the processing is a plugin that (by accident) can be hidden. To hide and unhide plugins, go to the installed tab of the plugin manager

Here you can hide plugins by removing the little tick mark in front of a plug-in or unhiding it by adding the little tick mark.
If you encounter any issues or have questions about specific plugins, consult the QGIS Documentation or reach out to the QGIS community for support.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/QGIS 4 on macOS 27.2.md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: QGIS 4 on macOS 27.2
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Solved in the QGIS nightly build of 26 November 2026 
                  
                

The QGIS nightly build from 26 November 2026 (the development version 4.5.0, build 0fddd5b) starts normally on macOS 27.2: the workaround below is not needed with it. A nightly build is a test version of the next QGIS and can have other faults. Until a released version of QGIS has the fix, use either the nightly build or the workaround.


The problem. After updating a Mac to macOS 27.2, QGIS 4.2 closes a few seconds after you start it, before the window appears, or macOS reports that it quit unexpectedly. This is a known fault (QGIS issue 67981). It is not caused by your projects or settings, and reinstalling QGIS does not help.
The cause. Some of the small images QGIS uses (its Dock icon and some mouse cursors) contain a colour profile. Since 27.2, macOS fails on the way the version of Qt inside QGIS passes that profile on, and QGIS crashes. The real fix has to come from Qt and QGIS. Until then, the workaround below removes the colour profiles from a copy of QGIS.
The workaround (about five minutes)
The script makes a copy of QGIS in the folder Applications in your home folder, patches the copy, and signs it for your Mac. The QGIS in /Applications is not changed.


Close QGIS if it is open.


Open Terminal (Finder › Applications › Utilities › Terminal).


Paste these two lines and press Return:
curl -fsSL semanticgis.org/Data/assets/scripts/qgis-macos27-patch.sh -o ~/Downloads/qgis-macos27-patch.sh
sh ~/Downloads/qgis-macos27-patch.sh



Wait. Copying takes a few minutes and signing a minute or two. The script prints Cursor images patched: 6, then Done. Start QGIS from …, and opens QGIS.


From now on start QGIS from the copy: open Finder, press ⇧⌘H (your home folder), open Applications and double-click QGIS-4.2.x-patched. Drag it to the Dock to keep it there. The old QGIS in the Dock will still crash.


You can read the script before running it. It uses only tools that come with macOS.
If something goes wrong

No QGIS 4 found in /Applications: give the path of your QGIS, e.g. sh ~/Downloads/qgis-macos27-patch.sh /Applications/QGIS-final-4_2_3.app.
… exists already: you have run it before. Drag QGIS-4.2.x-patched from your home folder’s Applications to the Trash and run the script again.
“Operation not permitted”: macOS protects an app from changes once it has been opened. Never open the copy before the script has finished; if you did, put it in the Trash and run the script again.
“QGIS … is damaged and can’t be opened”: the signing step did not finish. Put the copy in the Trash and run the script again, and bring the text Terminal printed to class if it fails again.
QGIS still crashes: bring the crash report (the text in the “quit unexpectedly” window, Report…) to class.

Notes

After updating QGIS the new version is unpatched. Check first whether it starts by itself (the fault may be fixed); if not, run the script again.
Disk space: the copy takes about 3.6 GB. Once a fixed QGIS is out, put the copy in the Trash.
Signed for your Mac only: the copy carries a local signature, not the QGIS project’s, so it runs on your Mac but should not be passed on to others. Everyone runs the script on their own Mac.
QGIS 3.44 LTR does not have this fault and can be used meanwhile. It may report a crash when you quit it; that happens after it has closed your project.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: QGIS
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
QGIS is an Open-Source (free to use) desktop GIS that can handle the needs of most Geospatial projects. In addition to the built-in functionality of QGIS, there are hundreds of so-called plugins that can extend the functionality of QGIS.
Installing QGIS.
Installing QGIS is relatively easy just go to www.qgis.org/download/. The website normally determines the OS you are using and gives you the option to download a Long-term version or the latest for your OS. I recommend using the latest. For Mac users please read the tips for the first launch, and on macOS 27.2 see QGIS 4 on macOS 27.2 For Windows users who know they want to use QGIS for more than just some months I recommend using the OSGeo4W installer since it is easier to update QGIS later.
Costimising QGIS
QGIS has a lot of options to customise how it looks and feels. It can, therefore, sometimes be difficult to follow documentation /Tutorials/Demos. There are two primary customisations you will need to master in order to make your QGIS look like the one someone else is using or in time look how you want it to look, and that is Changing the UI language and showing hiding and moving the UI panels
Extending QGIS
Plugins are a powerful feature in QGIS that allow you to extend the functionality of the software. Most plugins are available from the official QGIS Plugin Repository—the “app store” for QGIS. Read about installing and managing plugins in the note Managing QGIS plugins
Accessing data in QGIS
Once QGIS is installed and configured, the next task is typically to access some geospatial data. There are many different ways of doing this depending on the data type and method of access. To read more, read the article “Accessing data in QGIS“
Up and running with QGIS
This article takes you through the first basic steps of using QGIS from loading data to producing a map.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Aggregating a categorical raster to zones (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need



































RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesCategorical rasterraster, one band of class codesnominal (or ordinal) classese.g. a land-cover or land-use mapSymbology file.qml next to the raster—a Paletted/Unique values style whose labels name the classes; without it the columns get the raw codesZonespolygonsnominal zone typee.g. landscapes, municipalities, grid cellsComposition (output)the zones with one field per classratio (area or percentage)
Raster and zones in the same CRS.
Prepare the raster (Task Schema step 1)
Add the raster. A style file with the same name as the raster (<raster>.qml) loads automatically; otherwise Layer Properties › Symbology › Style › Load Style…. Check that the legend shows class names, not codes.
One zone per zone type (step 4, done first)
If several polygons share a type, Dissolve (Tool - QGIS) the zones by the type field first. The shares are then computed from summed areas, never averaged.
Tabulate (step 3)
Tabulate area (Tool - QGIS) (SemanticGIS plugin): Categorical raster the raster, Polygons the (dissolved) zones, Report as Percent of the zone’s classified pixels or Area. The output has one column per legend label; codes without a label get a column value <n>. Without the plugin, QGIS’s Zonal histogram gives the same counts with the codes as column names.
Chart (step 5)
Export the table (Export › Save Features As…, format MS Office Open XML spreadsheet, without geometry) and make a 100 % stacked bar chart, one bar per zone. Group small classes first.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Aggregating a continuous raster to zones (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Soil carbon and land use at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need



































RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesContinuous rasterraster, one band of valuesinterval or ratioe.g. soil organic carbon, elevation, a vegetation index; know its unit, depth or date and how it was madeZonespolygonsnominal zone typee.g. landscapesCategorical raster (optional)raster on the same gridnominal classesto summarise the surface per class, e.g. per land useStatistics (output)the zones with statistics fieldsratiocount, mean, median, …
Statistics per zone type (Task Schema steps 3–4)

If several polygons share a type, Dissolve (Tool - QGIS) the zones by the type field, so types are combined from cells, not from polygon means.
Zonal statistics (Tool - QGIS): Raster layer the surface, Statistics to calculate Count, Mean, Median (add Max to spot extremes).

Statistics per class (step 5)
Zonal statistics by class (Tool - QGIS) (SemanticGIS plugin): Categorical raster the classes, styled with their legend or with a .qml file, and Value raster the surface. The output table has one row per legend label, with count, area, mean, median, quartiles and standard deviation. The two rasters may differ in cell size and CRS.
Without the plugin: Raster layer zonal statistics (Raster analysis), with Input layer the surface and Zones layer the categorical raster. Both rasters need the same cell size and alignment. The output table has one row per class code, without names, with count, sum, minimum, maximum and mean.
To restrict either result to the zones, first Clip raster by mask layer the surface with the zones.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Aggregating points to zones (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Aggregating points to zones (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Aggregating points to zones (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked examples: Share of rented dwellings in Copenhagen (Example) and Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).
Data you need





























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesPointspointsfields of any levelthe population to aggregate, e.g. from Categories from register codes (Task); a 0/1 indicator field gives sharesZonespolygonsnominal zone idadministrative units, or a grid made with Create grid (Tool - QGIS)Summaries (output)the zones with summary fieldsratio counts, sums, means
Points and zones in the same projected CRS.
Summarise (Task Schema step 3)
Join attributes by location (summary) (Tool - QGIS):

Join to features in: the zones
Where the features: intersect
By comparing to: the points
Fields to summarise: the fields you need
Summaries to calculate: e.g. count, sum, mean, median
Discard records which could not be joined: unticked

The new fields are named <field>_<summary>. For a single count, Count points in polygon (Tool - QGIS) is quicker.
Check the sums (step 4)
Open the statistics panel (View › Statistics Panel) on the count field: its Sum should equal the number of points. A difference means points outside every zone, or on a border counted twice.
Minimum count (step 5)
Flag zones below the minimum with Field calculator (Tool - QGIS), e.g. coalesce("<field>_count", 0) < <minimum>, or handle it in the symbology (Comparable choropleth maps (Recipe - QGIS)).
A grid instead of given zones
Create grid (Tool - QGIS): Grid type Rectangle (Polygon) or Hexagon (Polygon), extent from the zones, spacing in metres, the project’s CRS. Then summarise as above with the grid as the zones.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Backdrop digitalisation (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Backdrop Digitalisation (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Backdrop digitalisation Task Schema.

Editorial note: the mechanics below (layer creation, edit mode, snapping, rings/holes) are grounded in the transcript of your “basic GIS operations in QGIS” video, supplied manually. That video covers general QGIS digitising over an OpenStreetMap basemap — it does not itself demonstrate reconciling hand-drawn field notes against an aerial photo, so that part of the write-up is a general reconstruction pending a source specific to backdrop digitalisation.

Load the backdrop
Add the orthophoto — as a WMS/WMTS connection or a local raster layer — and zoom to the extent of your study area. If it isn’t already georeferenced, see Georeferencing (Recipe - QGIS) first.
Build the empty layer (Task Schema step 1)
Layer → Create Layer → New GeoPackage Layer: browse to (or create) your project’s .gpkg file, name the table after the entity — not after the GeoPackage itself, which QGIS will otherwise default to — set the geometry type, and set the coordinate reference system (in Denmark, searching the EPSG code directly, e.g. 25832 for ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N, is faster than browsing the list). Add the attribute fields to match your Attribute Framework exactly before dismissing the dialog.
Digitise (Task Schema step 2)
Toggle the layer into edit mode using the pencil icon on the Digitizing toolbar, then use the corresponding Add Point / Add Line / Add Polygon Feature tool. Place vertices by clicking, and right-click to finish the feature — this immediately opens its attribute form, which you fill in directly from your field notes.
Interior exclusions (rings/holes): enable Advanced Digitizing, digitise the outer boundary as normal and finish it, then use Add Ring on that same feature to cut the interior hole. QGIS treats a ring as a hole precisely when the outer and inner boundaries belong to the same feature — a second, separately-owned polygon placed on top is not the same thing.
Enforce boundary topology (Task Schema step 4)
The magnet icon on the Snapping toolbar toggles snapping on; the settings beside it let you choose whether to snap to vertices, edges, or segments, and set a tolerance. Enable snapping before digitising the second of two features that must meet exactly, not after.
Save and close out (Task Schema step 5)
Once digitising is complete, do a final pass comparing the digitised layer against your original field notes.
ArcGIS
(To fill in: the equivalent layer-creation/editing/snapping workflow in ArcGIS Pro — same Task Schema, different interface.)

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Building heights from DHM (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Building heights from DHM (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Building heights from elevation models (Task) Schema, for Danish data. Used in Urban Design Visualisation (Example) (step 1).
Before you start
Install the SemanticGIS plugin (0.7.19 or later) and enter your free Datafordeleren key in the plugin panel’s Settings. The tools used here are in the Processing Toolbox (⚙ icon or Ctrl+Alt+T) under SemanticGIS; nothing else needs installing.

























ToolWhat it doesUrban context for a study area (Denmark)Fetches GeoDanmark for the study area, adds building heights and saves it all in one GeoPackage, with the terrainBuilding heights from elevation modelsHeight, eave height and roof type for any building layerClip project layers to one GeoPackageClips all visible layers to the study area and saves them, with stylesSurface partition 1 and 2Used in Surface partitioning (Recipe - QGIS)
1. Set up the project

New QGIS project. Project → Properties → CRS: EPSG:25832.
Save it in 02_qgis/.
Add an orthophoto as background from the SemanticGIS panel (search ortofoto), and zoom to your square. The tool in step 2 saves its own copy of the orthophoto for the study area.

2. Get the context data, with heights
Run SemanticGIS › Data access › Urban context for a study area (Denmark):

Study area: leave the layer empty, click … next to or a rectangle → Draw on Map Canvas, and drag a rectangle about 200–300 m around the square. (A polygon layer works too, for an irregular area.)
GeoDanmark layers: the defaults (buildings, kerbs, road centre lines, traffic islands, parking, squares, lakes, trees, fences) suit most squares.
GeoPackage: 02_qgis/context.gpkg.

After a minute or two, a group Urban context – context.gpkg appears with:

the GeoDanmark layers, cut to the study area, buildings coloured by height (road centre lines are switched off: they are only needed as hints);
the newest orthophoto (shown) and the OpenStreetMap map (switched off), as context_rasters/orthophoto.tif and openstreetmap.tif at 0.1 m, for backgrounds in drawings and in Blender;
Terrain (DTM) and Height above ground (nDSM), switched off, saved as context_rasters/terrain.tif and height_above_ground.tif. Copy terrain.tif to 03_exchange/ as terrain for Blender.

Write the attribution line from the log on your drawings.
Your own data instead
If you have your own footprints or height models, or work outside Denmark: clip your layers with Clip project layers to one GeoPackage, then run Building heights from elevation models on the buildings. Leave its surface and terrain model empty to use Danmarks Højdemodel, or choose your own rasters.
3. Check the heights













































FieldMeaningUsed forheightTop of the building / ridge above ground (m)LOD1 extrusioneaveEstimated eave height above ground (m)LOD2 extrusion, before modelling the roofroof_riseheight − eave (m)How far to raise the ridge in Blenderroof_typeflat or pitchedWhich buildings need a roofgroundTerrain elevation under the building (m, DVR90)Placing buildings on the terrainh_medianMedian height (m)Alternative LOD1 height for pitched roofsh_checkok, few pixels, no data, negativeFinding problems
Sort the attribute table by h_check. “Few pixels” is usually a shed. A very large roof_rise often means a lower wing inside the same footprint — check it against the orthophoto, and switch on Height above ground to see what the tool saw.
4. Export for Blender
Add an integer field lod: 2 for the 4–8 buildings that frame the square and show in your views, 1 for all others. Then export twice with Export → Save Features As…, each time selecting the buildings first (Select by Expression) and ticking Save only selected features:




















FileBuildingsFields to keep03_exchange/context_lod1.shp"lod" = 1id, height, ground03_exchange/context_lod2.shp"lod" = 2id, height, eave, roof_rise, roof_type, ground
Format ESRI Shapefile, CRS EPSG:25832. Shapefile field names are cut at 10 characters, which these names respect. Shapefile is only the transport format; the master data stays in context.gpkg.
Troubleshooting






























ProblemCauseFix”needs your own Datafordeleren API key”No key in the pluginGet one at Datafordeleren (free) and enter it in the SemanticGIS panel’s Settings”The study area is … m”The area is larger than 3 × 3 kmDraw a smaller study areaVery tall or very low buildingsTrees or street pixels inside the footprintIncrease the inward buffer (Advanced parameters of the height tool); fix outliers by handEave much too low, roof_rise very largeLower wing or annex inside the same footprintSet the eave by hand from orthophoto / site photos, or split the footprint and run the height tool on it again

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Categories from register codes (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Categories from register codes (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Categories from register codes (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).
Data you need





























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesRegister unitspoints or a tablecode fields: nominal; years and areas: ratioe.g. dwellings with use codes, construction years, rental codesCode listsdocumentation—the register’s own definitions of each codeUnits with categories (output)the same layernominal category, or a 0/1 indicator
Read and count the codes (Task Schema steps 2–3)
Read the code list for each field you consider. Then count the units per code: Processing Toolbox › Vector analysis › Statistics by categories, Field(s) with categories the code field, no value field. Note the empty values.
Decide and select (steps 4–5)
Write the decisions down first: which codes form the population, and which codes go into which category. Then Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS) for the population, e.g.
"<code field>" IN (<codes>) AND "<year field>" < <year>

Write the category (step 6)
Field calculator (Tool - QGIS), a text field:
CASE WHEN <condition 1> THEN '<category 1>'
     WHEN <condition 2> THEN '<category 2>'
     ELSE NULL END

or an integer 0/1 indicator: if(<condition>, 1, 0).
Check (step 7)
Count again per category (Statistics by categories on the new field): every unit should be in exactly one category, or left out on purpose.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Comparable choropleth maps (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Comparable choropleth maps (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Comparable choropleth maps (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Dwelling size by construction period in Copenhagen (Example).
Data you need























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesAggregated zones, one layer per grouppolygonsratio value field and a count fieldfrom Aggregating points to zones (Task), with the same zones and minimum countShared style (output)a .qml file—the same classes and colours for every map
Look at all groups’ values (Task Schema step 2)
Open the statistics panel on the value field of each layer and note the combined range.
One set of classes, with a class for too few (steps 3–4)
Layer Properties › Symbology › Categorized with an expression as Value (the ε button), so that zones with too few points get their own class:
CASE WHEN coalesce("<count field>", 0) < <minimum> THEN 'Too few'
     WHEN "<value field>" < <break 1> THEN 'under <break 1>'
     WHEN "<value field>" < <break 2> THEN '<break 1>–<break 2>'
     …
     ELSE '<last break> or more' END

Press Classify, put the categories in order, and give them one sequential colour scheme, with grey for “Too few”. With Graduated symbology (Tool - QGIS) instead, set the boundaries by hand (Fixed Interval or typed values) and add a rule for too few.
Same style on every map (step 5)
Style › Save Style… to a .qml file, then Style › Load Style… on the other layers; or Styles › Copy Style and Paste Style.
Compose (step 6)
Print layout (Tool - QGIS): a title that names the group, the legend, a scale bar, a north arrow and a source line on each map; the same extent and scale on all of them.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Distance to habitat (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Distance to habitat (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Distance to habitat (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need





























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesHabitat patchespolygons— (presence)e.g. from Nature content layer (Task), covering the study area plus a marginZones (optional)polygonsnominalfor summaries, e.g. landscapesDistance (output)rasterratio (metres)
A projected CRS in metres (EPSG:25832 for Danish data).
Rasterize the habitat (Task Schema steps 2–3)
Rasterize (Tool - QGIS) on the patches:

A fixed value to burn: 1; Pre-initialize the output image with value: 0
Output raster size units: Georeferenced units; width and height = the chosen cell size
Output extent: the study area plus its margin
Additional command-line parameters: -at (all touched), so features narrower than a cell are not lost

Compute distances (step 4)
Proximity (Tool - QGIS): A list of pixel values to use as target 1, Distance units Georeferenced coordinates, Output data type Float32.
Cut to the study area and summarise (steps 5–6)

Clip raster by extent (Raster extraction) to the study area.
Style it with Singleband pseudocolor, mode Discrete, with classes from the question (e.g. 50, 100, 200 m).
Per zone: Dissolve the zones by their type field if several polygons share a type, then Zonal statistics (Tool - QGIS) with Mean and Max.

Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Georeferencing (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Georeferencing (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Georeferencing (Task) Schema. Also referenced as a prerequisite step from Backdrop digitalisation.
Tool: Raster → Georeferencer

Open the Georeferencer and load the un-referenced image (scanned map, un-referenced aerial photo).
Place control points on the image and, for each, either type in its known real-world coordinates directly, or (with a reference layer such as an existing orthophoto loaded in the main QGIS canvas alongside the Georeferencer window) click the matching location on that reference layer to pick the coordinate pair visually.
Set the target CRS.
Choose the transformation type:

Linear/Helmert/first-order (affine): scales, rotates, and translates only. Assumes a flat surface with no lens distortion — appropriate for a flat scan or paper map with no optical distortion to correct.
Polynomial 2/3 (higher-order): warps the image using polynomial equations to correct non-linear distortion — appropriate for aerial or satellite photographs, where lens/perspective distortion is present, especially toward the image edges. Higher polynomial order corrects more precisely but needs more control points and more computation.


Run the transformation and check the reported residual/RMS error before accepting — a control point with an unexpectedly high residual is usually a mis-clicked point, not a transformation-order problem, and should be re-picked rather than compensated for by raising the polynomial order.
Save the georeferenced output.

(Open item: minimum recommended control-point count per transformation order in QGIS’s specific implementation, and the acceptable residual/RMS threshold — to fill in once verified against QGIS’s own documentation or a worked example.)
Use cases (tool-agnostic context, kept here for now)

Aerial photographs and satellite images — typically need higher-order rectification because of lens/perspective optical distortion.
Scanned maps — typically only need first-order/affine, since there is no lens distortion to correct.
Urban planning / GIS work generally — georeferencing aerial photographs is usually the prerequisite step before overlaying vector data such as roads, buildings, and zoning boundaries.

ArcGIS
(To fill in: the equivalent Georeferencing toolbar/pane workflow in ArcGIS Pro — same Task Schema, different interface.)

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Habitat network (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Habitat network (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Habitat network (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need





























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesHabitat patchespolygonsnominal type (optional)e.g. from Nature content layer (Task)Connection distancea numberratio (metres)from the species or species group in questionPatches with cluster (output)polygonsnominal cluster_id; ratio counts and areas
Build the clusters (Task Schema steps 3–5)
Buffer (Tool - QGIS) on the patches:

Distance: half the connection distance
Dissolve result: ticked
Keep disjoint results separate: ticked

This one dialog realises three Operators — dilation, dissolve and explode — and gives one feature per cluster. Then:

Renumber feature ids (Tool - QGIS) on the clusters. Without it, saving to a GeoPackage fails (UNIQUE constraint failed), because the clusters share fid values.
Field calculator (Tool - QGIS): an integer field cluster_id = $id.

Give each patch its cluster (step 6)
Join attributes by location (Tool - QGIS): Join to features in the patches, By comparing to the clusters, predicate intersect, field cluster_id, join type Take attributes of the first matching feature only (one-to-one).
Measure and classify (steps 7–8)
Field calculator (Tool - QGIS) on the joined patches:

n_in_cluster (integer) = count($id, group_by:="cluster_id")
cluster_area (decimal) = sum($area, group_by:="cluster_id")

Style the layer with Categorized on the expression
CASE WHEN "cluster_area" = maximum("cluster_area") THEN 'Main network'
     WHEN "n_in_cluster" = 1 THEN 'Isolated patch'
     ELSE 'Smaller cluster' END

Repeat with at least one other connection distance, as the Task’s choices recommend.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/History from yearly snapshots (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: History from yearly snapshots (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the History from yearly snapshots (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2 with the SemanticGIS plugin. Worked example: Crop rotations at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need



































RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesYearly registerWFS, one layer per year—a series the SemanticGIS catalogue knows; or a layer you have already merged, with a year fieldAreapolygons—the study area, e.g. landscapes; selected features only if you likeCode listtable: code, categorynominaltranslates each year’s codes into categories that mean the same in every yearHistory (output)polygons, one column per yearnominalplus summary fields
Fetch every year (Task Schema step 2)
Download snapshot series (SemanticGIS plugin): Series the register, First year and Last year, Area the study area with a Buffer if you want one, Clip features to the area on for area statistics. Read the log: it names the years without a layer and the fields some years lack, and gives the attribution line for the map.
Make the codes comparable (step 3)
Join attributes by field value: Input layer the series, Table field <code field>; Input layer 2 the code list, Table field 2 <code>; copy only the category fields you need; join type one-to-one. Check Unjoinable features: codes the list does not know get no category.
Count per category and year (step 4)
Statistics by categories: Field to calculate statistics on the expression $area / 10000 (hectares), Field(s) with categories <category> and the year field. The sum column is the area. Export it and pivot it with the years as columns.
Flatten (step 5)
Flatten snapshot series: Period field the year field, Fields to keep <category> (and any other field you want per year), Tolerance in metres, Column prefix y. The result has one column per year: y<year>_<category>.
Summarise each piece (step 6)

Unordered combination: Combination of values with the period columns; it adds the combination, the number of distinct values (…_n) and the number of years with a value (…_periods).
Years with a given category: Field calculator, an integer field with one term per year:
if("y<year1>_<category>" = '<value>', 1, 0) + if("y<year2>_<category>" = '<value>', 1, 0) + …
Write if(…, 1, 0), not the comparison alone: a comparison with an empty year gives NULL, and NULL makes the whole sum NULL.
The year of a category: CASE WHEN "y<year1>_<category>" = '<value>' THEN <year1> WHEN … END.

Map and count (step 7)
Area per summary value: Statistics by categories on the flattened layer with $area / 10000 and the summary field. For a map of the largest values: Symbology › Categorized on the summary field, Classify, sort by the area table and keep the largest; give the rest one grey class. For the number of years, Graduated with one class per year count.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, November 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Landscape delineation (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Landscape delineation (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Landscape delineation (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesEvidence layersraster or vector, anyanylayers that show landform, soils, water, historical and present land use, e.g. a geomorphological map, historical maps, a soil map, a terrain model with hillshade, an orthophotoLandscapes (output)polygonsnominal (landscape type)one text field for the type
Create the layer and the study area (Task Schema step 1)

Layer › Create Layer › New GeoPackage Layer…: geometry type Polygon, the project’s CRS (EPSG:25832 for Danish data), one text field for the landscape type.
Toggle editing, and on the Shape Digitizing toolbar choose Add Rectangle from Extent (or from 2 points). Draw the study area.

Load and read the evidence layers (steps 2–3)
Add the evidence layers, for example with the SemanticGIS plugin. Switch them on and off, and set the transparency of one over another, to see where landform, soil and land use change together.
Split the rectangle into landscapes (step 4)
On the Advanced Digitizing toolbar choose Split Features. Click a line across the rectangle along a boundary you have read in the evidence layers; right-click to finish. Repeat for every boundary.
Name the landscapes (step 5)
Open the attribute table and type the landscape type for each polygon. Use exactly the same spelling for the same type: a misspelt name becomes a separate landscape in every later summary. Save the edits.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Multi-criteria suitability (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Multi-criteria suitability (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Multi-criteria suitability (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Densification priorities in Copenhagen by multi-criteria analysis (Example).
Data you need





























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesUnitspolygons—e.g. parcelsCriteriaone field per criterion on the unitsdistances and areas: ratio; classes: ordinalraw values, or scores already rescaledSuitability and rank (output)new fields on the unitsinterval (suitability), ordinal (rank)one pair per scenario
Audit the criteria (Task Schema step 2)
For each criterion field: Processing Toolbox › Vector analysis › Basic statistics for fields gives count, empty values, minimum, maximum, mean, median and standard deviation. A mean far from the median, or a maximum many times the third quartile, means extreme values. Where a criterion has no meaning for a unit, set its value to NULL (Scoring criteria (Recipe - QGIS)) rather than leaving a score that looks real. A unit with a NULL criterion gets no suitability (a sum with NULL is NULL) and so no rank. Units that should not be ranked at all can be removed with Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS).
Score (step 3)
One score field per criterion, by Scoring criteria (Recipe - QGIS): divide by the maximum, min–max, z-score, log, thresholds, distance decay, a lookup table, or a percentile rank, with NULL for held-out units.
Weight and add (steps 4–5)
Field calculator (Tool - QGIS), a decimal field per scenario, e.g. suit_1:
- 0.4 * "p_station" - 0.2 * "p_centre" + 0.2 * "p_density" + 0.2 * "p_heritage"

A negative weight for a criterion where a high score is bad for the question. Keep the expression: it is the scenario’s documentation.
Rank and select (step 6)

Add autoincremental field (Tool - QGIS): Field name rank_1, Start values at 1, Sort expression "suit_1", Sort ascending off, Sort nulls first off, so units without a suitability come last.
Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS): "rank_1" <= 100 for the top 100.

Effective weights (step 7)
Basic statistics for fields on each rescaled criterion gives its standard deviation. The effective weight of a criterion is |weight| × standard deviation, divided by the sum of these over all criteria. With percentile ranks the effective weights equal the nominal ones.
Check (step 8)
Repeat weighting and ranking for the second scenario. Count the units in both top selections: "rank_1" <= 100 AND "rank_2" <= 100 in Select by expression.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, November 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Nature content layer (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Nature content layer (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Nature content layer (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need



































RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesProtected habitatspolygonsnominal habitat typee.g. the national register of protected nature typesWoodlandpolygons—area is computed from the geometryLinear habitats (hedges, streams)linesnominal type, if the source has onee.g. a type field that separates living hedges from fences, or open from piped streamsNature content (output)polygonsnominal (nature field)one layer, all sources
All sources for the study area plus a margin (about 1 km), in the same CRS.
Get the sources (Task Schema step 2)
Load each source for the map extent (e.g. with the SemanticGIS plugin) and save a local copy: Export › Save Features As… with Extent = map canvas, or all at once with Package layers (Tool - QGIS).
Select what qualifies (step 3)
Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS) on each source, with the conditions the Task’s choices call for, e.g.

a minimum size: $area >= <m²>
a type: "<type field>" = '<value>'

Give lines a width (step 4)
Buffer (Tool - QGIS) on each line layer with half the habitat strip’s width as Distance; Dissolve result off.
Label and merge (steps 5–6)

On each layer, Field calculator (Tool - QGIS): a text field nature, either a fixed label ('Woodland') or a source field ("<type field>").
Retain fields (Vector table) keeps only nature on each layer, so the merge does not stumble over different fields.
Merge vector layers (Tool - QGIS) with all layers and the project’s CRS as Destination CRS.

Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Network gaps and stepping stones (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Network gaps and stepping stones (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Network gaps and stepping stones (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example).
Data you need



































RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesPatches with clusterpolygonsnominal cluster_idfrom Habitat network (Task)Land where new habitat is possiblepolygons, or a raster to convertnominal land-use classese.g. farmland classes of a land-cover rasterExcluded land (optional)polygonsnominalroads, buildings: negative constraintsStrip width, minimum cluster sizenumbersratiofrom the Task’s choices
Each cluster’s own habitat (Task Schema steps 1–2)

Dissolve (Tool - QGIS) on the patches, Dissolve field(s) cluster_id: each cluster’s habitat without the buffer, so gaps are measured between real patches.
Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS) twice:

the main network: "cluster_id" = <id of the largest> (sort the attribute table by $area to find it)
the clusters to connect: "cluster_id" <> <id of the largest> AND $area >= <minimum m²>



Shortest connections (step 3)
Shortest line between features (Tool - QGIS): Source layer the clusters to connect, Destination layer the main network, Method Distance to Nearest Point on feature, Maximum number of neighbors 1.
Proposed new habitat (steps 4–6)

Buffer (Tool - QGIS) on the lines: Distance = half the strip width, End cap style Flat, Dissolve result ticked.
If the possible land is a raster: Reclassify by table with the possible classes → 1 (Use no data when no range matches), then Polygonize (raster to vector).
Clip (Tool - QGIS): the strip, with the possible land as Overlay layer (positive constraint).
Difference (Tool - QGIS): the result minus the habitat patches and any excluded land (negative constraints).
Sum the lengths of the lines and the area of the new habitat with the statistics panel.

Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Placing register units on the map (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Placing register units on the map (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Placing register units on the map (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Share of rented dwellings in Copenhagen (Example).
Data you need















































RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesUnitstable without geometryids: nominaleach unit with an id pointing to its address and one to its buildingAddressestablenominal idseach address with the id of its entrance (house number)Entrances (house numbers)tablenominal idseach with the id of its pointEntrance pointspoints, as WKT text or geometry—Buildings (alternative route)points, as WKT text or geometry—Units on points (output)pointsthe units’ fieldsone point per unit
Text files (CSV) are loaded with Layer › Add Layer › Add Delimited Text Layer…: tables with No geometry (attribute only table), point tables with Well known text (WKT), the geometry field, and the CRS.
Large national tables can be cut to the study area first with Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS) on a municipality field.
Select the units (Task Schema step 2)
Extract by expression (Tool - QGIS) on the unit table with the population’s conditions.
Join to the address point (steps 4–5)
Join attributes by field value (Tool - QGIS), with Join type one-to-one:

Units ← addresses: Table field the unit’s address id, Table field 2 the address’s id; copy the address text and the entrance id.
Result ← entrances: Table field the entrance id, Table field 2 the entrance’s id; copy the entrance text and the point id.
Points ← units: Input layer the point table, Table field its id, Input layer 2 the joined units, Table field 2 the point id, Join type one-to-many, Discard records which could not be joined ticked. The point layer must be the input, because the output takes its geometry; one-to-many gives one point for each unit at the same entrance.

Or join to the building point
One join: Input layer the building points, Table field their id, Input layer 2 the units, Table field 2 the unit’s building id, one-to-many, discard unmatched.
Count (step 6)
Compare the number of units with the number of points, and save Unjoinable features from first layer to see which units found no address or building.
Checked in QGIS 4.2.2, October 2026.

the-technology-stack/processing-environm.filePath: The technology stack/Processing Environments/QGIS/Recipes/Scoring criteria (Recipe - QGIS).md
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.title: Scoring criteria (Recipe — QGIS)
the-technology-stack/processing-environm.content:
Tool-bound implementation of the Scoring criteria (Task) Task Schema in QGIS 4.2. Worked example: Densification priorities in Copenhagen by multi-criteria analysis (Example).
Data you need





























RoleFormLevel of measurementNotesUnitsvector features—e.g. parcels or grid cellsCriteriona field on the unitsany; the function depends on ite.g. a distance in metres, a class 1–9Score (output)a new decimal fieldinterval, 0–100 (or z)NULL for held-out units
