workflow/part-3-getting-your-feet-wet/pr.title: Snapshot packages
workflow/part-3-getting-your-feet-wet/pr.content:
A snapshot package is a set of data frozen at a date, self-contained with everything needed to read it: the data files, the code lists their coded fields use, a machine-readable description and a README. The same format serves two purposes:

Example data on semanticgis.org, so that a worked example can be reproduced on anyone’s computer without API keys, with exactly the example’s numbers (Habitat network at Ledreborg (Example), Share of rented dwellings in Copenhagen (Example)).
Datasets published to a research group, so that what the group analysed can be found and read again later, even after the source has changed.

Live access is a different case: there the SemanticGIS plugin reads current data, and the code lists follow the source’s schema version.
What a snapshot contains
<snapshot>/
  snapshot.json        machine-readable description (a STAC Item)
  data files           GeoParquet, GeoPackage, Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (+ .qml styles)
  codelists/*.csv      one file per code list: code, name (name_en, description)
  README.txt           human-readable, generated from snapshot.json
  <name>_data.zip      everything above in one download

Choosing the data format

























DataFormatWhyLarge point or table layersGeoParquet (zstd)column-wise storage compresses repeated values to almost nothing: 349,743 dwellings take 6.6 MB, against 39 MB as GeoPackageSmall sets of several vector layersGeoPackageone file, several layers, styles insideRastersCloud Optimized GeoTIFF with a .qml style of the same namecompressed, tiled, readable over the web; QGIS loads the style automatically
Layers are extracted for the area plus a margin. Vector features are kept whole — every feature that touches the area, not cut at its edge — so that selections by size or length give the same result as on the source.
Code lists
Coded fields keep their codes, as the source registers them. The names travel with the snapshot in codelists/, one CSV per list, with its source and the date it was retrieved (e.g. a BBR list from teknik.bbr.dk). The codes are the data; the code list is how to read them at that date, and lists change between versions of a register.
To see the names in QGIS, join the code list to the layer by code (Layer Properties › Joins). The SemanticGIS plugin will be able to do this automatically from snapshot.json.
snapshot.json
A STAC Item, so that the same description can be read by catalogues and by the plugin:

properties: title, description, datetime (the date of the data), proj:code and proj:bbox (EPSG:25832), the sources with licence and attribution (semanticgis:sources).
assets: each file, with

for tables, the table extension’s table:columns: name, type, description, and for a coded field semanticgis:codelist, the key of its code-list asset;
for categorical rasters, the classification extension’s classification:classes (value, name, title);
for each code list, its source and retrieval date.


links: the examples or project pages that use the snapshot.

Licences and attribution
Every source is listed with its licence and the attribution line to put on a map, using the wording from the dataset’s page on semanticgis.org where it has been checked, and hentet ‹date› for downloaded data. A snapshot redistributes data, so the licence must allow it; where a source’s terms are not explicit, say so in the README.
Building a snapshot
In semanticGIS-code, scripts/snapshots.py builds the example snapshots: it extracts the data, fetches the code lists, writes snapshot.json, generates the README and zips the folder. New snapshots follow the same pattern.
The software environment
A snapshot fixes the data. The software can be fixed the same way, with an environment file or a container: see Reproducible environments.

workflow/part-4-the-deep-dive/the-four-n.title: The Four NOIR Data Types
workflow/part-4-the-deep-dive/the-four-n.content:
Nominal (N): Categorical data with no logical order or ranking, used to label variables without quantitative value.

Examples: Eye color, country names, gender.
Operations: Counting, mode.


Ordinal (O): Categorical data with a clear, inherent ordering or ranking, but the intervals between values are unknown or inconsistent.

Examples: Survey responses (satisfied, neutral, dissatisfied), education level, race positions (1st, 2nd).
Operations: Median, rank order.


Interval (I): Numerical data where the distance between two values is meaningful and equal. The zero point is arbitrary, meaning it does not represent a complete absence of the value.

Examples: Temperature in Celsius or Fahrenheit, time in 12-hour clock.
Operations: Addition, subtraction, mean.


Ratio (R): Numerical data that possesses all properties of interval data but includes a true, absolute zero point. The zero point implies the absence of the quantity.

Examples: Weight, height, age, income.
Operations: Multiplication, division, mean, median. 



Key Characteristics

Hierarchy: Each level includes the characteristics of the ones below it. Ratio is the most complex, while Nominal is the simplest.
Qualitative vs. Quantitative: Nominal and Ordinal are typically categorical (qualitative), while Interval and Ratio are numerical (quantitative).
Importance: Knowing the level of measurement helps determine the statistical tests and data visualization techniques to use.

index.title: Welcome
index.content:
SemanticGIS is a way of working with geospatial data that starts with the world, not with the software. First you say what you are looking at and which question you are asking of it. Then you find the data that stand for it, and choose the operations that turn the data into an answer. The software comes last. Each choice on the way is written down, so that others can follow it and the work can be repeated.
The site has two entrances.
1. Learning GIS the semantic way
For anyone who wants to learn GIS, or to plan and document a GIS project.
A GIS project is a workflow: a documented chain of reasoning from a spatial question to an answer. The workflow is built from reusable pieces, which run from domain-specific and tool-free at the top to tool-bound at the bottom:








































PieceWhat it isStart hereWorkflowThe route from question to answer, seen from five vantage points: scoping, data, analysis, communication and executionIntroduction, The workflowDomain hubsThe questions a field asks (landscape ecology, housing, hydrology…), with its own Tasks and worked ExamplesDomain hubsTasksA reusable unit of work, such as georeferencing or aggregating points to zones, described without reference to any softwareTasksOperatorsThe single transformations a Task is made of: buffer, clip, dissolve, zonal statisticsOperatorsRecipesHow a Task is carried out step by step in one piece of softwareQGIS RecipesToolsThe dialog in the software that realises one or more OperatorsQGIS Tools
Where to begin: follow a learning path. Learn GIS the semantic way is an open path for self-study, with no earlier GIS experience needed. Course paths follow the courses taught on site.
2. Finding data the semantic way
For anyone looking for the data that can answer a spatial question.
A data catalogue lists datasets by theme. SemanticGIS starts from the question instead. SPHERE organises the world in thematic spheres (Atmosphere, Biosphere, Hydrosphere, Geosphere and Anthroposphere) plus a Reference Framework. Leaves are the questions you can ask of the data, such as “Where are protected habitats?”, and each leaf links to the datasets that realise it. The leaves form a network rather than a tree: a leaf belongs wherever it is relevant.

































Start hereWhen you know…SPHEREthe question you want to askClassical Classificationsa theme from INSPIRE, ISO 19115 or UN-GGIM, and want to see where it lands in SPHEREReference Frameworkwhat the data must be located by: coordinate systems, administrative and statistical units, addressesBasemapsyou need a backdrop: topographic maps, orthophotos, historical maps or terrainData Portalsthe source, and want to know how to get data out of itAll entrances to the datathe register, the publisher or the collection method
In QGIS: the SemanticGIS plugin gives the same network as a panel in QGIS, and adds a service as a layer with one double-click.
